tutorials.title: Python HOME
tutorials.intro: Welcome to the Python tutorial. This page is the starting point for learning Python from the very beginning, one small topic at a time.

blocks.text: What you will learn here

This tutorial takes you from your first line of Python to real programs. You will learn variables, numbers, text, lists, dictionaries, conditions, and loops. Each topic is short, with examples you can run and small tasks you can try yourself.

items: Start with the basics: printing text, variables, and data types.
Learn to work with strings, lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries.
Make decisions with if statements and repeat work with loops.
Practise every topic with short exercises and code challenges.

blocks.text: How to use this tutorial

Follow the topics in order using the sidebar. Read the short explanation, run the example code, and then try the practice tasks at the end of each page. Typing the code yourself teaches far more than only reading it.

blocks.title: Your first taste of Python
blocks.code:
print("Hello, World!")
print(2 + 3)

blocks.text: The two lines above are a complete Python program. The first line prints a greeting, and the second line adds two numbers and prints the answer. You do not need to install anything special to try Python: the editor on this site can run the examples.

blocks.title: Python reads like plain English
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
print("Hello,", name)

blocks.text: You do not need any earlier programming experience. Every topic starts from zero and builds on the ones before it.
Keep a folder of your own practice files as you go. When you finish a topic, save one small program that uses what you just learned.

practice: Run the two example programs above and check that your output matches.
Change the greeting to print your own name.
Use print to work out 7 times 8 and 100 minus 37.
summary: This tutorial teaches Python from the very beginning, one topic at a time.
Follow the sidebar in order, run the examples, and try the practice tasks.
print shows text and numbers on the screen.
Typing the code yourself is the fastest way to learn.

tutorials.title: Python Intro
tutorials.intro: Python is a programming language that is easy to read and powerful enough for real work. This page explains what Python is and where it is used.

blocks.text: What is Python?

Python is a programming language created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. It is designed to be easy to read, so its code looks close to plain English. Python is free to use, and it runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux.
What can you build with Python?
Python is used for websites, data analysis, automation, games, and artificial intelligence. Large companies use Python in production every day, and it is the most common language in data science.

items: Web development: sites and web apps with frameworks like Django and Flask.
Data science: analysing numbers and drawing charts with pandas and matplotlib.
Artificial intelligence: building models with libraries like TensorFlow and PyTorch.
Automation: renaming files, sending emails, and doing repetitive jobs automatically.

blocks.title: Python is short and clear
blocks.code:
numbers = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
print(sum(numbers))
print(max(numbers))
print(sorted(numbers))

blocks.text: Why Python is a good first language

In some languages, adding up a list of numbers takes many lines of code. In Python, one built-in function does it. Python comes with many ready-made tools, so you spend your time solving the problem instead of writing the same basic steps again and again.

blocks.title: Borrowing the math library
blocks.code:
import math
print(math.sqrt(144))
print(math.pi)

blocks.text: A library is a collection of ready-made code written by other programmers. Importing a library is like borrowing a toolbox instead of building every tool from scratch.

practice: Make a list of your five favourite numbers and print its sum and its largest value.
Import the math module and print the square root of 81.
Write one sentence about what you would like to build with Python.
summary: Python is a free, easy-to-read programming language first released in 1991.
It is used for websites, data science, AI, automation, and games.
Built-in functions like sum and max do common jobs in one line.
Libraries give you ready-made tools you can import and reuse.

tutorials.title: Python Get Started
tutorials.intro: This page shows you how to get Python running and how to write and run your first program. You only need a computer and a few minutes.

blocks.text: Installing Python

Many computers already have Python installed. To check, open a terminal and type python3 --version. If you see a version number like Python 3.12.3, Python is ready. If not, download it from python.org and run the installer. During installation on Windows, tick the box that says Add Python to PATH.
Running Python line by line
Type python3 in the terminal to open the interactive prompt. You can type one line at a time and see the answer at once. Type exit() to leave. This is handy for quick tests.

blocks.title: Trying lines in the prompt
blocks.code:
print("Hello, World!")
print(2 + 3)

blocks.text: Running a Python file

Real programs live in files ending in .py. Write your code in a file called hello.py, then run it from the terminal with python3 hello.py. Python reads the file from top to bottom and runs each line in order.

blocks.title: hello.py
blocks.code:
print("Hello, everyone!")
print("My name is Ada.")
print("I am learning Python.")
blocks.output:
Hello, everyone!
My name is Ada.
I am learning Python.

blocks.text: On some computers the command is python instead of python3. Both run the same language, so use whichever one prints a version number on your machine.
Save practice programs with clear names like greeting.py or calculator.py. A good name saves you from opening every file to find one.

practice: Check which Python version is installed on your computer.
Create a file called aboutme.py that prints your name and your city, then run it.
Change one line in your file, save it, and run it again to see the new output.
summary: Check Python with python3 --version, or install it from python.org.
Type python3 to test single lines in the interactive prompt.
Save programs in .py files and run them with python3 file.py.
print can show several values at once, separated by spaces.

tutorials.title: Syntax
tutorials.intro: Syntax is the set of rules for writing correct Python code. This page covers the most important rules: indentation, line endings, and comments.

blocks.text: Python runs top to bottom
Python reads your file from the first line to the last line, and runs each line in order. If a line has an error, the lines after it do not run, so always fix the first error shown.

blocks.title: Lines run in order
blocks.code:
print("First")
print("Second")
print("Third")

blocks.text: Indentation groups lines together

Indentation is not decoration in Python. The lines under an if statement or a loop must be indented by the same amount, usually four spaces. A line with the wrong indentation either fails or belongs to the wrong block.

blocks.title: Indented lines belong to the if
blocks.code:
age = 18
if age >= 18:
    print("You can vote")
    print("Welcome")

blocks.text: No semicolons needed

Unlike some languages, Python does not need a semicolon at the end of each line. One statement per line is the normal style. You can put two short statements on one line with a semicolon, but it is rarely a good idea because it is harder to read.

blocks.title: One statement per line
blocks.code:
x = 5
y = 10
print(x + y)

blocks.text: Python is case sensitive, so Print and print are different names. The function is print with a small p, and writing Print gives a NameError.

practice: Write three print lines and run them, then swap two lines and run again.
Write an if statement with two indented print lines inside it.
Deliberately remove the indentation from one line and read the error Python gives you.
summary: Python runs code from top to bottom, one line at a time.
Indentation groups lines into blocks, usually four spaces per level.
Statements do not need semicolons at the end.
Python is case sensitive: print and Print are different names.

tutorials.title: Statements
tutorials.intro: A statement is one instruction that Python carries out. This page explains the kinds of statements you will write and how they fit together in a program.

blocks.text: What is a statement?

A statement is a single instruction, like assigning a value to a variable or printing a result. A program is a list of statements that run in order. Each statement does one small job, and together they do something useful.

blocks.title: Three statements, one program
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 17
print(name, "is", age, "years old")

blocks.text: Simple and compound statements

A simple statement fits on one line, such as an assignment or a print. A compound statement, such as if or for, has a header line ending in a colon and then an indented block of statements underneath it. The block runs only when the header says so.

blocks.title: A compound statement with a block
blocks.code:
score = 85
if score >= 50:
    print("Pass")
    print("Well done")

blocks.text: Long statements over several lines
A statement can be split over several lines if it sits inside brackets. This is common for long lists or function calls. Python knows the statement is not finished until the brackets close.

blocks.title: One statement across two lines
blocks.code:
total = (10 + 20
         + 30)
print(total)

blocks.text: An empty line between statements is fine and makes code easier to read. Python ignores blank lines.

practice: Write a program with five statements: two assignments, two prints, and one calculation.
Write an if statement with three indented lines inside it.
Split a long addition over two lines inside brackets and print the result.
summary: A statement is one instruction, and a program is a list of statements.
Simple statements fit on one line; compound statements have an indented block.
A statement inside brackets can span several lines.
Blank lines are ignored and help make code readable.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about Python syntax and statements. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that stores your name, your age, and your favourite number in three variables. Then print three lines: a greeting with your name, a line saying your age next year, and a line showing your favourite number doubled. Use one statement per line, and use a compound if statement to print a bonus line when your age is 18 or more.
Hints

items: Assign values with the equals sign, like name = "Ada".
Age next year is age + 1, and doubling a number is number * 2.
An if statement needs a colon at the end of its first line and an indented block under it.
print can show several values at once, separated by commas.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution. The values are the sample values used for the output below; your own program will print your own name, age, and number.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 20
favourite = 7
print("Hello,", name)
print("Next year you will be", age + 1)
print("Your favourite number doubled is", favourite * 2)
if age >= 18:
    print("You are an adult")
blocks.output:
Hello, Ada
Next year you will be 21
Your favourite number doubled is 14
You are an adult

blocks.text: Notice how each statement does one job: three assignments, three prints, and one if block. If your program prints the same four lines with your own values, you have solved the challenge.

blocks.title: Check: the same program with different values
blocks.code:
name = "Ravi"
age = 15
favourite = 3
print("Hello,", name)
print("Next year you will be", age + 1)
print("Your favourite number doubled is", favourite * 2)
if age >= 18:
    print("You are an adult")
blocks.output:
Hello, Ravi
Next year you will be 16
Your favourite number doubled is 6

blocks.text: In the second run the bonus line does not print, because 15 is less than 18. That is the if statement working correctly, not a mistake.

practice: Solve the challenge with your own name, age, and favourite number.
Add a fourth variable for your city and print a line about it.
Change the if condition so the bonus line prints when your age is under 18 instead.
summary: A program is built from simple statements that run in order.
Assignments store values, and print shows results.
An if statement runs its indented block only when its condition is true.
Test your program with different values to check every branch.

tutorials.title: Print Text
tutorials.intro: The print function is how a Python program shows text on the screen. This page covers printing text, joining words, and controlling how print ends a line.

blocks.text: Printing text
The print function shows whatever you put inside its brackets. To print text, put it inside quotes. Single quotes and double quotes work the same way, so pick one style and use it most of the time.

blocks.title: Printing lines of text
blocks.code:
print("Hello, World!")
print('Python is fun')
print("I am learning to code")
blocks.output:
Hello, World!
Python is fun
I am learning to code

blocks.text: Printing several values at once
When you pass several values separated by commas, print puts a space between them. You can mix text and numbers in the same line this way, without converting anything yourself.

blocks.title: Several values in one print
blocks.code:
print("My age is", 17)
print("Python", "is", "fun")
print("2 + 3 =", 2 + 3)
blocks.output:
My age is 17
Python is fun
2 + 3 = 5

blocks.text: Changing the separator and the ending

Print has two useful settings. The sep setting controls what goes between the values, and the end setting controls what comes after the last value. By default, sep is a space and end is a new line. Changing end to a space keeps the next print on the same line.

blocks.title: sep and end in action
blocks.code:
print(1, 2, 3, sep="-")
print("Hello", end=" ")
print("World")

blocks.text: Python 3 needs parentheses around print. Writing print "Hello" without them is old Python 2 style and gives a syntax error in Python 3.

practice: Print your name, your city, and your favourite food on three separate lines.
Print one line that mixes text and a number, like My age is 17.
Use sep to print the numbers 1, 2, and 3 joined with a slash, like 1/2/3.
summary: print shows text or numbers on the screen.
Text goes inside single or double quotes.
Several values in one print are joined with a space by default.
sep changes the joiner and end changes what comes after the line.

tutorials.title: Print Numbers
tutorials.intro: Print can show numbers, answers to calculations, and numbers stored in variables. This page shows how Python prints numbers and how to control their format.

blocks.text: Printing numbers directly

You can print a number on its own, or print the result of a calculation. Python works out the calculation first and then prints the answer. Whole numbers print as they are, and division always gives a decimal result.

blocks.title: Numbers and calculations
blocks.code:
print(42)
print(2 + 3)
print(10 - 4)
print(3 * 4)
print(7 / 2)

blocks.text: Printing numbers from variables

When a number is stored in a variable, printing the variable shows its value. If you change the variable and print it again, the new value is shown. This is how programs show results that change while they run.

blocks.title: Variables and their values
blocks.code:
price = 199
quantity = 3
print(price)
print(price * quantity)
print("Total:", price * quantity)

blocks.text: Controlling decimal places

Some calculations give long decimals. The round function limits a number to a chosen number of decimal places, and an f-string can format a number while it is printed. Formatting only changes the printed text, not the stored value.

blocks.title: Rounding and formatting numbers
blocks.code:
print(10 / 3)
print(round(10 / 3, 2))
print(f"Pi is about {3.14159:.2f}")

blocks.text: Division with a single slash always gives a float, even when the answer is whole. 8 / 2 prints 4.0, not 4. Use double slash for whole-number division.

practice: Print the answers to 7 times 8, 100 minus 37, and 25 divided by 5.
Store a price and a quantity in variables, then print their total.
Print 10 divided by 3 rounded to two decimal places.
summary: print shows numbers and the answers to calculations.
Division with a single slash always gives a decimal result.
Printing a variable shows its current value.
round and f-strings control how many decimal places are shown.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about printing text and numbers. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that prints a simple receipt. Store the name of an item, its price, and how many were bought. Then print three lines: the item name, the quantity and price, and the total cost. Use sep to print the date as 16-11-2026 on one line, and use end to print two words on the same line at the end.
Hints

items: The total cost is price times quantity.
print with commas puts a space between values.
sep changes what goes between the values, for example sep="-".
end=" " keeps the next print on the same line.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution, using the sample values shown in the output.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
item = "Notebook"
price = 45
quantity = 4
print("Item:", item)
print("Quantity:", quantity, "Price:", price)
print("Total:", price * quantity)
print(16, 11, 2026, sep="-")
print("Thank", end=" ")
print("you!")
blocks.output:
Item: Notebook
Quantity: 4 Price: 45
Total: 180
16-11-2026
Thank you!

blocks.text: The receipt prints five lines. The date uses sep to join the day, month, and year with dashes, and the last two words join into one line because end was set to a space.

blocks.title: Check: formatting a decimal total
blocks.code:
price = 19.99
quantity = 3
print("Total:", round(price * quantity, 2))

blocks.text: When money is involved, always round the total to two decimal places, or the printed total can show a long string of decimal digits.

practice: Solve the challenge with your own item, price, and quantity.
Add a line that prints the price of one item rounded to two decimal places.
Print the date 1-1-2027 using sep, then print Good bye on one line using end.
summary: print can mix text, numbers, and variables in one line.
sep controls what goes between values, and end controls what follows the line.
The total cost is price times quantity.
Round money totals to two decimal places before printing them.

tutorials.title: Comments
tutorials.intro: A comment is a note for humans that Python ignores completely. Comments explain why code is written the way it is, so you and others can understand it later.

blocks.text: Single-line comments
Anything after a hash sign on a line is a comment. Python ignores it and runs only the code before it. A comment can sit on its own line or at the end of a line of code.

blocks.title: Comments are ignored by Python
blocks.code:
# This program greets the user
print("Hello!")  # print a greeting
# print("This line never runs")

blocks.text: What makes a good comment

Good comments explain the reason behind a line, not just what it does. When you return to a program after a week, a good comment reminds you what you were thinking, and that saves you from reading every line again to work it out.

blocks.title: A comment that explains the why
blocks.code:
# Prices are in rupees, so divide by 83 to show dollars
price_in_dollars = 830 / 83
print(price_in_dollars)

blocks.text: Multi-line comments

Python has no special multi-line comment syntax. For a longer note, write several lines that each start with a hash sign. You can also use a triple-quoted string on its own as a note, but it is really a string that Python creates and throws away, so hash lines are the clearer choice.

blocks.title: Several hash lines for a long note
blocks.code:
# This program works out a bill.
# It adds the price of each item
# and then prints the total.
print(10 + 20 + 30)

blocks.text: You can use comments to turn off a line of code while testing. Put a hash in front of it, run the program, and remove the hash when you want the line back.

practice: Write a program with a comment at the top saying what it does, then print your name.
Add a comment at the end of a line of code explaining what that line does.
Comment out one print line, run the program, then remove the hash and run it again.
summary: A comment starts with a hash sign and is ignored by Python.
Good comments explain why code is written a certain way.
Use one hash line per line for longer notes.
Comments can temporarily switch off a line while you test.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about comments. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that works out the total cost of three items and prints it. Add a comment at the top saying what the program does, a comment next to each price explaining what the item is, and a comment above the total explaining how it is worked out. Then comment out the most expensive item, run the program, and check the new total.
Hints

items: Store each price in its own variable, like pen = 10.
A comment starts with a hash sign and can sit at the end of a line.
The total is the sum of the three prices.
Putting a hash in front of a line stops Python from running it.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution with the sample prices shown in the output.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
# This program works out the total cost of three items
pen = 10      # a blue pen
notebook = 45  # a ruled notebook
bag = 350     # a school bag
# Add the three prices together to get the total
total = pen + notebook + bag
print("Total:", total)

blocks.text: Each comment says something useful: what the program does, what each price is for, and how the total is worked out. Comments like these help a reader understand the program without guessing.

blocks.title: The same program with the bag commented out
blocks.code:
# This program works out the total cost of three items
pen = 10      # a blue pen
notebook = 45  # a ruled notebook
# bag = 350     # a school bag
# Add the three prices together to get the total
total = pen + notebook
print("Total:", total)

blocks.text: Commenting out the bag also meant removing it from the total, because the name bag no longer exists. A commented-out variable cannot be used anywhere else in the program.

practice: Solve the challenge with three items of your own.
Write a program with a three-line comment at the top explaining what it does.
Comment out a line in one of your earlier programs and check what changes.
summary: Comments explain a program to humans and are ignored by Python.
Put a useful comment at the top of a program and next to tricky lines.
A hash at the start of a line switches that line off.
A commented-out variable cannot be used anywhere else.

tutorials.title: Python Variables
tutorials.intro: A variable is a named box that stores a value so you can use it later. Almost every program you write will use variables.

blocks.text: What is a variable?

A variable is a name that stores a value. You create one with an equals sign, like age = 17. The name goes on the left and the value on the right. After that, writing age anywhere in the program means the value 17. If you assign a new value to the same name, the old value is replaced.

blocks.title: Creating and using variables
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 17
height = 5.6
is_student = True
print(name)
print(age)
print(height)
print(is_student)

blocks.text: Variables can change
A variable is not fixed. You can give it a new value at any time, and the next time you use it, you get the new value. This is how programs keep track of things that change, like a score or a total.

blocks.title: Changing a variable
blocks.code:
score = 0
print(score)
score = 10
print(score)
score = score + 5
print(score)

blocks.text: Variables in calculations
You can use variables in calculations just like numbers. Python looks up each value, works out the answer, and you can store the answer in a new variable or print it directly.

blocks.title: Maths with variables
blocks.code:
length = 5
width = 4
area = length * width
print("Area:", area)

blocks.text: Python figures out the type of a value from the value itself, so you never declare a type when you create a variable. The same name can even hold a different type later, although good programs usually keep one name for one kind of value.

practice: Create variables for your name, your age, your height, and whether you like Python, then print all four.
Create a variable called score, set it to 0, add 10 to it, and print it.
Store the length and width of a rectangle and print its area.
summary: A variable is a name that stores a value for later use.
Create one with an equals sign: name = "Ada".
Assigning a new value replaces the old one.
Variables can be used in calculations like numbers.

tutorials.title: Variable Names
tutorials.intro: Variable names must follow a few rules, and good names make your code easy to read. This page covers the rules and the naming style most Python programmers use.

blocks.text: The rules for names

A variable name must start with a letter or an underscore, and it can only contain letters, digits, and underscores. It cannot contain spaces, and it cannot start with a digit. It also cannot be a Python keyword like if, for, or class.

blocks.title: Valid names
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
age2 = 17
_my_score = 90
total_price = 250
print(name, age2, _my_score, total_price)

blocks.text: Names that do not work

A name with a space in it, like my age, is a syntax error, because Python reads it as two separate names. A name that starts with a digit, like 2age, is also an error. A name that is a keyword, like class, cannot be used as a variable either.

blocks.title: Case matters
blocks.code:
age = 17
Age = 18
print(age)
print(Age)

blocks.text: Good naming style

Python programmers use lowercase letters with underscores between words, a style called snake_case. Names should say what the value is, such as total_price instead of tp, so your code reads like a sentence.

items: Use short but clear names: age, price, first_name.
Use snake_case: total_price, not totalPrice or TotalPrice.
Avoid single letters except for very short loops, like i in a loop.
Do not use Python keywords as names: if, for, while, class, import.

blocks.text: Python is case sensitive, so age and Age are two different variables. Pick one style, usually lowercase with underscores, and use it everywhere.

practice: Create three variables with good snake_case names and print them.
Try using a name with a space in it and read the error Python gives you.
Rename a variable called x in one of your programs to a clear name like total_marks.
summary: Names must start with a letter or underscore and contain only letters, digits, and underscores.
Names cannot contain spaces or be Python keywords.
Python is case sensitive: age and Age are different variables.
Use lowercase snake_case names that say what the value is.

tutorials.title: Assign Multiple Values
tutorials.intro: Python lets you assign values to several variables in one line. This page shows the shortcuts for setting up many variables at once.

blocks.text: Several variables in one line

You can assign a different value to each of several variables in a single line. Write the names on the left separated by commas, and the values on the right separated by commas. Python matches them in order: the first name gets the first value, and so on.

blocks.title: One line, three variables
blocks.code:
name, age, city = "Ada", 17, "Mumbai"
print(name)
print(age)
print(city)

blocks.text: The same value for several variables
You can also give the same value to several variables at once by chaining the assignments with equals signs. This is handy when several counters or flags all start at the same value.

blocks.title: One value, three names
blocks.code:
x = y = z = 0
print(x, y, z)
x = 5
print(x, y, z)

blocks.text: Swapping two variables is a famous use of this trick. Writing a, b = b, a swaps their values in one line, with no temporary variable needed.

blocks.title: Swapping two values
blocks.code:
a = 10
b = 20
a, b = b, a
print(a)
print(b)

blocks.text: For numbers and strings, chained assignment like x = y = z = 0 gives each name its own copy, so changing one does not change the others. For lists it is different, because all three names would point to the same list.

practice: Assign your name, age, and city to three variables in one line and print them.
Set three counters to 0 in one line, then change one and print all three.
Swap the values of two variables in one line and print the result.
summary: Assign several variables in one line with commas on both sides.
Chained assignment gives the same value to several names at once.
A list or tuple can be unpacked into separate variables.
a, b = b, a swaps two values in one line.

tutorials.title: Output Variables
tutorials.intro: Once a value is stored in a variable, you often need to show it. This page covers the ways to print variables, alone and mixed with text and other values.

blocks.text: Printing a variable
Printing a variable shows its current value. If the value changes later, printing the variable again shows the new value. This is the simplest way to see what your program is doing while it runs.

blocks.title: Printing variables
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 17
print(name)
print(age)

blocks.text: Mixing text and variables
The print function can take several values separated by commas, and it puts a space between them. This lets you build a sentence from text and variables without converting anything yourself.

blocks.title: Text and variables together
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 17
print("My name is", name)
print("I am", age, "years old")
blocks.output:
My name is Ada
I am 17 years old

blocks.text: The clearest way: f-strings
An f-string places variables directly inside a string, inside curly braces. It is shorter and easier to read than joining pieces with plus, and it handles numbers automatically.

blocks.title: Building sentences with f-strings
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 17
print(f"My name is {name} and I am {age} years old.")
blocks.output: My name is Ada and I am 17 years old.

blocks.text: print with commas adds spaces between values automatically. With plus, you control every space yourself, which is why f-strings are usually the easiest choice.

practice: Store your name and age in variables and print a sentence about yourself three ways: with commas, with plus, and with an f-string.
Print two variables on one line separated by a dash using sep.
Store a price in a variable and print it inside a sentence like The price is 199 rupees.
summary: print(variable) shows the current value of a variable.
print with commas joins text and values with spaces.
Plus joins strings, but numbers must be converted with str first.
f-strings place variables inside curly braces and are the clearest way to build sentences.

tutorials.title: Global Variables
tutorials.intro: A variable created outside a function is called a global variable. This page explains how global and local variables differ, and how to change a global variable from inside a function.

blocks.text: What is a global variable?

A variable created at the top level of a file, outside any function, is a global variable. Every function in the file can read it. A variable created inside a function is a local variable, and it only exists while that function is running.

blocks.title: A global variable read inside a function
blocks.code:
city = "Mumbai"

def show_city():
    print("City:", city)

show_city()
print(city)

blocks.text: Local variables stay inside their function
A local variable is created when the function runs and disappears when the function ends. Trying to use it outside the function gives a NameError, because the name does not exist there.

blocks.title: A local variable cannot be used outside
blocks.code:
def make_message():
    text = "Hello from inside"
    print(text)

make_message()

blocks.text: Changing a global variable inside a function

Reading a global variable inside a function is easy, but changing it needs the global keyword. Without it, Python treats the assignment as creating a new local variable with the same name, and the global value stays unchanged.

blocks.title: The global keyword
blocks.code:
score = 0

def add_points(points):
    global score
    score = score + points

add_points(10)
add_points(5)
print(score)

blocks.text: Use global variables sparingly. A function that reads and changes globals is harder to test and reuse than one that takes values as parameters and returns a result.

practice: Create a global variable and read it inside a function, then print it outside.
Write a function that changes a global counter using the global keyword.
Write a function with a local variable and try to print that variable outside the function to see the error.
summary: A global variable is created outside a function and can be read anywhere.
A local variable exists only while its function is running.
Use the global keyword to change a global variable from inside a function.
Without global, an assignment inside a function creates a local variable instead.

tutorials.title: Variable Exercises
tutorials.intro: A set of practice exercises on variables. Try each one yourself, then check your answer against the solution below it.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: Your details
Create variables for your name, your age, and your city. Then print a sentence that uses all three, like My name is Ada, I am 17 years old, and I live in Mumbai.

blocks.title: Exercise 1: answer
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 17
city = "Mumbai"
print(f"My name is {name}, I am {age} years old, and I live in {city}.")
blocks.output: My name is Ada, I am 17 years old, and I live in Mumbai.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: Swap two numbers
Store 10 in a and 20 in b. Then swap their values so that a becomes 20 and b becomes 10, using only one line for the swap. Print both values before and after the swap.

blocks.title: Exercise 2: answer
blocks.code:
a = 10
b = 20
print("Before:", a, b)
a, b = b, a
print("After:", a, b)

blocks.text: Exercise 3: A simple bill
A pen costs 10 rupees and a notebook costs 45 rupees. Store the two prices and the quantities bought (3 pens and 2 notebooks) in variables. Then work out and print the total cost.

blocks.title: Exercise 3: answer
blocks.code:
pen_price = 10
notebook_price = 45
pens = 3
notebooks = 2
total = pen_price * pens + notebook_price * notebooks
print("Total:", total)

blocks.text: If an exercise feels hard, break it into smaller steps. Write one variable, print it, and check it before moving on to the next step.

practice: Do Exercise 1 with your own name, age, and city.
Write a program that stores the length and width of a room and prints its area.
Store your marks in three subjects and print the total and the average.
summary: Variables store values under names you choose.
f-strings build sentences from text and variables.
a, b = b, a swaps two values in one line.
Break a big exercise into small steps and check each one.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about variables. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program for a small shop. Store the name of a product, its price, and how many are in stock. Then sell 3 items: reduce the stock by 3 and add the money earned to a total_sales variable that starts at 0. Print the product name, the items left in stock, and the total money earned.
Hints

items: Start total_sales at 0 before the sale.
Selling 3 items means stock = stock - 3.
Money earned is price times 3.
Use an f-string to print a clear sentence for each result.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution, using the sample values shown in the output.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
product = "Notebook"
price = 45
stock = 10
total_sales = 0
stock = stock - 3
total_sales = total_sales + price * 3
print(f"Product: {product}")
print(f"Items left in stock: {stock}")
print(f"Total money earned: {total_sales}")
blocks.output:
Product: Notebook
Items left in stock: 7
Total money earned: 135

blocks.text: The stock drops from 10 to 7, and the money earned is 45 times 3, which is 135. The variables stock and total_sales change during the program, which is exactly what variables are for.

blocks.title: Check: selling 3 more items
blocks.code:
product = "Notebook"
price = 45
stock = 7
total_sales = 135
stock = stock - 3
total_sales = total_sales + price * 3
print(f"Items left in stock: {stock}")
print(f"Total money earned: {total_sales}")
blocks.output:
Items left in stock: 4
Total money earned: 270

blocks.text: When a value changes over time, like stock or total sales, print it after each change while you are learning, so you can see the change happen.

practice: Solve the challenge with your own product, price, and stock.
Sell 5 more items in the same program and print the new stock and total.
Add a variable for the shop name and print it at the top of the output.
summary: Variables hold values that change as the program runs.
Update a variable by assigning a new value based on the old one.
Money earned is price times the number of items sold.
Print values after each change to check your program step by step.

tutorials.title: Data Types
tutorials.intro: Every value in Python has a type, which tells Python what you can do with it. This page introduces the main types and how to check them.

blocks.text: What is a data type?

A data type is the kind of a value. Numbers, text, and true-or-false values are different types, and Python treats them differently. You cannot add a number to text, but you can add two numbers. The type decides which operations make sense.

blocks.title: Checking types with type()
blocks.code:
print(type(10))
print(type(3.5))
print(type("Ada"))
print(type(True))

blocks.text: The main types

items: int is a whole number, like 17 or -4.
float is a number with a decimal point, like 5.6 or 3.14.
str is text inside quotes, like "Ada" or "Hello".
bool is either True or False, used for yes-or-no facts.
list is an ordered collection of values, like [1, 2, 3].
tuple is an ordered collection that cannot change, like (1, 2).
set is an unordered collection of unique values, like {1, 2}.
dict is a collection of key and value pairs, like {"name": "Ada"}.

blocks.text: Python finds the type for you

Python figures out the type from the value itself, so you never declare a type when you create a variable. The same name can even hold a different type later, although good programs usually keep one name for one kind of value.

blocks.title: Types of collections
blocks.code:
print(type([1, 2, 3]))
print(type((1, 2)))
print(type({1, 2}))
print(type({"name": "Ada"}))

blocks.text: The type of a value decides what you can do with it. Adding two ints gives a number, adding two strings joins them, but adding an int and a string gives a TypeError.

practice: Use type() to print the type of 100, 9.99, "hello", and False.
Create one variable of each main type and print its type.
Try adding a number and a string and read the error message.
summary: Every value has a type, and the type decides what you can do with it.
The main types are int, float, str, bool, list, tuple, set, and dict.
type() shows the type of any value.
Python finds the type from the value, so you never declare it.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about data types. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that creates one variable of each type: an int, a float, a str, a bool, a list, and a dict. Print each variable together with its type, using type(). Then change the int variable to hold a string and print its type again, to prove that a variable can change type.
Hints

items: type(value) gives the type, and print can show a value and its type together.
A list uses square brackets and a dict uses curly brackets with key and value pairs.
Assigning a new value to a name replaces the old value and its type.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution, using the sample values shown in the output.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
age = 17
height = 5.6
name = "Ada"
is_student = True
scores = [85, 90, 78]
student = {"name": "Ada", "age": 17}
print(age, type(age))
print(height, type(height))
print(name, type(name))
print(is_student, type(is_student))
print(scores, type(scores))
print(student, type(student))

blocks.text: A variable in Python is only a name pointing at a value. When you assign a new value of a different type, the name simply points at the new value.

blocks.title: A variable can change its type
blocks.code:
age = 17
print(age, type(age))
age = "seventeen"
print(age, type(age))

blocks.text: Changing a variable's type is allowed, but it is usually a bad habit in real programs, because the reader expects one name to hold one kind of value.

practice: Solve the challenge with your own values for each type.
Create a tuple and a set, then print each with its type.
Change a string variable to hold a number and print its type before and after.
summary: type() shows the type of any value.
The main types are int, float, str, bool, list, tuple, set, and dict.
A variable can hold a different type after a new assignment.
In real programs, keep one name for one kind of value.

tutorials.title: Numbers
tutorials.intro: Python has three kinds of numbers: integers, floats, and complex numbers. This page covers the first two, which you will use every day, and the arithmetic you can do with them.

blocks.text: Integers and floats

An int is a whole number, like 17 or -4, with no limit on its size. A float is a number with a decimal point, like 5.6 or 3.14. Any number with a decimal point in it is a float, even if the decimal part is zero, so 7.0 is a float and 7 is an int.

blocks.title: Ints and floats
blocks.code:
print(type(17))
print(type(5.6))
print(type(7.0))
print(2 + 3)
print(2.5 + 1.5)

blocks.text: Arithmetic with numbers

Python supports the usual arithmetic: plus, minus, multiply, divide, and power. Division with a single slash always gives a float. Double slash gives whole-number division, and the percent sign gives the remainder.

blocks.title: The arithmetic operators
blocks.code:
print(10 + 3)
print(10 - 3)
print(10 * 3)
print(10 / 3)
print(10 // 3)
print(10 % 3)
print(2 ** 3)

blocks.text: Floats are not always exact

Computers store decimal numbers in binary, so some decimals cannot be stored exactly. Adding 0.1 and 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. For money, round the result to two decimal places, or work in the smallest unit, like paise instead of rupees.

blocks.title: A float surprise, and the fix
blocks.code:
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 2))

blocks.text: Complex numbers, like 3 + 4j, are the third kind of number in Python. They are used in maths and engineering, but you will rarely need them in everyday programs.

practice: Print the answers to 15 divided by 4 using both / and //, and the remainder using %.
Work out 2 to the power of 10 with ** and print the answer.
Print 0.1 + 0.2, then print it rounded to one decimal place.
summary: int is a whole number and float is a number with a decimal point.
Division with / always gives a float; // gives whole-number division.
% gives the remainder and ** gives the power.
Floats can be slightly inexact, so round money to two decimals.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about numbers. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that takes a total bill of 1000 rupees and splits it equally between 3 friends. Print how much each friend pays as a whole number of rupees using whole-number division, how many rupees are left over, and the exact share rounded to two decimal places. Then print the square of 12.
Hints

items: // gives whole-number division and % gives the remainder.
/ gives the exact division as a float.
round(value, 2) limits a number to two decimal places.
** is the power operator, so 12 ** 2 is 12 squared.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution, using the sample values shown in the output.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
bill = 1000
friends = 3
print("Each friend pays:", bill // friends)
print("Left over:", bill % friends)
print("Exact share:", round(bill / friends, 2))
print("Square of 12:", 12 ** 2)
blocks.output:
Each friend pays: 333
Left over: 1
Exact share: 333.33
Square of 12: 144

blocks.text: The bill does not split evenly: 3 times 333 is 999, so 1 rupee is left over. The exact share is 333.33 rupees when rounded to two decimal places.

blocks.title: Check: a bill that splits evenly
blocks.code:
bill = 900
friends = 3
print("Each friend pays:", bill // friends)
print("Left over:", bill % friends)
print("Exact share:", round(bill / friends, 2))
blocks.output:
Each friend pays: 300
Left over: 0
Exact share: 300.0

blocks.text: When you split money, decide what happens to the leftover rupees first. In real programs, one person often pays the extra rupee.

practice: Solve the challenge with a bill of 500 rupees split between 4 friends.
Print the cube of 5 and the remainder of 100 divided by 7.
Work out the average of 85, 90, and 78 and print it rounded to one decimal place.
summary: // gives the whole-number share and % gives the leftover.
/ gives the exact share as a float.
round(value, 2) shows money to two decimal places.
** raises a number to a power.

tutorials.title: Casting
tutorials.intro: Casting means converting a value from one type to another. You will learn the int, float, str, and bool functions and when each one is useful.

blocks.text: What is casting?

Casting means changing a value from one type to another. The text "42" and the number 42 look similar, but Python treats them very differently. You cannot add 8 to the text "42", but after converting it to a number with int, the addition works and gives 50.

blocks.title: Converting between types
blocks.code:
print(int("42") + 8)
print(float("3.5") + 1)
print(str(100) + " points")
print(int(3.9))

blocks.text: What each conversion does

Converting a decimal number to int cuts off the part after the decimal point. It does not round the number. So int(3.9) gives 3, not 4. Converting a whole number to float adds .0, so float(7) gives 7.0. Converting a number to str makes text, which you can join with other text using plus.

blocks.title: More conversions, including bool
blocks.code:
print(float(7))
print(int(7.9))
print(bool(1))
print(bool(0))
print(bool(""))

blocks.text: The bool function follows a simple rule. Zero, empty text, and empty lists are False, and almost everything else is True. This rule is handy when you test whether a user typed anything at all, or whether a number is zero.

blocks.title: Casting input to a number
blocks.code:
age_text = "17"
age = int(age_text)
print("Next year you will be", age + 1)

blocks.text: Not every conversion works. int("3.5") fails with an error, because the text 3.5 is not a whole number. Convert it to float first, then to int, like int(float("3.5")), which gives 3.
The most common use of casting is with input. Since input always returns text, wrap it in int or float right away when you need a number.

practice: Convert the string "25" to a number, add 5 to it, and print the answer.
Convert 9.99 to an int and print the result, then explain why it is 9 and not 10.
Try int("hello") and read the error message, then explain in your own words why it failed.
summary: Casting converts a value from one type to another.
int makes whole numbers, float makes decimal numbers, and str makes text.
Converting a float to int cuts off the decimal part without rounding.
Zero and empty text become False, and almost everything else becomes True.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about casting. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that starts with the text values "25" and "3.5". Convert the first one to an int and the second one to a float, add them together, and print the result. Then convert the sum to a string and print a sentence like The total is 28.5. Finally, print what happens when you convert the float 28.5 to an int.
Hints

items: int("25") gives the number 25 and float("3.5") gives 3.5.
Adding an int and a float gives a float.
str(number) turns a number into text you can join with plus.
int(28.5) cuts off the decimal part and gives 28.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution, using the sample values shown in the output.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
first = int("25")
second = float("3.5")
total = first + second
print(total)
print("The total is " + str(total))
print(int(total))

blocks.text: The sum is 28.5, a float, because one of the two numbers was a float. Converting 28.5 to an int cuts off the .5 and leaves 28, without rounding up.

blocks.title: Check: the same idea with different values
blocks.code:
first = int("100")
second = float("0.99")
total = first + second
print(total)
print("The total is " + str(total))
print(int(total))

blocks.text: If the text cannot become a number, like int("hello"), Python stops with a ValueError. In real programs, that conversion should sit inside a try block.

practice: Solve the challenge with the text values "40" and "2.5".
Convert the string "99" to a float and print its type.
Convert the float 7.9 to an int and to a string, and print both results.
summary: int and float turn text into numbers; str turns numbers into text.
Adding an int and a float gives a float.
int cuts off the decimal part without rounding.
A conversion that cannot work raises a ValueError.

tutorials.title: Python Strings
tutorials.intro: A string is text in Python. This page explains how to create strings, measure them, join them, and pick out single characters.

blocks.text: What is a string?

A string is a sequence of characters, such as letters, digits, spaces, and symbols. You create a string by writing text inside single or double quotes. Both kinds of quotes work the same way, so pick one style and use it most of the time. An empty pair of quotes makes an empty string with no characters at all.

blocks.title: Length and joining
blocks.code:
name = "Python"
print(len(name))
print(name + " is fun")
print("Hello, " + "World!")

blocks.text: Picking out single characters

Every character in a string has a position number, called an index. Counting starts at zero, so the first character is at index 0 and the second is at index 1. You can also count from the end with negative numbers, so index -1 is the last character and index -2 is the second last.

blocks.title: Indexing a string
blocks.code:
name = "Python"
print(name[0])
print(name[1])
print(name[-1])
print(name[-2])

blocks.text: Repeating and searching

The star operator repeats a string, so repeating the text ha three times gives hahaha, which is useful for drawing lines or patterns. You can also test whether one string contains another with the in keyword, which gives True or False.

blocks.title: Repeating and searching
blocks.code:
print("ha" * 3)
print("a" in "banana")
print("z" in "banana")
print("Python" == "Python")

blocks.text: Strings are immutable, which means you cannot change one character in place. Writing name[0] = "J" gives an error. To change a string, build a new one from pieces instead.

practice: Store your name in a variable and print its length and its first and last letters.
Join your first and last name with a space and print the result.
Check whether the letter e appears in your favourite food, using the in keyword.
summary: A string is text inside single or double quotes.
len counts the characters in a string, including spaces.
Indexes start at 0, and negative indexes count from the end.
Plus joins strings, star repeats them, and in tests for a piece inside a string.

tutorials.title: Slicing Strings
tutorials.intro: Slicing cuts out part of a string. It is how you take the first word, the last letters, or a reversed copy of any text.

blocks.text: What is slicing?

Slicing takes a piece of a string using square brackets with a start and a stop, written as text[start:stop]. The slice starts at the start index and stops just before the stop index, so the character at the stop index is not included. This rule takes a little practice, but it makes slices easy to measure: the length of text[2:5] is always 3.

blocks.title: Basic slices
blocks.code:
text = "Python Programming"
print(text[0:6])
print(text[7:])
print(text[:6])
print(text[-11:])

blocks.text: Leaving out the start or the stop

You can leave out the start or the stop. Leaving out the start means from the beginning, and leaving out the stop means to the end. Leaving out both gives a copy of the whole string. These shortcuts keep slices short and readable.

blocks.title: Shortcuts for slices
blocks.code:
word = "Hello"
print(word[:3])
print(word[2:])
print(word[:])
print(word[-2:])

blocks.text: Steps and reversing

A slice can also take a third number, the step, written as text[start:stop:step]. A step of 2 takes every second character, and a step of -1 walks backwards through the string. The slice text[::-1] is a famous Python trick that reverses a whole string in one short expression.

blocks.title: Steps and a reversed string
blocks.code:
word = "Hello"
print(word[1:4])
print(word[::2])
print(word[::-1])
print(word[0] + word[-1])

blocks.text: Slicing never gives an error when the indexes are too big. text[0:100] on a short string simply gives the whole string, while text[100] on its own gives an IndexError.

practice: Take the string "Hello, World!" and slice out just the word "World".
Reverse your name with a slice and print the result.
Slice the first three and last three characters of "Programming" and print both pieces.
summary: A slice text[start:stop] starts at start and stops just before stop.
Leaving out start or stop means from the beginning or to the end.
A third number is the step, and [::-1] reverses a string.
Slicing past the end never errors; it just gives what is there.

tutorials.title: Modify Strings
tutorials.intro: Strings cannot be changed in place, but Python gives you many ways to build a new, changed string from an old one. This page covers the most useful ones.

blocks.text: Strings are immutable

A string in Python cannot be changed after it is created. Writing name[0] = "J" gives a TypeError. To change a string, you build a new string from pieces of the old one and store it in a variable, often the same variable.

blocks.title: Building a new string from pieces
blocks.code:
name = "Python"
name = "J" + name[1:]
print(name)
name = name.replace("J", "P")
print(name)

blocks.text: Changing case

The upper, lower, and title methods return a new string with the case changed. Upper makes every letter capital, lower makes every letter small, and title capitalises the first letter of every word. These are handy when user input arrives in mixed case and you need one clean form to compare or store.

blocks.title: Changing case
blocks.code:
text = "hello world"
print(text.upper())
print(text.title())
print("HELLO".lower())

blocks.text: Cleaning spaces and replacing text
The strip method removes spaces from both ends of a string, which is useful for cleaning up user input. The replace method swaps one piece of text for another, everywhere it appears.

blocks.title: Strip and replace
blocks.code:
text = "  hello world  "
print(text.strip())
print("hello".replace("l", "L"))
print("banana".replace("a", "o"))

blocks.text: String methods return a new string and never change the original, because strings are immutable. You must store the result, like name = name.strip(), or the cleaned text is lost.

practice: Take the string "  PYTHON is FUN  ", strip it, and print it in lowercase.
Replace every space in your name with a dash using replace, and print the result.
Change the first letter of "python" to a capital by building a new string from pieces.
summary: Strings are immutable: you cannot change one character in place.
Build a new string from pieces, or use a method that returns a new string.
upper, lower, and title change the case of a string.
strip removes spaces from the ends, and replace swaps one piece for another.

tutorials.title: Concatenate Strings
tutorials.intro: Concatenation means joining strings together into one longer string. This page shows the ways to join strings and which one to use when.

blocks.text: Joining with plus

The plus sign joins two strings, gluing the second string onto the end of the first. This is called concatenation. You can join as many strings as you like in one expression, but remember to add spaces yourself where you need them.

blocks.title: Joining strings with plus
blocks.code:
first = "Ada"
last = "Lovelace"
full = first + " " + last
print(full)
print("Hello, " + full + "!")

blocks.text: Joining a list with join

When you have a list of strings, the join method is the cleanest way to glue them together. You call it on the separator string, and pass the list. Join is faster than adding strings in a loop, and it puts the separator between every pair of items.

blocks.title: Joining a list of words
blocks.code:
words = ["Python", "is", "fun"]
print(" ".join(words))
print("-".join(["2026", "11", "16"]))
print(", ".join(["apple", "banana", "mango"]))
blocks.output:
Python is fun
2026-11-16
apple, banana, mango

blocks.text: Joining numbers and text

Plus can only join text with text. Trying to join a string and a number with plus gives a TypeError, so you must convert the number to text first with str. An f-string avoids this problem entirely, because it converts values for you.

blocks.title: Numbers need converting, or use an f-string
blocks.code:
age = 17
print("Age: " + str(age))
print(f"Age: {age}")
print("Score: " + str(95) + " out of 100")

blocks.text: For joining many strings in a loop, build a list and join it once at the end. Adding strings with plus inside a loop is slow, because each plus makes a whole new string.

practice: Join your first and last name with a space and print the result.
Join the list ["red", "green", "blue"] with a comma and a space.
Print a sentence with your age in it using an f-string and then using plus with str.
summary: Plus joins two strings; remember to add spaces yourself.
join glues a list of strings together with a separator.
Plus cannot join a string and a number; convert the number with str first.
f-strings are the clearest way to build sentences with values inside them.

tutorials.title: Format Strings
tutorials.intro: Formatting means putting values into a string in a controlled way. This page covers f-strings and the format method, including how to control numbers.

blocks.text: F-strings: the modern way

Put the letter f just before the opening quote of a string, and anything inside curly braces is evaluated and placed into the string. The variable is replaced by its value, so you no longer need to join pieces with plus signs or commas.

blocks.title: Your first f-string
blocks.code:
name = "Asha"
age = 20
print(f"My name is {name} and I am {age} years old.")
blocks.output: My name is Asha and I am 20 years old.

blocks.text: Calculations inside f-strings
The braces can hold more than a variable name. You can put any expression inside them: arithmetic, a method call, or a value formatted to a fixed number of decimal places.

blocks.title: Expressions and number formatting
blocks.code:
price = 199
quantity = 3
print(f"Total: Rs. {price * quantity}")
pi = 3.14159
print(f"Pi rounded: {pi:.2f}")

blocks.text: Formatting numbers
The format inside the braces controls how a number looks. A colon followed by .2f shows two decimal places, a comma adds thousands separators, and a percent sign shows the value as a percentage.
Inside an f-string you cannot use the same kind of quote as the one that opens the string. Use single quotes inside a double-quoted f-string, or the other way round.

practice: Create variables for your name, city, and age, then print one sentence about yourself with a single f-string.
Use an f-string to print the total price of 4 notebooks at Rs. 45 each, with the calculation inside the braces.
Format the number 1234.5678 to two decimal places inside an f-string.
summary: An f-string starts with f before the quote and evaluates expressions in curly braces.
Braces can hold variables, arithmetic, method calls, and conditions.
:.2f formats a number to two decimal places, and a comma adds thousands separators.
The format method does the same job with placeholders, but f-strings are clearer.

tutorials.title: Escape Characters
tutorials.intro: Some characters are hard to type inside a string. Escape characters let you put new lines, tabs, and quotes inside a string.

blocks.text: What is an escape character?

An escape sequence is a backslash followed by a letter, and Python turns it into a special character. A backslash tells Python that the next character is special, not ordinary text, so the string can hold characters that would otherwise end it or break it.

items: Backslash n makes a new line inside a string.
Backslash t makes a tab, a wider gap of spaces.
Backslash backslash prints one real backslash.
Backslash quote prints a quote mark inside a quoted string.

blocks.title: New line and tab
blocks.code:
print("Hello\nWorld")
print("Name:\tAda")

blocks.text: Quotes inside a string

A string in double quotes cannot contain a plain double quote, because Python would think the string ends there. A backslash before the quote solves it. The simpler trick is to wrap the string in the other kind of quote: use single quotes around text that contains double quotes, and double quotes around text that contains single quotes.

blocks.title: Quotes inside a string
blocks.code:
print('She said, "Hello!"')
print("It's a nice day")
print("She said, \"Hi\"")
blocks.output:
She said, "Hello!"
It's a nice day
She said, "Hi"

blocks.text: Backslashes and file paths

A Windows file path contains backslashes, and each one must be doubled in a normal string, or Python will read it as an escape sequence. A raw string, written with the letter r before the quote, treats backslashes as plain characters, which is much easier for paths.

blocks.title: Raw strings for paths
blocks.code:
print("C:\\Users\\Ada")
print(r"C:\Users\Ada")

practice: Print two lines of a poem using one print statement and a new line escape sequence.
Print the sentence: She said, "Python is fun!" using single quotes around the string.
Print a Windows-style path with a raw string, then print the same path with doubled backslashes.
summary: An escape sequence is a backslash followed by a letter.
Backslash n makes a new line and backslash t makes a tab.
Use the other kind of quote to avoid escaping quotes inside a string.
A raw string with r before the quote keeps backslashes as plain characters.

tutorials.title: String Methods
tutorials.intro: String methods are built-in tools that change, search, and split text. They are the fastest way to clean up real-world text.

blocks.text: What is a method?

A method is a function that belongs to a value. You call it by writing the value, a dot, and the method name, like text.upper(). String methods cover the everyday jobs of text: changing case, removing spaces, replacing words, and splitting sentences into lists.

blocks.title: Changing case and cleaning spaces
blocks.code:
text = "  hello world  "
print(text.strip())
print(text.strip().upper())
print("hello world".title())
print("hello".replace("l", "L"))
blocks.output:
hello world
HELLO WORLD
Hello World
heLLo

blocks.text: Searching inside a string

The count method tells you how many times a piece appears in a string. The find method tells you where a piece first appears, giving its index, or -1 when the piece is not there. The startswith and endswith methods answer yes-or-no questions about how a string begins or ends.

blocks.title: Counting, finding, and testing
blocks.code:
print("banana".count("a"))
print("hello".find("l"))
print("hello".find("z"))
print("Python".startswith("Py"))
print("Python".endswith("on"))

blocks.text: Splitting and joining

The split method breaks a string into a list of pieces at a separator you choose, such as a comma or a space. The join method does the opposite: it glues a list of strings together with a separator between them. Together they are the standard way to move between one long string and a list of words.

blocks.title: Split a string, join a list
blocks.code:
print("apple,banana,cherry".split(","))
print("hello world".split())
print("-".join(["2026", "11", "16"]))
print(" ".join(["Python", "is", "fun"]))

blocks.text: String methods return a new string and never change the original, because strings are immutable. You must store the result, like name = name.strip(), or the cleaned text is lost.

practice: Take the string "  PYTHON is FUN  ", strip it, and print it in lowercase.
Split the sentence "I love Python" into words and print how many words it has.
Check whether "42" is a digit string and whether "hello" is an alphabetic string.
summary: A method is called with a dot after the string, like text.upper().
strip removes spaces from both ends, and replace swaps one piece for another.
count and find search inside a string, and startswith and endswith test its edges.
split breaks a string into a list, and join glues a list into a string.

tutorials.title: String Exercises
tutorials.intro: A set of practice exercises on strings. Try each one yourself, then check your answer against the solution below it.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: First and last letters
Store your name in a variable. Print its length, its first letter, and its last letter, each on its own line.

blocks.title: Exercise 1: answer
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
print(len(name))
print(name[0])
print(name[-1])

blocks.text: Exercise 2: Reverse a word
Take the word "Python" and print it backwards using a slice with a step of -1.

blocks.title: Exercise 2: answer
blocks.code:
word = "Python"
print(word[::-1])

blocks.text: Exercise 3: Clean up messy input
A user typed "  HELLO WORLD  " with extra spaces and capital letters. Strip the spaces, make it lowercase, and then title case, and print each result.

blocks.title: Exercise 3: answer
blocks.code:
text = "  HELLO WORLD  "
clean = text.strip()
print(clean.lower())
print(clean.title())

blocks.text: If an exercise feels hard, break it into smaller steps. Work out one piece, print it, and check it before moving on to the next piece.

practice: Do Exercise 1 with your own name.
Slice the word "Programming" to get just "gram".
Count how many times the letter a appears in the word "banana" using count.
summary: Indexes start at 0, and negative indexes count from the end.
A slice with a step of -1 reverses a string.
strip, lower, and title clean up messy text.
split turns a sentence into a list of words.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about strings. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that takes a full name like "ada lovelace" and prints it in title case. Then print the first name only, the last name only, and the full name backwards. Finally, print whether the name contains the letter a, and how many times the letter a appears.
Hints

items: title() capitalises the first letter of every word.
split() breaks the name into a list of words.
A slice with a step of -1 reverses a string.
in tests whether a piece is inside a string, and count tells you how many times it appears.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution, using the sample name shown in the output.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
name = "ada lovelace"
name = name.title()
print(name)
parts = name.split()
print(parts[0])
print(parts[1])
print(name[::-1])
print("a" in name.lower())
print(name.lower().count("a"))
blocks.output:
Ada Lovelace
Ada
Lovelace
ecalevoL adA
True
3

blocks.text: The name is cleaned to title case first, then split into two words. The reversed string is built with a slice, and the letter count uses the lowercase version so that the capital A at the start is counted too.

blocks.title: Check: the same program with another name
blocks.code:
name = "alan turing"
name = name.title()
print(name)
parts = name.split()
print(parts[0], parts[1])
print(name[::-1])
blocks.output:
Alan Turing
Alan Turing
gniruT nalA

blocks.text: When you count or search for a letter, convert the string to lowercase first, so that capital and small versions of the letter are treated the same.

practice: Solve the challenge with your own full name.
Print your name in uppercase, then slice out the first three letters.
Count how many times the letter e appears in your favourite food.
summary: title() fixes the case of a name, and split() breaks it into words.
A slice with a step of -1 reverses a string.
in tests for a piece inside a string, and count tells you how many times it appears.
Convert to lowercase before counting a letter, so capitals are counted too.

tutorials.title: Booleans
tutorials.intro: A boolean is a value that is either True or False. Booleans are the result of every comparison, and they are what if statements test.

blocks.text: What is a boolean?

A boolean has only two possible values: True and False. They are written with a capital first letter in Python. Booleans answer yes-or-no questions, such as whether a user is old enough or whether a list is empty.

blocks.title: Booleans from comparisons
blocks.code:
print(10 > 9)
print(10 == 9)
print(10 < 9)
print(5 == 5)

blocks.text: Booleans from the bool function

The bool function turns any value into True or False. Zero, empty text, and empty collections are False, and almost everything else is True. This rule is handy when you test whether a user typed anything at all, or whether a number is zero.

blocks.title: What is True and what is False
blocks.code:
print(bool(1))
print(bool(0))
print(bool("hello"))
print(bool(""))
print(bool([]))
print(bool([0]))
blocks.output:
True
False
True
False
False
True

blocks.text: Booleans in if statements
An if statement runs its block when its condition is True and skips it when the condition is False. You can store a boolean in a variable first, which makes the condition easy to read.

blocks.title: A boolean variable in an if
blocks.code:
age = 20
can_vote = age >= 18
print(can_vote)
if can_vote:
    print("You can vote")

blocks.text: True and False are also numbers in Python: True is 1 and False is 0. So True + True gives 2. This is a useful fact, but do not rely on it in normal code.

practice: Print the results of 5 > 3, 5 == 3, and 5 != 3.
Use bool() on 0, 1, "", "hi", and [] and print the results.
Store a boolean called is_raining and print a different message depending on its value.
summary: A boolean is either True or False, written with a capital first letter.
Comparisons give booleans, and if statements test them.
Zero, empty text, and empty collections are False; almost everything else is True.
Storing a condition in a named boolean makes code easier to read.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about booleans. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that stores a user's age and whether they have a ticket. Print whether they can enter a show, which needs an age of 18 or more AND a ticket. Then print whether they can enter a different show, which needs an age of 18 or more OR a ticket. Test the program with two different sets of values.
Hints

items: age >= 18 gives a boolean that is True when the user is old enough.
and gives True only when both sides are True.
or gives True when at least one side is True.
Store each result in a variable with a clear name before printing it.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution, using the sample values shown in the output.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
age = 20
has_ticket = True
old_enough = age >= 18
strict_show = old_enough and has_ticket
easy_show = old_enough or has_ticket
print("Strict show:", strict_show)
print("Easy show:", easy_show)
blocks.output:
Strict show: True
Easy show: True

blocks.text: With an age of 20 and a ticket, both shows allow entry. The second set of values shows the difference between and and or: a 15-year-old with a ticket fails the strict show but passes the easy one.

blocks.title: Check: a younger user with a ticket
blocks.code:
age = 15
has_ticket = True
old_enough = age >= 18
strict_show = old_enough and has_ticket
easy_show = old_enough or has_ticket
print("Strict show:", strict_show)
print("Easy show:", easy_show)
blocks.output:
Strict show: False
Easy show: True

blocks.text: When a condition gets long, store its parts in named booleans first. old_enough and has_ticket reads far better than age >= 18 and has_ticket == True.

practice: Solve the challenge with an age of 17 and no ticket, and work out both answers by hand first.
Write a program that prints whether a number is between 10 and 20 using and.
Use bool() to test whether an empty string and a non-empty string are True or False.
summary: Comparisons give booleans: True or False.
and needs both sides True; or needs at least one side True.
Storing conditions in named booleans makes code easy to read.
Test every combination of values when a rule has more than one condition.

tutorials.title: Python Operators
tutorials.intro: Operators are symbols that do something with values, like adding numbers or comparing them. This page gives you the map of all the operator groups in Python.

blocks.text: What is an operator?

An operator is a symbol that works on one or more values, called operands, and produces a result. For example, in 2 + 3, the plus sign is the operator and 2 and 3 are the operands. Python has groups of operators for maths, assignment, comparison, logic, identity, membership, and bit-level work.

blocks.title: One operator from each group
blocks.code:
print(10 + 5)
print(10 == 10)
print(True and False)
print("a" in "apple")
print(2 ** 3)

blocks.text: The operator groups

items: Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, %, //, and ** for maths.
Assignment: =, +=, -=, *=, and more, for storing values.
Comparison: ==, !=, >, <, >=, and <=, which give True or False.
Logical: and, or, and not, for combining booleans.
Identity: is and is not, for checking whether two names point to the same object.
Membership: in and not in, for checking whether a value is inside a collection.
Bitwise: &, |, ^, ~, <<, and >>, for working with single bits.

blocks.text: Operators have an order

When an expression has more than one operator, Python follows a fixed order called precedence. Brackets come first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction, and comparisons come last. When in doubt, use brackets to make the order clear.
The next pages in this section cover each operator group in detail, with examples for every operator in the group.

practice: Write one expression using each of these operators: +, -, *, /, %, and **.
Print the results of 5 == 5, 5 != 5, and 5 > 3.
Work out 2 + 3 * 4 by hand, then check your answer in Python.
summary: An operator works on values called operands and produces a result.
Python has arithmetic, assignment, comparison, logical, identity, membership, and bitwise operators.
Comparison operators give True or False.
Operators follow a fixed order, and brackets make the order clear.

tutorials.title: Arithmetic Operators
tutorials.intro: Arithmetic operators do maths with numbers. This page covers all seven of them, with examples for each one.

blocks.text: The seven arithmetic operators

items: Plus (+) adds two numbers.
Minus (-) subtracts one number from another.
Star (*) multiplies two numbers.
Slash (/) divides and always gives a float.
Double slash (//) divides and gives the whole-number part.
Percent (%) gives the remainder after division.
Double star (**) raises a number to a power.

blocks.title: All seven operators on 10 and 3
blocks.code:
print(10 + 3)
print(10 - 3)
print(10 * 3)
print(10 / 3)
print(10 // 3)
print(10 % 3)
print(2 ** 3)

blocks.text: Remainder and whole-number division

The remainder operator is useful for testing whether a number is even or odd, and for splitting things into groups. A number is even when number % 2 is 0. Whole-number division tells you how many full groups fit, and the remainder tells you what is left over.

blocks.title: Even or odd, and sharing sweets
blocks.code:
print(7 % 2)
print(8 % 2)
print(17 // 5)
print(17 % 5)

blocks.text: Powers
The double star raises a number to a power. 2 ** 10 is 1024, and a fractional power works as a root: 9 ** 0.5 is 3.0, the square root of 9.

blocks.title: Powers and roots
blocks.code:
print(2 ** 10)
print(3 ** 2)
print(9 ** 0.5)

blocks.text: Division with a single slash always gives a float, even when the answer is whole. 8 / 2 prints 4.0, not 4.

practice: Print the answers to 15 divided by 4 using both / and //, and the remainder using %.
Use % to test whether 21 and 30 are even or odd.
Work out 2 to the power of 10 and the square root of 144 using **.
summary: The seven arithmetic operators are +, -, *, /, //, %, and **.
/ always gives a float; // gives the whole-number part.
% gives the remainder, which tests even and odd numbers.
** raises a number to a power, and a fractional power gives a root.

tutorials.title: Assignment Operators
tutorials.intro: Assignment operators store a value in a variable, and the short forms combine a calculation with the assignment in one step.

blocks.text: The plain assignment

The single equals sign assigns a value to a variable. It does not test whether two values are equal; that is the job of the double equals sign. Mixing them up is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

blocks.title: Assigning a value
blocks.code:
x = 5
print(x)
x = 10
print(x)

blocks.text: Short forms that combine maths and assignment

Writing x = x + 3 is so common that Python gives you a shorter form: x += 3. It means exactly the same thing: add 3 to x and store the result back in x. There is a short form for every arithmetic operator.

blocks.title: The short forms in action
blocks.code:
x = 10
x += 3
print(x)
x -= 3
print(x)
x *= 2
print(x)
x /= 2
print(x)

blocks.text: The rest of the short forms
The same pattern works for whole-number division, remainder, and powers. Each one does the calculation and stores the result back in the same variable.

blocks.title: More short forms
blocks.code:
x = 10
x //= 3
print(x)
x %= 2
print(x)
x = 2
x **= 3
print(x)

blocks.text: A single equals sign assigns a value, and a double equals sign compares two values. If a condition behaves strangely, check your equals signs first.

practice: Start with x = 5, then use +=, -=, and *= to change it, printing after each step.
Use //= and %= on a number and print the results.
