tutorials.title: Copy Dictionaries
tutorials.intro: Copying a dictionary is trickier than it looks, because assigning a dictionary to a new name does not copy it. This page shows how to make a real copy.

blocks.text: Assignment does not copy

When you write b = a for a dictionary, both names point to the same dictionary. Changing the dictionary through b also changes what a sees, because there is only one dictionary. This is the same surprise as with lists.

blocks.title: Two names, one dictionary
blocks.code:
a = {"name": "Asha", "age": 20}
b = a
b["age"] = 21
print(a)
print(b)

blocks.text: Making a real copy
The copy method makes a separate dictionary with the same pairs. The dict function, dict(a), does the same thing. After a real copy, changing one dictionary does not affect the other.

blocks.title: Two ways to copy a dictionary
blocks.code:
a = {"name": "Asha", "age": 20}
b = a.copy()
c = dict(a)
b["age"] = 21
print(a)
print(b)
print(c)

blocks.text: Shallow copies and nested dictionaries

The copy method makes a shallow copy: it copies the outer dictionary, but the values inside are still shared. If a value is itself a dictionary or a list, changing it through the copy also changes the original. For a full independent copy of nested data, use copy.deepcopy.

blocks.title: A shallow copy shares nested values
blocks.code:
a = {"name": "Asha", "marks": {"Maths": 90}}
b = a.copy()
b["marks"]["Maths"] = 95
print(a)
print(b)

blocks.text: For a dictionary of plain numbers or strings, copy and dict(a) are both safe. Only nested dictionaries and lists need deepcopy, because only they share inner objects.

summary: Assigning a dictionary to a new name does not copy it; both names point to one dictionary.
copy and dict(a) make a separate dictionary with the same pairs.
A shallow copy shares nested dictionaries and lists.
For nested data, use copy.deepcopy for a full independent copy.

tutorials.title: Nested Dictionaries
tutorials.intro: A nested dictionary is a dictionary inside a dictionary. It is how you store structured data, like a student with an address, or a class full of students.

blocks.text: What is a nested dictionary?

A nested dictionary is a dictionary whose values are themselves dictionaries. The outer keys name the groups, and the inner keys name the details. This is a natural way to store data that has layers, like a school with classes, or a student with an address.

blocks.title: A dictionary of students

blocks.text: Reading nested values
You read a nested value by chaining the keys, one pair of square brackets for each level. The first key finds the inner dictionary, and the second key finds the value inside it.

blocks.title: Reading values at each level

blocks.text: Looping over nested dictionaries

To visit every value in a nested dictionary, loop over the outer items and then loop over the inner items. The outer loop gives you each group, and the inner loop gives you the details inside that group.

blocks.title: Looping through two levels

blocks.text: Reading a missing key at any level gives a KeyError. Use get at each level, like students.get("Asha", {}).get("age"), when you are not sure the keys exist.

Use get at each level when a key might be missing.

tutorials.title: Dictionary Methods
tutorials.intro: Dictionary methods let you read, add, update, and remove pairs safely and in fewer lines. This page is the reference for the methods you will use most.

blocks.text: Getting values safely

Reading a missing key with square brackets gives a KeyError and stops your program. The get method is safer, because it returns None when the key is missing instead of giving an error. You can also give get a second value, which it returns as a default when the key is not there.

blocks.title: Use get instead of square brackets
blocks.code:
user = {"name": "Rahul", "age": 25}
print(user.get("name"))
print(user.get("city"))
print(user.get("city", "Unknown"))

blocks.text: Updating and adding values

The update method adds or changes many pairs at once from another dictionary. If a key already exists, its value is replaced, and if it does not exist, the pair is added. The setdefault method returns the value for a key if the key exists, and if it does not exist, it adds the key with the value you give and then returns that value.

blocks.title: Update many pairs and use setdefault
blocks.code:
scores = {"Maths": 80}
scores.update({"English": 90, "Maths": 85})
scores.setdefault("Science", 75)
scores.setdefault("Maths", 100)
print(scores)

blocks.text: Removing items and reading keys

The pop method removes a pair by its key and returns the value that was removed, so you can use that value before it is gone. The popitem method removes the last pair that was added and returns it as a pair of key and value. The keys method gives you all the keys, and the values method gives you all the values.

blocks.title: Remove pairs and read keys and values
blocks.code:
book = {"title": "Python Basics", "pages": 200, "author": "Asha"}
print(book.pop("pages"))
print(book.popitem())
print(list(book.keys()))
print(list(book.values()))

blocks.text: The pop method gives a KeyError for a missing key unless you pass a default value, for example book.pop('pages', 0). The clear method removes every pair and leaves an empty dictionary.

practice: Create a dictionary for a user, then use get to read a key that does not exist, with a default value.
Create a dictionary of scores, update it with two new subjects, and use setdefault to add a third subject only if it is missing.
Create a dictionary, remove one pair with pop, print the removed value, and then print the keys that are left.
summary: get reads a value safely, with an optional default.
update changes many pairs at once.
setdefault adds a missing key without overwriting an old one.
pop and popitem remove pairs, and keys and values list what is left.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about dictionaries. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that stores a small phone book as a dictionary of names and numbers. Add two contacts, change one number, remove one contact with pop, and then print the phone book, the number of contacts, and the number for a name that is not in the book, using get with a default message. Finally, loop over the phone book and print each contact.
Hints

items: Assigning to a new key adds a contact; assigning to an old key changes its number.
pop removes a contact and returns its number.
get with a second argument returns that value when the name is missing.
items loops through names and numbers together.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution, using the sample contacts shown in the output.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
phonebook = {}
phonebook["Asha"] = 9876543210
phonebook["Ravi"] = 9123456780
phonebook["Asha"] = 9999999999
removed = phonebook.pop("Ravi")
print("Removed:", removed)
print(phonebook)
print("Contacts:", len(phonebook))
print("Meera:", phonebook.get("Meera", "Not found"))
for name, number in phonebook.items():
    print(name, number)
blocks.output:
Removed: 9123456780
{'Asha': 9999999999}
Contacts: 1
Meera: Not found
Asha 9999999999

blocks.text: Asha's number was changed from 9876543210 to 9999999999, and Ravi was removed. Only one contact is left, and looking up Meera gives the default message instead of an error.

blocks.title: Check: adding the contact back
blocks.code:
phonebook = {"Asha": 9999999999}
phonebook["Meera"] = 8888888888
print(phonebook)
print("Contacts:", len(phonebook))

blocks.text: A dictionary is the right tool whenever you look things up by name. If you find yourself searching a list for a matching name, a dictionary will do it faster and with less code.

tutorials.title: Python If
tutorials.intro: An if statement lets a program make decisions. With conditions, your code can take one path when something is true and a different path when it is false.

blocks.text: Making decisions in code

A program often needs to choose between two actions. If a user is old enough, they can vote. If not, they cannot. The if statement tests a condition, which is an expression that is either True or False. When the condition is True, Python runs the indented lines under the if. When it is False, Python skips them.

blocks.title: A simple if else choice

blocks.text: Comparison operators

Conditions are built with comparison operators. Two equals signs test whether values are equal, and a single equals sign is only for giving a value to a variable. Mixing them up is one of the most common beginner mistakes, so check your equals signs whenever a condition behaves strangely.

items: Double equals (==) tests whether two values are equal.
Not equals (!=) tests whether two values are different.
Greater than (>) and less than (<) compare numbers.
Greater than or equal (>=) and less than or equal (<=) include the boundary value.

blocks.text: More than two choices with elif

When there are more than two possible outcomes, use elif, short for else if. Python checks each condition from top to bottom and runs the first block whose condition is True. Once one block runs, the rest are skipped, so the order of your conditions matters.

blocks.title: Grading marks with elif

blocks.text: Indentation is not decoration in Python. The lines under an if must be indented by the same amount, usually four spaces. A line with the wrong indentation either fails or belongs to the wrong block.

practice: Ask the user for their age and print whether they can vote.
Ask the user for a number and print whether it is positive, negative, or zero.
Write a program that prints "Pass" when marks are 40 or more and "Fail" otherwise.
summary: if runs a block only when its condition is True, and else runs when it is False.
Use double equals (==) to compare values, not a single equals sign.
elif adds extra choices, checked from top to bottom.
Indentation groups the lines that belong to each if, elif, or else.

tutorials.title: Python Elif
tutorials.intro: Elif adds extra choices to an if statement. It lets a program pick one outcome out of many, checking the conditions in order.

blocks.text: What is elif?

Elif is short for else if. It sits between an if and an optional else, and it adds another condition to test. Python checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs the first block whose condition is True. Once one block runs, the rest are skipped.

blocks.title: Grading marks with elif

blocks.text: Order matters

In the grade example, the conditions are checked from highest to lowest. Marks of 72 fail the first test, since 72 is not 90 or more, and pass the second test, since 72 is 60 or more. If the order were reversed, every mark above 40 would stop at the first test and always get Grade C.

blocks.title: The wrong order gives the wrong answer

blocks.text: Elif with different kinds of tests

The conditions in an elif chain do not have to test the same variable. Each one can test something different, as long as only one of them should run. The chain still stops at the first True condition.

blocks.title: A greeting based on the hour

blocks.text: You can have as many elif blocks as you need, but a very long chain is a sign that a dictionary or a match statement might be clearer.

practice: Write a program that prints a grade from marks using four elif branches.
Write a program that prints a greeting based on the hour, using elif.
Change the order of the conditions in a grade program and see what goes wrong.
summary: elif adds another condition to an if statement.
Python checks conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first True one.
Order matters: check the most specific or highest values first.
The final else catches every value that matched nothing.

tutorials.title: Python Else
tutorials.intro: Else is the fallback of an if statement. It runs when every condition above it is False, so it catches everything the earlier tests missed.

blocks.text: What is else?

The else block runs when the if condition is False. It has no condition of its own, so it catches every case the if did not handle. Together, if and else cover every possibility: one of the two blocks always runs.

blocks.title: A simple if else choice

blocks.text: Else at the end of an elif chain

At the end of an if-elif chain, else catches every value that matched no condition. In a grade program, else is the natural place for the lowest grade, because it covers every mark below the lowest elif.

blocks.title: Else as the final fallback

blocks.text: Else is optional

An if statement does not need an else. When there is no else, a False condition simply means nothing happens and the program moves on. Add an else only when there is something to do in the False case.

blocks.title: An if without an else
blocks.code:
temperature = 28
if temperature > 30:
    print("It is hot")
print("Done")

blocks.text: An else must belong to an if or an elif. Writing else on its own, without an if above it, is a syntax error.

practice: Write a program that prints "Even" or "Odd" for a number, using if and else.
Write a grade program with an else for the lowest grade.
Write an if statement with no else, and check that nothing prints when the condition is False.
summary: else runs when the if condition is False.
At the end of an elif chain, else catches every value that matched nothing.
else is optional: an if can stand alone.
An else must follow an if or an elif.

tutorials.title: Shorthand If
tutorials.intro: Python lets you write short if statements on a single line. This page covers the one-line if, the one-line if-else, and when to use them.

blocks.text: A one-line if

When an if block has only one statement, you can put it on the same line as the if. This is called a shorthand if. It is handy for short, simple actions, but it should not be used for anything longer.

blocks.title: A one-line if

blocks.text: A one-line if-else

An if-else that only picks a value can be written as a ternary expression: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false. It is an expression, which means you can store its result, print it, or pass it to a function.

blocks.title: A ternary if-else
blocks.code:
age = 20
status = "adult" if age >= 18 else "minor"
print(status)
print("Pass" if 82 >= 40 else "Fail")

blocks.text: Short if-elif-else chains
You can also write a whole if-elif-else chain on one line, but it is rarely a good idea. The line gets long and hard to read, and a normal chain with indented blocks is clearer.

blocks.title: A short chain, kept readable
blocks.code:
marks = 72
grade = "A" if marks >= 90 else ("B" if marks >= 60 else ("C" if marks >= 40 else "D"))
print(grade)

blocks.text: Shorthand if is for short, simple actions only. If the block has more than one statement, or the condition is long, use the normal indented form.

practice: Write a one-line if that prints a message when a number is greater than 10.
Use a ternary to store "Pass" or "Fail" from a marks value of 35.
Rewrite a one-line if-else as a normal if-else with indented blocks.
summary: A one-line if fits a single short statement on the same line as the if.
A ternary picks one of two values: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false.
Shorthand forms are for short, simple cases only.
Use normal indented blocks when the logic is longer or has several statements.

tutorials.title: Logical Operators
tutorials.intro: Logical operators combine conditions inside an if statement. They are how you say both of these must be true, or at least one of them must be true.

blocks.text: And, or, and not in conditions

The and operator gives True only when both sides are True. The or operator gives True when at least one side is True. The not operator flips a boolean. Together, they let you build conditions with more than one part.

blocks.title: Combining two conditions

blocks.text: Using or for either condition
Sometimes either condition is enough. A shop gives a discount to students or to senior citizens, so either one qualifies. The or operator covers that case.

blocks.title: Either condition is enough

blocks.text: Using not to flip a condition
The not operator flips a condition. It is useful when you want to test the opposite of something, like whether a list is empty or whether a user is not logged in.

blocks.title: Flipping a condition with not
blocks.output:
Please log in
No tasks left

blocks.text: And has higher precedence than or, so a and b or c means (a and b) or c. Use brackets when the grouping is not obvious.

practice: Write a program that prints a message only when a number is between 10 and 20, using and.
Write a program that gives a discount to students or senior citizens, using or.
Write a program that prints a message when a list is empty, using not.
summary: and needs both sides True; or needs at least one side True.
not flips a condition.
Logical operators combine comparisons into bigger conditions.
Use brackets when the grouping of and and or is not obvious.

tutorials.title: Nested If
tutorials.intro: A nested if is an if statement inside another if statement. It lets you test a second condition only after the first one is true.

blocks.text: What is a nested if?

A nested if is an if statement placed inside the block of another if statement. The inner if is only tested when the outer condition is True. This is useful when a decision has two layers, like checking whether a user is old enough and then checking whether they have a ticket.

blocks.title: Two layers of checks

blocks.text: Nested if versus and

The same two checks can often be written as one condition with and. Use a nested if when the inner check needs its own message, and use and when both checks lead to the same outcome. The nested form is clearer when each layer has a different message.

blocks.title: The same checks with and

blocks.text: Three levels of nesting

Nesting can go deeper, but each level adds indentation and makes the code harder to follow. Three levels is usually the most you should use; deeper than that, it is better to use and, or a function that returns early.

blocks.title: Three levels, kept short

blocks.text: Every level of nesting adds four spaces of indentation. Keep nesting shallow, and combine simple conditions with and instead of nesting them.

practice: Write a nested if that checks age and then checks for a ticket, with a different message for each case.
Rewrite your nested if using and, and compare the two versions.
Write a nested if that checks whether a number is positive, and then whether it is even.
summary: A nested if is an if statement inside another if statement.
The inner if is only tested when the outer condition is True.
Use nesting when each layer needs its own message; use and otherwise.
Keep nesting shallow: three levels is usually the most you should use.

tutorials.title: Pass Statement
tutorials.intro: The pass statement does nothing. It is a placeholder for code you have not written yet, so that a block that must exist can stay empty.

blocks.text: What is pass?

Python needs at least one statement inside every block. An if, a loop, or a function with an empty block is a syntax error. The pass statement fills that gap: it does nothing, but it counts as a statement, so the block is valid.

blocks.title: Pass as a placeholder

blocks.text: Pass in a function you have not written yet
When you plan a program, you often know the names of the functions before you know how they work. Writing pass inside each one lets the program run while you fill them in one by one.

blocks.title: A function with pass inside

blocks.text: Pass in a loop
Pass is also useful in a loop when you want to skip a case for now. The loop still runs for every item, but the pass branch does nothing, which is clearer than leaving the branch empty.

blocks.title: Pass inside a loop
blocks.output:
1 is odd
3 is odd
5 is odd

blocks.text: Pass is not the same as continue. Continue skips the rest of the current round of a loop, while pass does nothing and the loop carries on normally.

practice: Write an if statement with pass in its block and print a line after it.
Write a function with pass inside it, then call it and check that nothing happens.
Write a loop that uses pass for even numbers and prints odd numbers.
summary: pass does nothing; it is a placeholder for code not written yet.
Every block needs at least one statement, and pass fills that gap.
Use pass in functions and branches you plan to fill in later.
pass is not continue: it does nothing and the loop carries on normally.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about if statements. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that works out the ticket price for a visitor. Children under 5 enter free. Children from 5 to 12 pay 50 rupees. Adults from 13 to 59 pay 100 rupees. Seniors aged 60 or more pay 60 rupees. Print the price for a given age, and add a message saying whether the visitor is a child, an adult, or a senior.
Hints

items: Use an if-elif-else chain, checking the ages from youngest to oldest.
Each branch should set the price and the category, then print them.
Test with ages on both sides of every boundary: 4, 5, 12, 13, 59, and 60.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution, using the sample age shown in the output.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
age = 10
if age < 5:
    price = 0
    category = "child"
elif age <= 12:
    price = 50
    category = "child"
elif age < 60:
    price = 100
    category = "adult"
else:
    price = 60
    category = "senior"
print(f"Age {age}: {category}, Rs. {price}")

blocks.text: An age of 10 falls into the second branch, so the price is 50 rupees. The chain checks the conditions in order and runs only the first one that is true.

blocks.title: Check: a senior and a baby
blocks.output:
Age 3: child, Rs. 0
Age 65: senior, Rs. 60

blocks.text: When a rule has boundaries, test the values on both sides of every boundary. A single wrong comparison, like < instead of <=, shows up at once.

practice: Solve the challenge with an age of 45 and check the price.
Add a branch for students aged 13 to 25 who pay 70 rupees.
Write a program that prints the grade for marks of 88 using an elif chain.
summary: An if-elif-else chain picks one outcome out of many.
Check conditions in order and run only the first True one.
Each branch can set several values before printing.
Test boundary values on both sides of every limit.

tutorials.title: Match
tutorials.intro: The match statement compares one value against several patterns, called cases. It is a clean way to choose between many values.

blocks.text: What is match case?

The match statement compares one value against several patterns, called cases. Python runs the block of the first case that matches the value. It is like a switch in other languages. Match case was added in Python 3.10, so it needs a modern version of Python to run.

blocks.title: Matching a day number to a name
blocks.code:
day = 3
match day:
    case 1:
        print("Monday")
    case 2:
        print("Tuesday")
    case 3:
        print("Wednesday")
    case _:
        print("Invalid day")

blocks.text: The default case

The last case uses an underscore, which matches anything. It works like the else in an if statement and catches every value that did not match an earlier case. Without it, a value with no matching case would simply do nothing, which is usually a mistake.

blocks.title: The underscore case catches everything else
blocks.code:
day = 9
match day:
    case 1:
        print("Monday")
    case 2:
        print("Tuesday")
    case _:
        print("Invalid day")

blocks.text: Match case in a calculator

Match case is a natural fit for the calculator from earlier lessons. Each operation is one case, and the underscore case handles unknown operations. Compare this version with the if and elif version and notice how much shorter and clearer it is.

blocks.title: Calculator with match case
blocks.code:
op = "*"
a = 6
b = 7
match op:
    case "+":
        print(a + b)
    case "-":
        print(a - b)
    case "*":
        print(a * b)
    case "/":
        print(a / b)
    case _:
        print("Unknown operation")

blocks.text: Match case needs Python 3.10 or newer. On an older version, the same code fails with a syntax error, so use if and elif when you are not sure which version will run your program.

practice: Write a match case program that prints the name of a month from its number, 1 to 12.
Rewrite the calculator exercise using match case instead of if and elif.
Write a match case that prints "Weekend" for Saturday and Sunday and "Weekday" for other days.
summary: match compares one value against several cases and runs the first match.
The underscore case matches anything, like else in an if statement.
A vertical bar in a case means or, so one case can match several values.
Match case needs Python 3.10 or newer.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about match case. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that takes a month number from 1 to 12 and prints the season: Winter for December, January, and February; Spring for March, April, and May; Summer for June, July, and August; and Autumn for September, October, and November. Use a match statement with one case per season, and an underscore case for an invalid month number.
Hints

items: A case can match several values with a vertical bar: case 12 | 1 | 2.
The underscore case catches every month number that is not 1 to 12.
Write one case per season, so the program has four cases plus the default.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution, using the sample month shown in the output.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
month = 11
match month:
    case 12 | 1 | 2:
        print("Winter")
    case 3 | 4 | 5:
        print("Spring")
    case 6 | 7 | 8:
        print("Summer")
    case 9 | 10 | 11:
        print("Autumn")
    case _:
        print("Invalid month")

blocks.text: Month 11 matches the last season case, so the program prints Autumn. Each case groups three months with vertical bars, which is much shorter than writing three separate cases per season.

blocks.title: Check: a winter month and an invalid month
blocks.code:
for month in [1, 15]:
    match month:
        case 12 | 1 | 2:
            print("Winter")
        case 3 | 4 | 5:
            print("Spring")
        case 6 | 7 | 8:
            print("Summer")
        case 9 | 10 | 11:
            print("Autumn")
        case _:
            print("Invalid month")

blocks.text: When several values should do the same thing, group them in one case with vertical bars instead of writing the same block three times.

practice: Solve the challenge with a month of 7 and check the season.
Write a match case that prints the number of days in a month from its number.
Write a match case that prints "Weekend" for 6 and 7 and "Weekday" for 1 to 5.
summary: match compares one value against several cases and runs the first match.
A vertical bar groups several values into one case.
The underscore case catches every value that matched nothing.
Group values that share an outcome instead of repeating the same block.

tutorials.title: While Loops
tutorials.intro: A while loop repeats a block as long as a condition stays true. Use it when you do not know in advance how many times the loop must run.

blocks.text: What is a while loop?

A while loop checks a condition before each round. If the condition is True, it runs the block, then checks again. If the condition is False, it stops and the program moves on. Unlike a for loop, a while loop does not walk through a list. It simply repeats until something changes.

blocks.title: Counting with a while loop
blocks.code:
count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count = count + 1

blocks.text: The counter must change

The counter line inside the loop is the most important part. It changes the value the condition tests, so the loop can eventually stop. Without it, count would stay 1 forever, the condition would always be True, and the program would print 1 forever. That is called an infinite loop.

blocks.title: Counting down
blocks.code:
count = 5
while count >= 1:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("Blast off!")

blocks.text: When to use while instead of for

Use a for loop when you know the items in advance, like the numbers 1 to 10 or the fruits in a list. Use a while loop when the number of rounds depends on something that happens during the loop, like a user typing the right password or a total reaching a target. The example below adds numbers until the total passes a limit, and nobody knows in advance how many rounds that takes.

blocks.title: Adding until a target is reached
blocks.code:
total = 0
num = 1
while total < 20:
    total = total + num
    num = num + 1
print("Total:", total)

practice: Use a while loop to print the numbers from 10 down to 1.
Use a while loop to add the numbers 1, 2, 3, and so on until the total is more than 50, then print the total.
Write a loop that keeps asking the user for a number until they type 0.
summary: A while loop repeats its block as long as its condition is True.
Something inside the loop must change the condition, or it never stops.
Use for when you know the items, and while when the rounds depend on what happens.
Press Ctrl and C to stop a loop that runs forever.

tutorials.title: Code Challenge
tutorials.intro: A small challenge to test what you learned about while loops. Try it yourself before reading the solution.

blocks.text: The challenge

Write a program that plays a guessing game. The secret number is 7. Keep asking the player for a guess until they guess correctly. After each wrong guess, print whether the secret number is higher or lower than the guess. When they guess correctly, print how many guesses it took.
Hints

items: A while True loop keeps asking until a break stops it.
Count each guess with a counter that starts at 0 and adds 1 each round.
Compare the guess with the secret number to print Higher or Lower.
Break out of the loop when the guess is correct.

blocks.text: The solution
Here is one correct solution. The sample run below uses a fixed list of guesses instead of real input, so the output is the same every time: the player guesses 3, then 9, then 7.

blocks.title: Solution
blocks.code:
secret = 7
guesses = [3, 9, 7]
tries = 0
i = 0
while True:
    guess = guesses[i]
    i = i + 1
    tries = tries + 1
    print("Guess:", guess)
    if guess < secret:
        print("Higher")
    elif guess > secret:
        print("Lower")
    else:
        print("Correct! You guessed it in", tries, "tries")
        break
blocks.output:
Guess: 3
Higher
Guess: 9
Lower
Guess: 7
Correct! You guessed it in 3 tries

blocks.text: The loop runs three times. The first guess is too low, the second is too high, and the third is correct, so the break ends the loop. In the real game, replace the fixed list with input, like guess = int(input("Guess a number: ")).

blocks.title: The same game with real input
blocks.output:
Guess a number: 3
Higher
Guess a number: 9
Lower
Guess a number: 7
Correct! You guessed it in 3 tries

blocks.text: A while True loop with a break is the standard pattern for a game that keeps going until the player wins. Make sure every path through the loop can reach a break.

summary: A while True loop repeats until a break stops it.
