An inner class is written in the body of an outer class, indented one level inside it. It belongs to the outer class, so you reach it through the outer class name: Outer.Inner. The inner class is a normal class in every other way: it has its own __init__, its own attributes, and its own methods.

Inner classes are for grouping. A university has departments, and a department is hard to imagine on its own outside a university. Putting Department inside University says that clearly in the code, and keeps the two names together instead of having two separate top-level classes.

blocks.title: A Department class inside a University class

blocks.text: Creating the inner object from a method

The outer class can also build inner objects for you. A method on the outer class can create and return an inner object, so the caller never writes the long Outer.Inner name. The Car below has a build_engine method that returns an Engine, and the engine works on its own once it is built.

blocks.title: A method that builds an inner Engine
blocks.output:
Engine with 120 hp started.
City Motors

items: An inner class is defined inside the body of an outer class.
Reach it through the outer class: Outer.Inner.
It is a normal class with its own attributes and methods.
An outer method can build and return an inner object.
Use inner classes only when the inner class belongs to the outer one.

blocks.text: An inner class does not automatically see the outer object's data. A Department object has no access to the University object's name unless you pass it in. If the inner class needs the outer data, pass it as an argument when you create it.

practice: Create a class called School with an inner class called Classroom that stores a room number and prints it.
Add a method to School that creates a Classroom and returns it, then call the method and print the room number.
Create a class called Computer with an inner class called CPU that stores a speed and has a method that prints it.
summary: An inner class is a class defined inside another class.
It is reached through the outer class name: Outer.Inner.
It groups a helper class with the class it belongs to.
The inner class does not automatically see the outer object's data.

tutorials.title: Python File Handling
tutorials.intro: File handling is how a Python program saves data to a file and reads it back later. Variables forget everything when a program ends, but files keep the data.

blocks.text: A program stores its data in variables while it runs. When the program ends, those variables disappear. Files solve this problem. Notes, scores, settings and logs all live in files between runs. Python opens a file, reads or writes through it, and closes it when done. The built-in open function opens a file. It takes the file path and a mode. The mode w writes a file and erases anything already in it. The mode r reads a file and is the default when you leave the mode out. The mode a appends, adding new text at the end without touching what is already there. The with statement closes the file automatically, even if something goes wrong in the middle. Always use the with statement with open. It closes the file for you, so you never forget and never leave a file locked.
Opening a file

items: r reads a file. The file must already exist, or open raises an error.
w writes a file. It creates the file if needed and erases old content.
a appends to a file. It creates the file if needed and keeps old content.
x creates a new file and raises an error if the file already exists.

blocks.text: Writing and reading a file

This example writes two lines to a demo file in the /tmp folder, then reads the whole file back and prints it. The examples in this section use /tmp/demo.txt so you can run them anywhere without cluttering your project folder. The final blank line in the output comes from print adding a newline after text that already ends with one. Opening a file with w erases it at once, before you write anything. Double-check the file name and the mode before you run code that opens with w.

blocks.title: Writing and reading a file
blocks.code:
with open("/tmp/demo.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello Python\n")
    f.write("File handling is easy\n")

with open("/tmp/demo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
blocks.output:
Hello Python
File handling is easy

blocks.text: Appending to a file
This example writes one line, then reopens the same file in append mode to add a second line. Reading it back shows both lines, because append mode kept the first line instead of erasing it.

blocks.title: Adding lines without erasing
blocks.code:
with open("/tmp/demo.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Day 1: Started Python\n")

with open("/tmp/demo.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Day 2: Learned files\n")

with open("/tmp/demo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
blocks.output:
Day 1: Started Python
Day 2: Learned files

practice: Write your name and age to a file named /tmp/me.txt, then read it back and print it.
Append three lines of a diary to the same file over three separate runs and read the result.
Try opening a file that does not exist in r mode and read the error message it gives.
summary: Files let programs save data that survives after the program ends.
open with mode w writes, r reads, and a appends to a file.
The with statement closes the file automatically.
Opening with w erases existing content, so check the mode first.

tutorials.title: Python Read Files
tutorials.intro: Reading a file means opening it and pulling its text into your program. Python gives you three reading methods: read, readline and readlines.

blocks.text: The read method returns the whole file as one string. The readline method returns a single line each time you call it, and returns an empty string when the file ends. The readlines method returns a list with one string per line. Each method suits a different job, so pick the one that matches the shape of data you need. This example first creates a demo file with two lines, then reads it all at once with read. Passing a number to read, like read(5), reads only that many characters instead of the whole file.
Reading the whole file

blocks.title: read and read with a size
blocks.code:
with open("/tmp/demo.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello Python\n")
    f.write("File handling is easy\n")

with open("/tmp/demo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

with open("/tmp/demo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read(5))
blocks.output:
Hello Python
File handling is easy

Hello

blocks.text: Reading one line at a time

Each call to readline returns the next line, including its newline character at the end. That is why the output below has a blank line after each printed line: the line already ends with a newline, and print adds one more. A common pattern is to loop over the file object directly, which reads one line at a time and uses far less memory on large files. For most jobs, loop over the file object directly instead of readlines: for line in f reads one line at a time and uses far less memory on large files.

blocks.title: readline and looping over lines
blocks.code:
with open("/tmp/demo.txt") as f:
    print(f.readline())
    print(f.readline())

with open("/tmp/demo.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())
blocks.output:
Hello Python

File handling is easy

Hello Python
File handling is easy

blocks.text: Reading all lines as a list

The readlines method is handy when you want to loop over lines or pick one by position, because a list supports indexing and loops. Each line in the list keeps its newline character at the end. Every line returned by readline or readlines ends with a newline character, except possibly the last line of the file. Strip it with line.strip when you want the clean text.

blocks.title: readlines returns a list of lines
blocks.code:
with open("/tmp/demo.txt") as f:
    print(f.readlines())

practice: Write five lines to a file, then use readline in a loop to print each line with its line number.
Use readlines to load a file into a list and print only the second line.
Use read(10) to print the first ten characters of a file, then read(10) again to print the next ten.
summary: read returns the whole file as one string, or a set number of characters.
readline returns one line per call, and an empty string at the end.
readlines returns a list with one string per line.
Lines keep their newline characters, so strip them when you need clean text.

tutorials.title: Python Write/Create Files
tutorials.intro: Writing to a file creates it if it does not exist, or replaces its content. Appending adds new text at the end without touching what is already there.

blocks.text: Creating a file with w

Opening a file in w mode creates the file if it does not exist. If it does exist, w erases its old content at once, before you write anything. The write method adds one string at a time. It does not add a newline for you, so include \n at the end of each line yourself.

blocks.title: Creating a file and writing lines
blocks.code:
with open("/tmp/demo.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello Python\n")
    f.write("File handling is easy\n")

with open("/tmp/demo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
blocks.output:
Hello Python
File handling is easy

blocks.text: Writing many lines at once

The writelines method writes a list of strings in one call. Like write, it does not add newlines for you. Each string in the list must already end with \n if you want it on its own line. Build your text with a list and join it, or use writelines, instead of calling write dozens of times in a loop. It is faster and easier to read.

blocks.title: writelines writes a list of strings
blocks.code:
lines = ["Line one\n", "Line two\n", "Line three\n"]

with open("/tmp/demo.txt", "w") as f:
    f.writelines(lines)

with open("/tmp/demo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
blocks.output:
Line one
Line two
Line three

blocks.text: Appending with a

The a mode adds text at the end of a file and keeps everything already in it. It also creates the file if it does not exist yet. This example writes one line, then appends a second line in a separate open call. Reading the file back shows both lines. Opening a file with w erases it at once, before you write anything. If you only want to add to a file, use a. If you want to fail rather than overwrite an existing file, use x mode instead.

blocks.title: Appending keeps the old content
blocks.code:
with open("/tmp/demo.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Day 1: Started Python\n")

with open("/tmp/demo.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Day 2: Learned files\n")

with open("/tmp/demo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
blocks.output:
Day 1: Started Python
Day 2: Learned files

practice: Create a file /tmp/shopping.txt and write three shopping items into it, one per line.
Use writelines to write the numbers 1 to 5 into a file, each on its own line.
Append your favourite quote to the shopping file and read the whole file back.
summary: Mode w creates a file or erases its old content, then writes.
Mode a adds text at the end and keeps the old content.
write adds one string; writelines adds a list of strings.
Neither write nor writelines adds newlines for you.

tutorials.title: Python Delete Files
tutorials.intro: Python deletes files with the os module. Always check that a file exists first, so a missing file does not crash your program with an error.

blocks.text: Deleting a file with os.remove

The os module has a remove function that deletes a file by its path. Once deleted, the file is gone. It does not go to a recycle bin, so there is no undo. This example creates a demo file, checks that it exists, deletes it, and checks again.

blocks.title: Creating and deleting a file
blocks.code:
import os

with open("/tmp/temp.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("delete me\n")

print(os.path.exists("/tmp/temp.txt"))
os.remove("/tmp/temp.txt")
print(os.path.exists("/tmp/temp.txt"))

blocks.text: Deleting a file that does not exist

Calling os.remove on a missing file raises a FileNotFoundError and stops your program. The safe pattern is to check with os.path.exists first, or to catch the error with try and except. The second way is better when another program might delete the file between your check and your remove call.

blocks.title: Safe delete with a check and with try
blocks.output:
File not found
File not found

blocks.text: Deleting a folder

The os module can also delete folders, but only empty ones. The os.rmdir function deletes an empty folder. For a folder with files inside it, use shutil.rmtree, which deletes the folder and everything in it. That is a dangerous call, so double-check the folder path before you run it.

items: os.remove(path) deletes one file.
os.rmdir(path) deletes one empty folder.
shutil.rmtree(path) deletes a folder and everything inside it.
None of these move anything to a recycle bin. Deletion is final.

blocks.text: Deleting is final. There is no undo and no recycle bin. Never delete a path that comes from user input without checking it first.

practice: Create a file, delete it with os.remove, and print os.path.exists before and after.
Write a small function safe_delete(path) that only deletes the file when it exists.
Try os.remove on a file that does not exist without a check, and read the error message.
summary: os.remove deletes a file by its path.
Deleting a missing file raises FileNotFoundError.
Check with os.path.exists or catch the error with try and except.
Deletion is final, so double-check the path before you delete.

tutorials.title: NumPy Tutorial
tutorials.intro: NumPy is the standard Python library for numbers and arrays. It makes maths on lists of numbers fast, and it is the base that Pandas, SciPy and most data science tools are built on.

blocks.text: A plain Python list can hold numbers, but maths on a list is slow and clumsy. NumPy gives you the array: a list of numbers of one type that supports maths on the whole array at once. Adding 2 to an array adds 2 to every element. NumPy also gives you functions for averages, totals, reshaping and random numbers. Install NumPy with pip. The command below installs it into your current Python environment. After installing, import it in your code. The usual short name is np.
Installing NumPy

blocks.title: Installing and importing NumPy
blocks.code: pip install numpy

blocks.text: Your first array

The np.array function turns a list into an array. Maths then works on the whole array at once. Multiplying the array by 2 doubles every element, and the mean method returns the average of all the elements. The examples in this tutorial were run with NumPy 1.26.4, and the outputs below are the real outputs.

blocks.title: Creating an array and doing maths on it
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
print(arr)
print(arr * 2)
print(arr.mean())

blocks.text: Two-dimensional arrays

An array can have rows and columns, like a table. Adding two arrays of the same shape adds them element by element. The arange function builds an array of evenly spaced numbers, and reshape changes a flat array into rows and columns without changing its data. NumPy has many small helpers for building arrays. zeros makes an array of zeros, ones makes an array of ones, and arange makes a range of numbers with a step. The sqrt function works on a whole array at once, element by element. When you need maths on a whole column of numbers, reach for NumPy instead of a loop. One line of NumPy usually replaces a loop and runs much faster.

blocks.title: 2D arrays, addition and reshape
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
b = np.array([[10, 20], [30, 40]])
print(a + b)

c = np.arange(1, 7).reshape(2, 3)
print(c)
print(c.sum(), c.max(), c.min())

blocks.title: zeros, arange and sqrt
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.zeros(3))
print(np.arange(0, 10, 2))
print(np.sqrt(np.array([4.0, 9.0, 16.0])))

practice: Create an array of the numbers 10 to 20 and print its sum and average.
Create a 3 by 3 array with arange and reshape, then print its largest value.
Make an array of temperatures in Celsius and convert the whole array to Fahrenheit with one line.
summary: NumPy adds fast arrays to Python, with maths on the whole array at once.
Install it with pip install numpy and import it as np.
np.array turns a list into an array; arange and reshape build new ones.
NumPy is the base library that Pandas and SciPy are built on.

tutorials.title: Pandas Tutorial
tutorials.intro: Pandas is the Python library for working with tables of data. It reads CSV files and spreadsheets into a table you can filter, sort and summarise with a few lines of code.

blocks.text: Real data usually comes as a table: rows of records and columns of fields, like a spreadsheet or a CSV file. Pandas gives you the DataFrame, a table you can work with in code. You can pick a column, filter rows by a condition, sort by a value, and compute averages. Pandas is built on NumPy, so it is fast even on large tables. Install Pandas with pip. It brings NumPy along with it if NumPy is not already installed. After installing, import it in your code. The usual short name is pd.
Installing Pandas

blocks.title: Installing and importing Pandas
blocks.code: pip install pandas

blocks.text: Your first DataFrame

The simplest way to make a DataFrame is from a dictionary, where each key is a column name and each value is a list of values. Printing the DataFrame shows a neat table with a row number on the left. The examples in this tutorial were run with Pandas 2.1.4, and the outputs below are the real outputs.

blocks.title: A DataFrame from a dictionary
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Name": ["Asha", "Ravi", "Meera"],
    "Age": [25, 30, 22],
    "City": ["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune"]
})
print(df)
print(df["Age"].mean())
blocks.output:
Name  Age    City
0   Asha   25  Mumbai
1  Ravi   30  Delhi
2  Meera   22    Pune
25.666666666666668

blocks.text: Filtering and sorting rows

A comparison on a column gives a list of true and false values, one per row. Putting that inside square brackets keeps only the rows where the condition is true. The sort_values method orders the rows by a column, smallest first by default. Most real data lives in CSV files, and read_csv loads one into a DataFrame in a single call. This example writes a small CSV file first, then reads it back and finds the average marks. The Series type is a single column of a DataFrame, and it has its own sum and mean methods. The CSV example above reads /tmp/marks.csv, which was created in the file handling section by writing two rows of names and marks. Create that file first, or use any CSV file of your own. Use df.head() to print just the first five rows of a big table, and df.info() to see the column names and types at a glance.

blocks.title: Filtering rows and sorting
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Name": ["Asha", "Ravi", "Meera"],
    "Age": [25, 30, 22],
    "City": ["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune"]
})
print(df[df["Age"] > 24])
print(df.sort_values("Age"))
blocks.output:
Name  Age    City
0  Asha   25  Mumbai
1  Ravi   30  Delhi
   Name  Age    City
2  Meera   22    Pune
0  Asha   25  Mumbai
1  Ravi   30  Delhi

blocks.title: Reading a CSV file and summarising it
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("/tmp/marks.csv")
print(df)
print(df["Marks"].mean())

practice: Make a DataFrame of five students with names and marks, then print the average marks.
Filter the DataFrame to show only students with marks above 80.
Save your DataFrame to a CSV file with df.to_csv, then read it back with read_csv.
summary: Pandas turns tables of data into DataFrames you can filter, sort and summarise.
Install it with pip install pandas and import it as pd.
A DataFrame can be built from a dictionary or read from a CSV file.
Filtering uses a true/false condition; sorting uses sort_values.

tutorials.title: SciPy Tutorial
tutorials.intro: SciPy is the Python library for scientific computing. It builds on NumPy and adds ready-made tools for statistics, optimisation, signal processing and more.

blocks.text: NumPy handles arrays and basic maths. SciPy goes further: it solves equations, finds the best value of a function, works with statistics, and processes signals and images. Scientists and engineers use it when a problem needs more than plain arithmetic. SciPy is built on top of NumPy, so you normally use the two together. Install SciPy with pip. It is a large package, so the install takes a little longer than NumPy. After installing, import the part you need, such as scipy.stats for statistics or scipy.optimize for optimisation. SciPy is not installed in this learning environment, so the examples below show the standard output you get when you run them on a machine where SciPy is installed.
Installing SciPy

blocks.title: Installing SciPy
blocks.code: pip install scipy

blocks.text: Constants and simple maths

The scipy.constants module holds physical and mathematical constants, so you never have to type them from memory. The pi constant below is the same value Python gives you from the math module, but SciPy also holds constants like the speed of light and the golden ratio in one place. The stats module has functions for describing data and testing ideas about it. The describe function returns the count, the smallest and largest values, the mean, and more, all in one call. The example below describes five numbers. Its output is the standard output for that code. The optimize module finds the input that makes a function smallest or largest. The minimize_scalar function takes a function and searches for its lowest point. The function below is smallest when x is 3, so the answer is 3. Its output is the standard output for that code. Do not install SciPy just to use one constant. For small jobs, NumPy and the math module are enough. Reach for SciPy when you need statistics, optimisation or signal work.

blocks.title: A constant from SciPy
blocks.code:
from scipy import constants

print(constants.pi)

blocks.title: Describing data with scipy.stats
blocks.code:
from scipy import stats

result = stats.describe([2, 4, 6, 8, 10])
print(result.nobs)
print(result.mean)

blocks.title: Finding the minimum of a function
blocks.code:
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar

result = minimize_scalar(lambda x: (x - 3) ** 2)
print(result.x)

items: scipy.stats covers statistics: describing data and testing hypotheses.
scipy.optimize covers finding minimums and solving equations.
scipy.signal covers filtering and analysing signals.
scipy.integrate covers numerical integration of functions.

practice: Install SciPy and print constants.golden to see the golden ratio.
Use stats.describe on the list [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and read the mean and variance.
Use minimize_scalar to find the minimum of the function (x + 2) squared.
summary: SciPy adds scientific tools on top of NumPy: statistics, optimisation and more.
Install it with pip install scipy.
Import only the part you need, like scipy.stats or scipy.optimize.
For small jobs, NumPy and math are usually enough.

tutorials.title: Django Tutorial
tutorials.intro: Django is the Python framework for building websites. It handles web addresses, pages, forms and databases for you, so you can focus on what your site does.

blocks.text: A website needs many pieces: pages to show, addresses to route, forms to accept, and a database to store data. Django gives you all of these in one framework, with a fixed structure that keeps large projects organised. It follows the model, view and template pattern: models describe your data, views hold your logic, and templates hold your pages. Install Django with pip. Django is not installed in this learning environment, so the examples below show the standard output you get when you run them on a machine where Django is installed. After installing, the django-admin command becomes available on your computer.
Installing Django

blocks.title: Installing Django
blocks.code: pip install django

blocks.text: Starting a project

The startproject command creates a new Django project folder with all the files Django needs. Replace mysite with the name of your own project. Inside the project, the startapp command creates an app, which is one feature of your site, like a blog or a shop. A view is a Python function that takes a request and returns a response. This view returns a short piece of text. To see it in a browser, you connect the view to a web address in the urls.py file, then start the development server. The runserver command starts a small web server on your own computer for testing. Django prints the address where your site is running, and you open that address in your browser. The server reloads itself when you change your code, so you can see your edits at once. Never use runserver for a real public site; it is for development only. Django is a big framework. Learn it one piece at a time: first a view and a page, then a model and a form, then the admin site.

blocks.title: Creating a project and an app
blocks.code:
django-admin startproject mysite
cd mysite
python manage.py startapp blog

blocks.title: A view that returns Hello, Django
Starting the development server
blocks.code: python manage.py runserver

items: Models describe your data and Django builds the database tables for you.
Views hold the logic: what happens when someone visits a page.
Templates hold the HTML pages your visitors see.
The admin site is built in: you get a ready-made dashboard for your data.

practice: Install Django and create a project named mysite with django-admin startproject.
Add a view that returns your name, connect it to an address in urls.py, and run the server.
Create an app inside your project and open the built-in admin site at /admin.
summary: Django is a full framework for building websites with Python.
Install it with pip install django.
A project holds apps; each app has models, views and templates.
The development server runs on your own computer for testing only.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Intro
tutorials.intro: Matplotlib is the most used Python library for drawing charts. It turns lists of numbers into line charts, bar charts, scatter plots, and more.

blocks.text: What is Matplotlib?

Matplotlib draws charts from your data. You give it lists of numbers, and it draws the picture. A chart made with Matplotlib is called a figure, and inside a figure you draw one or more plots, each with data points, axes, and optional labels, a title, and a legend. It works with plain Python lists and with NumPy arrays, and it is often used together with NumPy and pandas: NumPy supplies the numbers, pandas supplies the table, and Matplotlib draws the picture.
Check that Matplotlib is installed
The first step is to check the installed version. Import the library and print its version number.

blocks.title: Check the version
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
print(matplotlib.__version__)

blocks.text: The line matplotlib.use("Agg") picks a backend that draws charts without opening a window. Use it at the top of every script that runs without a screen, for example on a server or in an online editor.
Your first chart

The next example plots the numbers 1, 4, 9, and 16 against 1, 2, 3, and 4. The result is a line that rises steeply, because the y values grow faster than the x values. The chart is saved to a file instead of shown on screen.

blocks.title: Plot four points
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = [1, 2, 3, 4]
y = [1, 4, 9, 16]
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_intro.png")
print("Saved chart with 4 points")

blocks.text: The plt.plot() call draws the line, and plt.savefig() writes the chart to a PNG file. Open the file to see the chart: a single rising line with points at (1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 9), and (4, 16).

practice: Print the Matplotlib version installed on your machine.
Plot the points x = [0, 1, 2, 3] and y = [0, 2, 4, 6] and save the chart to a file.
Change the y values to [0, 1, 8, 27] and describe how the shape of the line changes.
summary: Matplotlib turns lists of numbers into charts.
matplotlib.use("Agg") lets charts run without a screen.
plt.plot(x, y) draws a line chart from two lists.
plt.savefig() writes the chart to an image file.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Get Started
tutorials.intro: This tutorial shows how to install Matplotlib and run your first chart. If Matplotlib is already installed, you can skip straight to the example.

blocks.text: Install Matplotlib

Install Matplotlib with pip, the Python package installer. Run this command in your terminal. You only need to do it once. If you use Anaconda, Matplotlib is usually already installed. If not, run conda install matplotlib in the Anaconda terminal instead. The exact version numbers in the output depend on when you install it; the last line is the one that matters.

blocks.code: pip install matplotlib
blocks.title: Install with pip
blocks.output: Successfully installed contourpy-1.4.0 cycler-0.12.1 fonttools-4.68.0 kiwisolver-1.5.1 matplotlib-3.11.2 numpy-2.5.5 packaging-26.3 pillow-13.0.0 pyparsing-3.3.3 python-dateutil-4.0.0 tzdata-2026.6

blocks.text: Check the install
After installing, check that Python can import the library and print its version. If this runs without an error, the install worked.

blocks.title: Verify the install
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
print(matplotlib.__version__)
print("Matplotlib is ready to use")

blocks.text: Draw your first chart

Most Matplotlib work starts with importing matplotlib.pyplot, usually shortened to plt. The example below plots y = x squared for x values 0 to 3, so the line curves upward. It saves the chart to a file and prints the data it plotted.

blocks.title: First line chart
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = [0, 1, 2, 3]
y = [0, 1, 4, 9]
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_start.png")
print(x)
print(y)

blocks.text: Three functions do most of the work in every Matplotlib script: plt.plot() draws the data, plt.savefig() or plt.show() displays it, and plt.close() frees the figure when you are done. Use plt.show() when you run code on your own computer with a screen, and plt.savefig() when you run code on a server or in an online editor without a screen.

practice: Run pip install matplotlib in your terminal, then print the version to confirm it worked.
Plot x = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] and y = [0, 3, 6, 9, 12] and save the chart.
Try plt.show() instead of plt.savefig() and see what happens on your machine.
summary: Install Matplotlib with pip install matplotlib.
Import it as matplotlib.pyplot, usually shortened to plt.
plt.plot(x, y) draws the chart from two lists.
plt.savefig() saves the chart; plt.show() displays it on screen.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Pyplot
tutorials.intro: Pyplot is the part of Matplotlib you use most. It gives you simple functions like plot(), title(), and show() that build a chart step by step.

blocks.text: What is pyplot?

Pyplot is a collection of functions that make Matplotlib easy to use. Each function changes the current figure: plot() adds a line, title() adds a title, xlabel() labels an axis. You call them one after another, and the chart grows. The usual import is import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, a convention used in almost all Matplotlib examples, so keep it.
Plot a line
The plot() function takes x values and y values and draws a line through the points. This example plots three points on a straight diagonal line and then reads the data back from the line object.

blocks.title: Plot with pyplot
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

line, = plt.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])
print(list(line.get_xdata()))
print(list(line.get_ydata()))

blocks.text: The line object returned by plot() stores the data you plotted. The get_xdata() and get_ydata() methods read that data back, which is handy when you want to check what a chart contains.
Add a title
A chart without a title is hard to read. The title() function adds a heading above the chart. This example plots four sales numbers and titles the chart Sales in January.

blocks.title: Add a chart title
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [10, 20, 25, 30])
plt.title("Sales in January")
print(plt.gca().get_title())

blocks.text: The gca() function means get current axes. It returns the plot you are working on, so get_title() reads the title you just set. Pyplot keeps track of the current figure and the current axes for you, which is why you can call plt.plot() and plt.title() without naming a figure.

practice: Plot the points (0, 0), (1, 5), (2, 10) and give the chart a title.
Plot two lines on the same chart by calling plt.plot() twice before saving.
Read the title back with plt.gca().get_title() and print it.
summary: Pyplot is the simple function interface to Matplotlib.
Import it as import matplotlib.pyplot as plt.
plt.plot(x, y) draws a line through the given points.
plt.title() adds a heading above the chart.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Plotting
tutorials.intro: Plotting means drawing data as a chart. This tutorial covers the basics: plotting x and y values, and what happens when you give only y values.

blocks.text: Plot x against y
The plot() function takes two lists: xpoints for the horizontal axis and ypoints for the vertical axis. It draws a line through each pair of values, in order.

blocks.title: Plot x and y
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

xpoints = [1, 2, 6, 8]
ypoints = [3, 8, 1, 10]
plt.plot(xpoints, ypoints)
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_plot.png")
print(xpoints)
print(ypoints)

blocks.text: The line connects the points (1, 3), (2, 8), (6, 1), and (8, 10). It goes up, then drops sharply, then rises again. The shape of the line tells the story of the data at a glance.
Plot only y values
If you pass only one list, Matplotlib uses it as the y values and uses 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on as the x values. This is useful when your data is just a sequence of measurements in order.

blocks.title: Plot y values only
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

line, = plt.plot([3, 8, 1, 10])
print(list(line.get_xdata()))
print(list(line.get_ydata()))

blocks.text: The x values are filled in automatically as 0, 1, 2, and 3. The points are (0, 3), (1, 8), (2, 1), and (3, 10), the same shape as before but starting at x = 0.
The two lists must have the same length. If x has 4 values and y has 3, plot() raises an error instead of drawing anything.
Give x and y clear variable names like days and sales, not xpoints and ypoints, when the data means something real. It makes the code much easier to read later.

practice: Plot x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] against y = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] and save the chart.
Plot only the list [5, 3, 9, 2, 7] and print the automatic x values.
Plot the same data twice: once with x values and once without, and compare the two charts.
summary: plt.plot(x, y) draws a line through pairs of values.
With only one list, x defaults to 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on.
The line connects the points in the order you give them.
The x and y lists must have the same length.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Markers
tutorials.intro: A marker is the symbol drawn at each data point. By default a line chart shows only the line, but markers make the actual data points easy to see.

blocks.text: What is a marker?

A marker is a small shape drawn at every data point: a circle, a square, a star, or many other shapes. Lines show the trend, markers show where the real measurements are. Pass marker="o" to plot() to draw a circle at each point, so the chart becomes a rising line with four visible circles at the data points.

blocks.title: Circle markers
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

line, = plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16], marker="o")
print(line.get_marker())

blocks.text: Change the marker size
The ms keyword sets the marker size in points. The default size is 6. This example uses size 12, so the circles are twice as large and stand out clearly.

blocks.title: Bigger markers
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

line, = plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16], marker="o", ms=12)
print(line.get_marker())
print(line.get_markersize())

blocks.text: Other marker shapes

items: "o" draws a circle.
"s" draws a square.
"*" draws a star.
"^" draws an upward triangle.
"D" draws a diamond.
"." draws a tiny point.

blocks.text: You can also combine the marker, line style, and color in one short string. For example, "o:r" means circle markers, a dotted line, and the color red. This is called the format string. Use markers when the exact data points matter, for example in a science experiment, and use a plain line when only the overall trend matters.

practice: Plot [1, 2, 3, 4] against [2, 3, 5, 7] with square markers.
Plot the same data with star markers of size 15.
Try the format string "s--b" and work out what each character means.
summary: Markers are symbols drawn at each data point.
marker="o" draws circles; other letters draw other shapes.
ms sets the marker size in points.
A format string like "o:r" combines marker, line, and color.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Line
tutorials.intro: The line connects your data points. You can change its style, its color, and its width to make the chart clearer or to tell two lines apart.

blocks.text: Line styles

The linestyle keyword changes how the line looks. The common choices are solid, dotted, dashed, and dashdot. A dotted line is useful when you want a line to look lighter or less dominant than a solid one.

blocks.title: Dotted line
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

line, = plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16], linestyle="dotted")
print(line.get_linestyle())

blocks.text: Matplotlib stores the dotted style as the short code ":". The other short codes are "-" for solid, "--" for dashed, and "-." for dashdot. You can use either the full word or the short code.
Line color and width
The color keyword sets the line color, and linewidth sets its thickness in points. This example draws a thick red line, which stands out strongly against the white background.

blocks.title: Red thick line
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

line, = plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16], color="r", linewidth=3)
print(line.get_color())
print(line.get_linewidth())

blocks.text: Common colors

items: "r" is red, "g" is green, "b" is blue.
"c" is cyan, "m" is magenta, "y" is yellow.
"k" is black, "w" is white.
You can also use full color names like "red" or "hotpink".

blocks.text: When you plot two lines on one chart, give them different colors and different line styles. Then a reader can tell them apart even in a black and white printout.

practice: Plot a dashed green line through [1, 2, 3, 4] and [1, 4, 9, 16].
Plot two lines on one chart: a solid blue line and a dotted red line.
Draw a line with linewidth 5 and describe how it looks compared to the default width.
summary: linestyle changes the line: solid, dotted, dashed, or dashdot.
color sets the line color; single letters like "r" are shortcuts.
linewidth sets the thickness in points.
Different colors and styles help readers tell lines apart.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Labels
tutorials.intro: Labels explain what a chart shows. The title names the chart, and the axis labels explain what the numbers on each axis mean.

blocks.text: Why labels matter
A chart without labels is a puzzle. The reader can see a line going up, but cannot tell what is being measured. A title and two axis labels turn the same chart into a clear message.
Add a title and axis labels

The title() function adds a heading, xlabel() labels the horizontal axis, and ylabel() labels the vertical axis. This example charts test scores against hours studied, so each label says exactly what its axis measures.

blocks.title: Title and axis labels
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16])
plt.xlabel("Hours studied")
plt.ylabel("Test score")
plt.title("Study time and scores")
print(plt.gca().get_xlabel())
print(plt.gca().get_ylabel())
print(plt.gca().get_title())
blocks.output:
Hours studied
Test score
Study time and scores

blocks.text: Style the title
The fontdict keyword lets you style the title text. You can set the font family, the size, and the color. This example uses a serif font at size 15.

blocks.title: Styled title
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16])
plt.title("Study time and scores", fontdict={"family": "serif", "size": 15})
print(plt.gca().get_title())
print(plt.gca().title.get_fontsize())

blocks.text: You can style the axis labels the same way. Pass fontdict to xlabel() or ylabel() with the family, size, and color you want.
Keep labels short and plain. "Hours studied" is better than "Number of hours spent studying for the test". The reader should understand each label in one second.

practice: Plot monthly rainfall and label both axes and the title.
Make the title size 20 and print the font size to confirm it.
Change the x label color to red using fontdict and save the chart.
summary: plt.title() names the chart.
plt.xlabel() and plt.ylabel() explain the axes.
fontdict styles the text with family, size, and color.
Good labels let a reader understand the chart in seconds.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Grid
tutorials.intro: Grid lines are faint lines that run across the chart behind the data. They help the reader read exact values off the axes.

blocks.text: What is a grid?

A grid is a set of horizontal and vertical lines lined up with the tick marks on the axes. It turns the empty space of a chart into a sheet of graph paper, so the eye can follow a point across to its value on an axis. Call plt.grid() to draw grid lines on both axes, as in the example below, which plots four points and adds a grid.

blocks.title: Grid on both axes
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16])
plt.grid()
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_grid.png")
print("Grid lines are on")

blocks.text: Grid on one axis only

The axis keyword limits the grid to one direction. Use axis="x" for vertical lines only, or axis="y" for horizontal lines only. Horizontal lines are usually the most useful, because most charts are read by looking across to the y values.
Style the grid lines
Grid lines can be styled like any other line. This example makes them green, dashed, and thin, so they guide the eye without competing with the data line.

blocks.title: Styled grid
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16])
plt.grid(color="green", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.5)
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_grid2.png")
print("Grid lines are green and dashed")
blocks.output: Grid lines are green and dashed

blocks.text: The color, linestyle, and linewidth keywords work the same way here as they do for plot(). Keep grid lines light and thin: they are helpers, not the main content. Turn the grid off again with plt.grid(False), which is useful when you draw a chart that should look clean, like a pie chart or a presentation slide.

practice: Plot [1, 2, 3, 4] against [10, 20, 15, 25] and add a grid.
Add a grid on the y-axis only and save the chart.
Style the grid with a light grey color and a dotted line, then compare it with the default grid.
summary: plt.grid() draws grid lines lined up with the tick marks.
axis="x" or axis="y" limits the grid to one direction.
Grid lines take color, linestyle, and linewidth like other lines.
Keep grid lines faint so the data stays the focus.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Subplot
tutorials.intro: A subplot is one small chart inside a bigger figure. Subplots let you show several related charts side by side so the reader can compare them.

blocks.text: What is a subplot?
A figure can hold more than one plot. Each plot sits in its own cell of a grid, like tiles on a wall. For example, a figure with 1 row and 2 columns holds two charts next to each other.
Two charts side by side
The subplot() function takes three numbers: rows, columns, and the position of the plot you are about to draw. This example draws a rising line on the left and a falling line on the right.

blocks.title: Two subplots
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])
plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.plot([1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1])
print(len(plt.gcf().get_axes()))

blocks.text: The call subplot(1, 2, 1) selects the first cell of a 1 by 2 grid, and subplot(1, 2, 2) selects the second. Each plot() call draws into whichever cell is currently selected.
The subplots() shortcut

The subplots() function creates the figure and all its axes in one call and returns them as a grid. This example makes a 2 by 2 grid, draws in the top left and bottom right cells, and gives each chart a title.

blocks.title: Four subplots at once
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2)
axes[0, 0].plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])
axes[0, 0].set_title("Top left")
axes[1, 1].plot([1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1])
axes[1, 1].set_title("Bottom right")
print(len(fig.axes))
print(axes[0, 0].get_title())
print(axes[1, 1].get_title())

blocks.text: With subplots() you address each cell by its row and column, like axes[0, 0] for the top left. This is clearer than subplot() when a figure has many cells. Give the figure a title for the whole page with fig.suptitle(), while each subplot keeps its own small title as well.

practice: Draw two subplots: a rising line on the left and a falling line on the right.
Make a 2 by 2 grid with subplots() and draw a different line in each cell.
Add a figure title with fig.suptitle() and save the chart.
summary: Subplots are small charts arranged in a grid inside one figure.
plt.subplot(rows, columns, position) selects one cell to draw in.
plt.subplots(rows, columns) creates the figure and all axes at once.
Address each cell by row and column, like axes[0, 0].

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Scatter
tutorials.intro: A scatter plot draws one dot per data point, with no connecting line. It is the best chart for asking whether two things are related.

blocks.text: What is a scatter plot?

A scatter plot takes two lists, x and y, and draws a dot at each pair of values. Because there is no line, the reader sees the raw pattern: dots that rise together, dots that fall, or dots with no pattern at all.
Draw a scatter plot

The scatter() function draws the dots. This example plots ten pairs of numbers. The dots spread across the chart with no clear upward or downward trend, which suggests the two numbers are not strongly related.

blocks.title: Scatter plot
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = [5, 7, 8, 7, 2, 17, 2, 9, 4, 11]
y = [99, 86, 87, 88, 111, 86, 103, 87, 94, 78]
plt.scatter(x, y)
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_scatter.png")
print(len(x))
print("points plotted")

blocks.text: Sizes and colors

Every dot can have its own size and color. The s keyword takes a list of sizes, and the c keyword takes a list of colors. This lets one chart show three things at once: the x value, the y value, and a third value shown by size or color.

blocks.title: Sizes and colors
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = [5, 7, 8, 7, 2]
y = [99, 86, 87, 88, 111]
sizes = [100, 200, 300, 400, 500]
colors = ["red", "green", "blue", "orange", "purple"]
plt.scatter(x, y, s=sizes, c=colors)
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_scatter2.png")
print(sizes)
print(colors)

blocks.text: The dots grow from size 100 to size 500 across the chart, and each dot has a different color. The size and color lists must match the length of the x and y lists.
Use the alpha keyword to make dots see-through, for example alpha=0.5. Overlapping dots then look darker, which shows where many points pile up.

practice: Scatter-plot study hours against test scores for five students.
Give each dot a size from a third list, for example the number of books each student read.
Color the dots by group, for example red for one class and blue for another.
summary: plt.scatter(x, y) draws one dot per pair of values.
Scatter plots show whether two variables move together.
s sets the dot sizes and c sets the dot colors.
Sizes and colors can show a third value on the same chart.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Bars
tutorials.intro: A bar chart draws one rectangle per category. The length of each bar shows its value, which makes comparisons between categories easy at a glance.

blocks.text: What is a bar chart?
A bar chart compares values across categories. Each category gets a bar, and taller bars mean larger values. Bar charts work best when the categories have names, like products, months, or teams.
Draw vertical bars
The bar() function takes a list of category names and a list of values. This example charts four categories, A to D. Category B is the tallest at 8, and category C is the shortest at 1.

blocks.title: Vertical bar chart
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
y = [3, 8, 1, 10]
bars = plt.bar(x, y)
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_bar.png")
print(len(bars))
print("bars drawn")

blocks.text: Draw horizontal bars

The barh() function draws the bars sideways. Horizontal bars are better when the category names are long, because there is more room to read them. This example draws the same four values as green horizontal bars.

blocks.title: Horizontal bar chart
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
y = [3, 8, 1, 10]
bars = plt.barh(x, y, color="green")
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_barh.png")
print(len(bars))
print(bars[0].get_width())

blocks.text: The first bar belongs to category A and has a width of 3, which matches the first value in the list. Each bar object stores its own size, so you can read values back from the chart.
Use the width keyword to make vertical bars thinner or thicker. A width of 0.5 leaves clear gaps between bars, which usually looks cleaner than bars that touch.

practice: Draw a bar chart of the marks of four students in a test.
Draw the same chart horizontally with barh() and color the bars orange.
Add a title and label the y-axis "Marks" on your chart.
summary: plt.bar(x, y) draws vertical bars, one per category.
plt.barh(x, y) draws horizontal bars.
The height or length of each bar shows its value.
Horizontal bars suit long category names.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Histograms
tutorials.intro: A histogram shows how numbers are spread out. It groups values into bins and draws one bar per bin, so you can see where most values fall.

blocks.text: What is a histogram?

A histogram answers a simple question: how are my numbers distributed? It splits the range of values into equal groups called bins, counts how many values fall in each bin, and draws a bar for each count. Tall bars show where values pile up.
Draw a histogram
The hist() function takes a list of numbers and a number of bins. This example uses the ages of twelve people, split into five bins. The counts show most people are in the younger bins.

blocks.title: Histogram of ages
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ages = [22, 25, 25, 27, 30, 31, 31, 33, 35, 40, 42, 45]
n, bins, patches = plt.hist(ages, bins=5)
print([int(v) for v in n])

blocks.text: The hist() function returns three things: n, the counts in each bin; bins, the edges of the bins; and patches, the bar objects. The counts add up to 12, the number of ages in the list.
Change the number of bins
More bins give a finer picture, fewer bins give a rougher one. With ten bins the same twelve ages spread out into ten thin bars, which shows the gaps between values more clearly.

blocks.title: Ten bins
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ages = [22, 25, 25, 27, 30, 31, 31, 33, 35, 40, 42, 45]
n, bins, patches = plt.hist(ages, bins=10)
print(len(n))
print("bins in the histogram")

blocks.text: A histogram is not a bar chart. In a bar chart each bar is a category. In a histogram each bar is a range of numbers, and the bars touch each other because the ranges are next to each other.

practice: Make a histogram of twenty test scores with 5 bins.
Redraw it with 10 bins and describe how the picture changes.
Print the bin counts and check that they add up to the number of values.
summary: plt.hist(values, bins=n) groups numbers into bins and counts them.
Each bar shows how many values fall in one range.
More bins give a finer picture; fewer bins give a rougher one.
hist() returns the counts, the bin edges, and the bar objects.

tutorials.title: Matplotlib Pie Charts
tutorials.intro: A pie chart shows parts of a whole as slices of a circle. Each slice is sized by its share of the total, which makes proportions easy to see.

blocks.text: What is a pie chart?
A pie chart turns numbers into slices of a circle. A value that is half the total gets half the circle. Pie charts work well when you want to show shares, like the share of each fruit sold in a shop.
Draw a pie chart
The pie() function takes a list of values. This example splits a total of 100 into four slices of 35, 25, 25, and 15. The biggest slice takes just over a third of the circle.

blocks.title: Simple pie chart
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sizes = [35, 25, 25, 15]
plt.pie(sizes)
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_pie.png")
print(sum(sizes))

blocks.text: Add labels and pull out a slice

The labels keyword names each slice, and the explode keyword pulls one slice slightly away from the rest to draw attention to it. This example labels the four fruits and pulls the Apples slice out by 0.1.

blocks.title: Labels and explode
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

labels = ["Apples", "Bananas", "Cherries", "Dates"]
sizes = [35, 25, 25, 15]
explode = [0.1, 0, 0, 0]
plt.pie(sizes, labels=labels, explode=explode)
plt.savefig("/tmp/mpl_pie2.png")
print(labels)
print(sum(sizes))

blocks.text: The explode list has one number per slice. A value of 0.1 moves the slice out by a tenth of the radius, while 0 keeps the other slices in place.
Pie charts work best with a few slices, ideally five or fewer. With many slices the small ones become hard to read, and a bar chart is usually clearer.

practice: Draw a pie chart of how you spend a week: study, sleep, play, and other.
Add labels to each slice and explode the biggest slice.
Try seven slices and decide for yourself whether the chart is still easy to read.
summary: plt.pie(values) draws slices sized by their share of the total.
labels names each slice.
explode pulls a slice away from the circle to highlight it.
Pie charts suit a few slices; use a bar chart for many categories.

tutorials.title: Getting Started
tutorials.intro: Machine learning is a way to make computers learn from data instead of following fixed rules. In this section you will build small machine learning ideas yourself, using only NumPy and plain Python.

blocks.text: What Is Machine Learning?

A normal program follows instructions you write step by step. A machine learning program looks at examples and finds a pattern on its own. You give it data, it learns a rule from that data, and then it uses the rule on new data. For example, if you show a program the heights of 100 people, it can learn the average height. Then it can guess the height of a new person it has never seen. That guess is called a prediction.
What You Need

You only need Python and NumPy for this whole section. NumPy is a library for working with numbers and arrays. Every example here runs with NumPy alone, so you do not need to install any machine learning library.

blocks.title: Check NumPy and find an average
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.__version__)
data = np.array([3, 5, 7, 9])
print(data.mean())

blocks.text: The mean, or average, is the simplest kind of learning. The program looked at four numbers and found the single number that best sums them up. That is the whole idea in miniature: data in, a learned value out.
A Tiny Prediction
Here the average height of five people becomes a prediction for the next person. It is a rough guess, but it shows the pattern of all machine learning: learn from old data, predict new data.

blocks.title: Predict with an average
blocks.code:
heights = [150, 160, 170, 180, 190]
print(sum(heights) / len(heights))
print("Prediction for a new person:", sum(heights) / len(heights))

blocks.text: Every topic in this section follows the same shape: a small fixed dataset, a few lines of NumPy or plain Python, and a result you can check by hand.

practice: Create a NumPy array of your own five numbers and print its mean.
Change the heights list so it has 8 people and print the new average.
Predict the next value in the list [10, 20, 30, 40] using the average, then check how close your guess is.
summary: Machine learning finds patterns in data instead of following fixed rules.
A prediction is a guess a program makes about new data.
NumPy is all you need for every example in this section.
The average is the simplest learned value: data in, one number out.

tutorials.title: Mean Median Mode
tutorials.intro: Mean, median and mode are three ways to describe the middle of a dataset. They are the first numbers you compute before any real machine learning begins.

blocks.text: Mean: The Average
The mean is the sum of all values divided by how many values there are. It is the most common average, but one very large or very small value can pull it away from the rest of the data.
Median: The Middle Value

The median is the value in the middle when the data is sorted. If there are 13 values, the median is the 7th one. The median is not pushed around by extreme values, so it is safer when the data has outliers.
Mode: The Most Common Value

blocks.title: Mean, median and mode of car speeds
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from statistics import mode

speed = [99, 86, 87, 88, 111, 86, 103, 87, 94, 78, 77, 85, 86]
print(np.mean(speed))
print(np.median(speed))
print(mode(speed))

blocks.text: The mode is the value that appears most often. It is the only one of the three that works well with non-numeric data too, like the most common colour in a list. The mean is about 89.8, the median is 87, and the mode is 86 because 86 appears three times. The mean is higher than the median because the fast speed of 111 pulls it up.
Mode with a Counter

When you want the most common value and how many times it appears, use collections.Counter. It counts every value for you, and most_common(1) gives the winner. If two values tie for most common, statistics.mode returns the one it finds first. Counter.most_common shows you the counts, so a tie is easy to spot.

blocks.title: Find the mode with Counter
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from collections import Counter

scores = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4]
print(Counter(scores).most_common(1))
print(np.mean(scores))
print(np.median(scores))

practice: Take the list [4, 8, 6, 5, 3, 2, 8, 9, 2, 5] and print its mean, median and mode.
Add the value 100 to that list and see how much the mean moves compared with the median.
Use Counter on the list ['red', 'blue', 'red', 'green', 'red'] to find the most common colour.
summary: Mean is the sum divided by the count; it is sensitive to extreme values.
Median is the middle value after sorting; it resists outliers.
Mode is the most frequent value; it also works for text.
Compare all three to understand the shape of your data.

tutorials.title: Standard Deviation
tutorials.intro: Standard deviation tells you how spread out numbers are around their mean. A small value means the numbers are close together, and a large value means they are far apart.

blocks.text: Why the Mean Is Not Enough
Two groups can have the same mean but look very different. One group might have all values near 82, while the other ranges from 60 to 104. The mean hides that difference. Standard deviation shows it.
How It Is Calculated

First find the mean. Then find how far each value is from the mean, square those distances, and take their average. The square root of that average is the standard deviation. Squaring stops positive and negative distances from cancelling out.

blocks.title: Standard deviation of a small list
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

speed = [86, 87, 88, 86, 87, 85, 86]
print(np.std(speed))
print(np.std(speed, ddof=1))

blocks.text: The standard deviation is about 0.9, so the speeds sit close to their mean of 86.6. The second number uses ddof=1, which is the sample version of the formula. It divides by one less than the count, and it is slightly larger.
Same Mean, Different Spread

These two lists both average 82, but the second list is far more spread out. Its standard deviation is about 15.8, while the first list is only about 1.4. If you only looked at the mean, you would think the lists are the same.

blocks.title: Compare the spread of two lists
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

a = [80, 81, 82, 83, 84]
b = [60, 70, 82, 94, 104]
print(np.mean(a), np.std(a))
print(np.mean(b), np.std(b))

blocks.text: In machine learning, features with a large spread can dominate features with a small spread. That is why scaling, covered later, matters.

practice: Compute the standard deviation of [10, 12, 23, 23, 16, 23, 21, 16] and of the same list with 100 added.
Make two lists with the same mean but very different standard deviations.
Compute np.std with ddof=0 and ddof=1 on a list of 4 numbers and note the difference.
summary: Standard deviation measures how far values spread from the mean.
A small value means the data is tightly packed; a large value means it is spread out.
np.std uses ddof=0 by default; ddof=1 gives the sample version.
Always check the spread, not just the mean, before trusting a dataset.

tutorials.title: Percentile
tutorials.intro: A percentile tells you what percentage of the data falls below a given value. The 90th percentile is the value that 90 percent of the data is below.

blocks.text: What a Percentile Means

If your score is in the 90th percentile, you scored higher than 90 percent of the people. Percentiles turn a raw number into a position inside the whole group. They are used for exam results, income, growth charts, and more.
The Median Is a Percentile

The 50th percentile is the median: half the data is below it and half is above it. The 25th percentile is the first quartile, and the 75th percentile is the third quartile. Together they split the data into four equal parts.

blocks.title: Percentiles of a list of ages
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

ages = [5, 31, 43, 48, 50, 41, 7, 11, 15, 39, 80, 82, 32, 2, 8, 6, 25, 36, 27, 61, 31]
print(np.percentile(ages, 75))
print(np.percentile(ages, 90))
print(np.percentile(ages, 50))

blocks.text: The 75th percentile is 43, so three quarters of the ages are 43 or below. The 90th percentile is 61, and the median age is 31. NumPy sorts the data for you, so the input order does not matter.
Finding a Percentile by Hand

To find what percentile a value sits at, count how many values are below it, divide by the total count, and multiply by 100. Here 6 of the 10 ages are below 40, so 40 is at the 60th percentile of this small list.

blocks.title: What percentile is the value 40 at?
blocks.code:
ages = [5, 31, 43, 48, 50, 41, 7, 11, 15, 39]
below = sum(1 for a in ages if a < 40)
print(below / len(ages) * 100)

blocks.text: Percentiles are safer than raw values when data is skewed. A salary of 50,000 means little on its own, but the 80th percentile tells you it beats 80 percent of salaries.

practice: Find the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of [12, 15, 18, 22, 25, 30, 33, 40].
Work out what percentile the value 25 is at in that same list, by counting.
Take any list of 20 numbers and check that np.percentile(list, 50) equals np.median(list).
summary: A percentile is the percentage of data below a value.
The 50th percentile is the median; the 25th and 75th are the quartiles.
np.percentile(data, n) finds the nth percentile for you.
Percentiles describe position in a group, which raw values cannot.

tutorials.title: Data Distribution
tutorials.intro: A data distribution shows how values are spread across a range. Some values appear often and some rarely, and that shape tells you a lot before you build any model.

blocks.text: What a Distribution Is

A distribution is a picture of how often each value occurs. If you group ages into bins like 0 to 10, 10 to 20, and so on, and count how many people fall in each bin, you have a distribution. Tall bins mean common values, short bins mean rare ones.
Uniform Distribution

In a uniform distribution every value is equally likely. Rolling a fair die gives a uniform distribution, because each face has the same chance. With random numbers between 0 and 5, each of the five bins below holds roughly the same count.

blocks.title: Histogram of uniform random numbers
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(0)
x = np.random.uniform(0.0, 5.0, 250)
counts, edges = np.histogram(x, bins=5)
print(counts)
print(np.round(edges, 2))

blocks.text: The five bins hold 51, 48, 53, 55 and 43 values. They are close to equal, which is exactly what uniform means. The edges show where each bin starts and ends.
Normal Distribution

In a normal distribution most values sit near the middle and fewer sit at the edges. Heights of people follow this shape: most people are near average height, very tall and very short people are rare. The histogram below peaks in the middle bin.

blocks.title: Histogram of normal random numbers
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(0)
x = np.random.normal(5.0, 1.0, 1000)
print(x.mean())
print(x.std())
counts, edges = np.histogram(x, bins=5)
print(counts)

blocks.text: np.random.seed(0) fixes the random numbers, so you get the same result every time you run the code. Always set a seed when you want reproducible examples.

practice: Generate 500 uniform numbers between 0 and 10 and print a 5-bin histogram.
Generate 500 normal numbers with mean 100 and standard deviation 15, then print the counts in 5 bins.
Change the seed from 0 to 1 in the uniform example and see how the counts change slightly.
summary: A distribution shows how often each value occurs.
Uniform means every value is equally likely; normal means values cluster near the middle.
np.histogram counts values into bins for you.
Set a random seed so your examples are reproducible.

tutorials.title: Normal Data Distribution
tutorials.intro: The normal distribution, also called the bell curve, is the most famous shape in statistics. Many real measurements follow it, and many machine learning methods assume it.

blocks.text: The Bell Curve

A normal distribution is shaped like a bell: high in the middle and low at both ends. It is fully described by two numbers, the mean and the standard deviation. The mean sets the centre of the bell, and the standard deviation sets how wide it is.
Making Normal Data with NumPy
np.random.normal takes the mean, the standard deviation, and how many values you want. With 100,000 values, the sample mean and standard deviation land almost exactly on 5.0 and 1.0.

blocks.title: Generate normal data and check it
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(0)
x = np.random.normal(5.0, 1.0, 100000)
print(round(float(x.mean()), 2))
print(round(float(x.std()), 2))

blocks.text: The 68-95-99.7 Rule

In a normal distribution, about 68 percent of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95 percent within two, and about 99.7 percent within three. This rule lets you judge whether a value is normal or unusual at a glance.

blocks.title: Check the 68-95-99.7 rule
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(0)
x = np.random.normal(5.0, 1.0, 100000)
for n in (1, 2, 3):
    inside = np.sum(np.abs(x - 5.0) < n * 1.0) / len(x) * 100
    print(n, round(float(inside), 1))

blocks.text: The results are 68.6, 95.4 and 99.7 percent, matching the rule. So a value more than three standard deviations from the mean is very rare, and in real data it is often an error or an outlier worth checking.
Real data is rarely perfectly normal, but close enough is common. Heights, test scores and measurement errors are all roughly normal.

practice: Generate normal data with mean 170 and standard deviation 10, then check what share falls within 160 to 180.
Generate normal data with mean 0 and standard deviation 2, and verify the 68-95-99.7 rule again.
Take the list [100, 102, 98, 101, 99, 150] and use the mean and standard deviation to decide which value looks like an outlier.
summary: The normal distribution is a bell curve set by its mean and standard deviation.
np.random.normal(mean, std, count) generates normal data.
About 68, 95 and 99.7 percent of values fall within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations.
Values beyond 3 standard deviations are rare and often outliers.

tutorials.title: Scatter Plot
tutorials.intro: A scatter plot draws one dot for each pair of values, with one value on the x-axis and the other on the y-axis. The pattern of the dots shows whether the two values move together.

blocks.text: Reading a Scatter Plot

Each dot is one observation. If the dots rise from left to right, large x values go with large y values. If they fall, large x values go with small y values. If they form a shapeless cloud, the two values are probably unrelated.
Correlation: A Number for the Pattern

Correlation measures how strongly two values move together, on a scale from -1 to 1. A value near 1 means a strong rising pattern, near -1 means a strong falling pattern, and near 0 means no clear pattern. np.corrcoef computes it for you.

blocks.title: Correlation between car age and speed

blocks.text: The correlation is about -0.76. That is a strong negative relationship: older cars in this list tend to be slower. The two-year-old car going 111 pulls against the pattern, but the overall trend is still clear.
Positive and Negative Patterns

Study hours and exam marks rise together, so their correlation is close to 1. Temperature and ice-cream sales also rise together. But temperature and hot-drink sales fall together: as it gets hotter, fewer hot drinks are sold, so the correlation is negative.

blocks.title: A strong positive and a strong negative case
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

study = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8])
marks = np.array([45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 72, 78, 85])
print(np.corrcoef(study, marks)[0, 1])
temp = np.array([30, 32, 35, 38, 40])
sales = np.array([90, 80, 70, 55, 40])
print(np.corrcoef(temp, sales)[0, 1])

blocks.text: Correlation is not causation. Two things can move together because a third thing drives them both, like ice-cream sales and sunburns both rising in summer.

practice: Compute the correlation between [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]. What value do you expect?
Compute the correlation between shoe size and height for five made-up people.
Make two lists with almost no relationship and check that the correlation is near 0.
summary: A scatter plot shows one dot per pair of values.
Correlation runs from -1 to 1 and measures how two values move together.
np.corrcoef(x, y) computes the correlation.
Correlation shows a pattern, not a cause.

tutorials.title: Linear Regression
tutorials.intro: Linear regression fits a straight line through data points. The line predicts the y value for any x value, and it is the simplest real machine learning model.

blocks.text: The Idea

Imagine a scatter plot of car age against top speed. The dots roughly fall along a downward line. Linear regression finds the straight line that sits closest to all the dots. Once you have the line, you can predict the speed of a car of any age.
Slope and Intercept

A line has the form y = slope times x plus intercept. The slope says how much y changes when x grows by one. The intercept is where the line crosses the y-axis. np.polyfit with degree 1 finds both numbers for you.

blocks.title: Fit a line to car age and speed
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([5, 7, 8, 7, 2, 17, 2, 9, 4, 11, 12, 9, 6])
y = np.array([99, 86, 87, 88, 111, 86, 103, 87, 94, 78, 77, 85, 86])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
print(slope)
print(intercept)

blocks.text: The slope is about -1.75, so each extra year of age costs about 1.75 units of speed. The intercept is about 103.1, which is the predicted speed of a brand-new car, where age is zero.
Predicting and Measuring Fit

To predict, plug a new x into the line. The R-squared score tells you how well the line fits: 1 is perfect and 0 means the line is no better than guessing the average. Here it is about 0.58, so age explains a bit more than half of the variation in speed.

blocks.title: Predict for a 10-year-old car and score the fit
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([5, 7, 8, 7, 2, 17, 2, 9, 4, 11, 12, 9, 6])
y = np.array([99, 86, 87, 88, 111, 86, 103, 87, 94, 78, 77, 85, 86])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
print(slope * 10 + intercept)
pred = slope * x + intercept
ss_res = np.sum((y - pred) ** 2)
ss_tot = np.sum((y - np.mean(y)) ** 2)
print(1 - ss_res / ss_tot)

blocks.text: A line only works when the real relationship is roughly straight. If the dots curve, you need polynomial regression, which is the next topic.

practice: Fit a line to study hours [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and marks [45, 50, 55, 60, 65], then predict the marks for 6 hours.
Predict the speed of a 20-year-old car with the line above. Does the answer look sensible?
Compute R-squared for the study hours data and explain why it is close to 1.
summary: Linear regression fits a straight line through the data.
np.polyfit(x, y, 1) returns the slope and intercept.
Predict with y = slope times x plus intercept.
R-squared measures how much of the variation the line explains.

tutorials.title: Polynomial Regression
tutorials.intro: Polynomial regression fits a curve instead of a straight line. When the data bends, a curve follows it far better than any line can.

blocks.text: When a Line Is Not Enough

Some relationships are curved. A ball thrown in the air rises and then falls, and its height over time is a curve, not a line. A straight line through that data would miss badly at both ends and in the middle.
A Curve Is a Polynomial

A degree 2 polynomial has the form y = a times x squared plus b times x plus c. It draws a parabola, which can bend once. np.polyfit with degree 2 finds a, b and c for you, just like degree 1 finds a line.

blocks.title: Fit a curve to curved data
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
y = np.array([2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 37])
a, b, c = np.polyfit(x, y, 2)
print(round(a, 2), round(b, 2), round(c, 2))
print(round(a * 7 ** 2 + b * 7 + c, 2))

blocks.text: The fitted curve is y = x squared plus 1, which matches the data exactly: 1 squared plus 1 is 2, 2 squared plus 1 is 5, and so on. Predicting x = 7 gives 50, which is the true next value.
Line Versus Curve

A straight line through the same data predicts 40.7 for x = 7, which is far from the true value of 50. The curve gets it exactly right. The gap between the two predictions shows how much the shape of the model matters.

blocks.title: Compare a line and a curve on the same data
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
y = np.array([2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 37])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
print("Line predicts x=7 as:", slope * 7 + intercept)
a, b, c = np.polyfit(x, y, 2)
print("Curve predicts x=7 as:", round(a * 7 ** 2 + b * 7 + c, 2))
print("True value is 50")
blocks.output:
Line predicts x=7 as: 40.66666666666668
Curve predicts x=7 as: 50.0
True value is 50

blocks.text: A higher degree is not always better. A degree 10 curve can twist through every point of noisy data and still predict new points badly. That mistake is called overfitting.
