summary: Quick sort picks a pivot and splits the list into smaller and larger parts.
It sorts each part the same way, by recursion.
The pivot ends up in its final place after one split.
It is fast on average, but a bad pivot slows it down.
It is the fastest sort most programmers write by hand.

tutorials.title: Counting Sort
tutorials.intro: Counting sort sorts by counting how many times each value appears, then writing the values out in order. It is very fast, but only works when the values are small integers.

blocks.text: Count, then write out

Counting sort does not compare values with each other at all. It counts how many times each value appears, then writes the values back out in order, repeating each one as many times as it was counted. That makes it extremely fast when the values are small integers, such as exam marks from 0 to 100. It is the wrong tool when the values are huge, because the counting list would have to cover every value up to the largest one.

The function below first finds the largest value, then makes a counting list with one slot per value from 0 up to that largest value. It walks the input once to fill the counts, then walks the counts to build the sorted result. On [4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1] it returns [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 8].

blocks.title: Counting sort on a small list

blocks.text: Seeing the counts

The counts list is the heart of the method. For [4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1] the counts are [0, 1, 2, 2, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1]: zero appears 0 times, one appears once, two appears twice, three appears twice, four appears once, and eight appears once. Reading that list from left to right gives the sorted order directly. The same function also sorts the fixed list from the other sorting tutorials, [64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90], but note that it builds a counting list of 91 slots to do it.

blocks.title: The counts list, and the fixed list sorted
blocks.code:
nums = [4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1]
counts = [0] * (max(nums) + 1)
for value in nums:
    counts[value] += 1
print(counts)
print(counting_sort([64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90]))

items: It counts occurrences instead of comparing values.
It is fast when the values are small integers in a narrow range.
It needs a counting list as large as the biggest value, so huge values waste memory.
It is stable when written with a cumulative count, and handles duplicates naturally.

blocks.text: Counting sort needs non-negative integers. To sort negative numbers, shift every value up by the smallest value first, sort, then shift back.

summary: Counting sort counts how often each value appears.
It writes the values out in order, repeating each one by its count.
It is very fast for small integers in a narrow range.
It needs a counting list as large as the biggest value.
It does not compare values, so it only works on integers.

tutorials.title: Radix Sort
tutorials.intro: Radix sort sorts numbers one digit at a time, from the last digit to the first, using a stable counting sort for each digit place.

blocks.text: Sort by digits, not by values

Radix sort never compares two whole numbers. It sorts by the ones digit, then by the tens digit, then by the hundreds digit, and so on, until every digit has been handled. The trick is that each digit pass must be stable: numbers with the same digit keep the order they had before the pass. That is why each pass uses counting sort, which is stable. After the last pass, the whole list is sorted.

The code below has a helper that counting-sorts a list by one digit place, and a main function that calls it for place 1, then 10, then 100, until the largest value has no more digits. It prints the list after each pass, so you can watch the order settle: after the ones pass, [170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66] becomes [170, 90, 802, 2, 24, 45, 75, 66], and after the hundreds pass it is fully sorted.

blocks.title: Radix sort, printing after each digit pass
blocks.code:
def counting_by_digit(items, place):
    counts = [0] * 10
    output = [0] * len(items)
    for value in items:
        digit = (value // place) % 10
        counts[digit] += 1
    for i in range(1, 10):
        counts[i] += counts[i - 1]
    for value in reversed(items):
        digit = (value // place) % 10
        counts[digit] -= 1
        output[counts[digit]] = value
    return output


def radix_sort(items):
    arr = items[:]
    place = 1
    while max(arr) // place > 0:
        arr = counting_by_digit(arr, place)
        print("After place", place, ":", arr)
        place *= 10
    return arr


print(radix_sort([170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66]))

blocks.text: The same fixed list

Radix sort also handles the fixed list used by the other sorts in this section. The list [64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90] has only two digits, so it needs two passes: ones, then tens. After the ones pass the list is [90, 11, 12, 22, 64, 34, 25], and after the tens pass it is [11, 12, 22, 25, 34, 64, 90], the same sorted result as every other sort.

blocks.title: Radix sort on the fixed list

items: It sorts one digit at a time, from the last digit to the first.
Each digit pass must be stable, or later passes will undo earlier work.
It is fast for integers with few digits, such as years or roll numbers.
It needs extra memory for the counting and output lists.

blocks.text: This second example reuses radix_sort and counting_by_digit from the code block above. Run both blocks together in the editor.

Each digit pass uses a stable counting sort.

tutorials.title: Merge Sort
tutorials.intro: Merge sort splits a list in half again and again until each piece has one item, then merges the pieces back together in sorted order. It is fast and stable.

blocks.text: Split, then merge

Merge sort is another divide-and-conquer algorithm. Split the list in half. Split each half in half again, and keep going until every piece has one item, which is already sorted. Then merge the pieces back together: take the smaller front item from either piece, append it to the result, and repeat until both pieces are used up. Merging two sorted lists is easy, because you only ever need to compare their first items.

The function below splits with a middle index, sorts each half by calling itself, and merges the two sorted halves by walking through them with two pointers. When one half runs out, the rest of the other half is appended as it is. On the fixed list [64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90] it returns [11, 12, 22, 25, 34, 64, 90], the same result as the other sorts.

blocks.title: Merge sort on the fixed list
blocks.code:
def merge_sort(items):
    if len(items) <= 1:
        return items
    mid = len(items) // 2
    left = merge_sort(items[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(items[mid:])
    result = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result


print(merge_sort([64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90]))

blocks.text: Merging two sorted lists

The merge step is worth seeing on its own. Take two sorted lists, [11, 25, 64] and [12, 22, 34, 90]. Compare the fronts: 11 is smaller than 12, so take 11. Now compare 25 with 12, take 12, then compare 25 with 22, take 22, and so on. The merge function below does exactly that, and the result is the same fully sorted list. Merge sort is stable because it takes from the left list first when the two front values are equal.

blocks.title: Merging two sorted lists
blocks.code:
def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result


print(merge([11, 25, 64], [12, 22, 34, 90]))

items: Split the list in half until each piece has one item.
Merge sorted pieces by comparing only their front items.
It is stable: equal values keep their original order.
It always takes about the same time, even on sorted or reversed lists.
It needs extra memory for the merged results.

blocks.text: Merge sort is the safe default when you need a guaranteed fast, stable sort and can afford the extra memory.

tutorials.title: MySQL Get Started
tutorials.intro: MySQL is a popular database system, and Python can connect to it with the mysql-connector-python package. This tutorial shows you how to install the package and connect to a MySQL server.

blocks.text: What You Need First

To follow this section you need two things installed on your own computer. First, a MySQL server, which is the database program that stores your data. You can download MySQL Community Server for free from the MySQL website and install it, choosing a root password during setup. Second, the Python package that lets Python talk to MySQL. Without a running MySQL server, none of the code in this section can connect, so install MySQL before you go further.

blocks.title: Install the connector
blocks.code: pip install mysql-connector-python

blocks.text: The package is called mysql-connector-python, and it is the official MySQL driver for Python. Once it is installed, import it in your code as mysql.connector. The next step is to open a connection to your server. You pass the host, your username, and your password. On your own computer the host is usually localhost, which means this computer.

blocks.title: Connect to MySQL
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword"
)

print(mydb)

blocks.text: If the connection works, print(mydb) shows a connection object, and no error appears. If you see an access denied error, check your username and password. If you see a connection refused error, MySQL is probably not running, so start the MySQL server first. Keep the connection object in a variable such as mydb, because every later example uses it to run SQL statements.

items: MySQL is the database server that stores tables and rows.
mysql-connector-python is the Python package that connects to it.
Install it with pip install mysql-connector-python.
Connect with mysql.connector.connect and your host, user, and password.
A connection object means the login worked.

blocks.text: Never share your real MySQL password in code you publish. The examples here use yourusername and yourpassword as placeholders, so replace them with your own login details.
Test the connection on its own first. If this small program works, every example in this section will work too.

Write a program that connects to your MySQL server with your own username and password and prints the connection object.
Change the password in your program to a wrong one on purpose, run it, and read the error message so you recognise it later.
summary: MySQL is a database server, and Python reaches it through the mysql-connector-python package.
Install the package with pip install mysql-connector-python.
Connect with mysql.connector.connect, passing host, user, and password.
A printed connection object means the connection worked.
You need a running MySQL server and the right login details before any later example can run.

tutorials.title: MySQL Create Database
tutorials.intro: A database is a container that holds your tables. Before you can create a table, you need a database to put it in, and you create it with the CREATE DATABASE statement.

blocks.text: Creating a Database

In MySQL, a database is like a folder for tables. One database can hold many tables, and each table holds rows of data. In this section we will create a database called mydatabase and use it for every MySQL example that follows. You create a database by running a CREATE DATABASE statement through a cursor. A cursor is the object that sends SQL to the server and brings results back.

blocks.title: Create a database in SQL
blocks.code: CREATE DATABASE mydatabase;

blocks.text: The same statement works from Python. Create a cursor from your connection, call execute with the SQL, and the database is created on the server. You do not need a database in the connection itself to create one, so connect without naming a database first.

blocks.title: Create a database from Python
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
mycursor.execute("CREATE DATABASE mydatabase")
print("Database created.")

blocks.text: If you run the code twice, MySQL will complain that the database already exists. That is normal. You can avoid the error with CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS mydatabase, which creates the database only when it is missing. After creating it, check that it exists with SHOW DATABASES, which lists every database on the server.

blocks.title: List all databases
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
mycursor.execute("SHOW DATABASES")

for db in mycursor:
  print(db)

items: A database holds tables, and a table holds rows.
CREATE DATABASE makes a new database.
Use a cursor and execute to run SQL from Python.
SHOW DATABASES lists the databases on the server.
IF NOT EXISTS stops the error when the database already exists.

blocks.text: Create the database once, then connect with database set to mydatabase in later examples so your tables go into the right place.

summary: A database is a container for tables.
CREATE DATABASE mydatabase creates a database called mydatabase.
Run SQL from Python with a cursor and its execute method.
SHOW DATABASES lists every database on the server.
Use IF NOT EXISTS to avoid an error when the database already exists.

tutorials.title: MySQL Create Table
tutorials.intro: A table stores your data in rows and columns. This tutorial creates the customers table that every later MySQL example in this section uses.

blocks.text: The Customers Table

A table is made of columns, and each column has a name and a data type. Our customers table has three columns. The id column is an integer and the primary key, which means every row has a different id and MySQL can find a row by its id. The name column holds text up to 255 characters, and the address column holds text up to 255 characters. VARCHAR(255) means a text value of up to 255 characters, and INT means a whole number.

blocks.title: Create the table in SQL

blocks.text: AUTO_INCREMENT means MySQL fills in the id for you, starting at 1 and going up by one for each new row. PRIMARY KEY means the id is unique for every row. From Python, connect to the mydatabase database this time, because the table must live inside a database. Then run the same CREATE TABLE statement with a cursor.

blocks.title: Create the table from Python
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword",
  database="mydatabase"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
mycursor.execute("CREATE TABLE customers (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(255), address VARCHAR(255))")
print("Table created.")

blocks.text: To check that the table exists, use SHOW TABLES, which lists the tables in the current database. To see the columns, use DESCRIBE customers, which shows each column name, its type, and whether it can be empty. If you try to create the same table twice, MySQL reports that it already exists, so use IF NOT EXISTS when you want the code to be safe to run again.

blocks.title: Check the table

items: A table has columns, each with a name and a data type.
INT stores whole numbers and VARCHAR(255) stores short text.
PRIMARY KEY means every row has a unique id.
AUTO_INCREMENT makes MySQL number new rows for you.
SHOW TABLES lists tables, and DESCRIBE shows the columns.

blocks.text: This customers table is the shared example for the whole MySQL section. Every later tutorial uses the same three columns, so do not change them.

CREATE TABLE defines the columns for a new table.
INT is for whole numbers and VARCHAR(255) is for short text.
PRIMARY KEY keeps every row unique, and AUTO_INCREMENT numbers new rows.
Connect to a database first, then create the table inside it.

tutorials.title: MySQL Insert
tutorials.intro: INSERT adds new rows to a table. This tutorial fills the customers table with six customers that every later MySQL example uses.

blocks.text: Inserting One Row

The INSERT INTO statement adds a row to a table. You name the table and the columns, then give the values in the same order. You do not give an id here, because the id column is AUTO_INCREMENT and MySQL fills it in for you. The first row is John, who lives at Highway 21. Always use placeholders, written as %s, for the values in Python, and pass the real values as a second argument. This keeps your data safe and handles quotes in text correctly.

blocks.title: Insert one row
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword",
  database="mydatabase"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
sql = "INSERT INTO customers (name, address) VALUES (%s, %s)"
val = ("John", "Highway 21")
mycursor.execute(sql, val)

mydb.commit()
print(mycursor.rowcount, "record inserted.")

blocks.text: The commit call is important. MySQL waits until you commit before it saves the change for good. If you forget commit, the row is lost when the program ends. The rowcount attribute tells you how many rows were affected, which is 1 for a single insert. The new row gets id 1 automatically.
Inserting Many Rows at Once

To insert many rows, use executemany with a list of value pairs. This is faster than running execute six times. The code below adds the other five customers, so the table ends up with six rows in total. The ids are given by MySQL in order, from 1 to 6.

blocks.title: Insert many rows
blocks.code:
mycursor = mydb.cursor()
sql = "INSERT INTO customers (name, address) VALUES (%s, %s)"
val = [
  ("Peter", "Lowstreet 4"),
  ("Amy", "Apple st 652"),
  ("Hannah", "Mountain 21"),
  ("Michael", "Valley 345"),
  ("Sandy", "Ocean blvd 2")
]

mycursor.executemany(sql, val)
mydb.commit()
print(mycursor.rowcount, "records inserted.")

blocks.text: After both programs run, the customers table holds six rows. This is the fixed sample data for the whole MySQL section, so every result table in later tutorials comes from these rows. The last inserted id is available as mycursor.lastrowid, which is 6 after the second program.

blocks.title: The six customers
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM customers;
blocks.output:
id | name    | address
1  | John    | Highway 21
2  | Peter   | Lowstreet 4
3  | Amy     | Apple st 652
4  | Hannah  | Mountain 21
5  | Michael | Valley 345
6  | Sandy   | Ocean blvd 2

items: INSERT INTO adds rows to a table.
Use %s placeholders and pass values separately.
Call commit to save the change.
executemany inserts a list of rows in one go.
rowcount tells you how many rows were inserted.

summary: INSERT INTO adds new rows to a table.
Use %s placeholders and pass the values separately.
Call mydb.commit() to save the inserted rows.
executemany inserts many rows from a list of values.
The customers table now holds six rows, used by every later MySQL tutorial.

tutorials.title: MySQL Select
tutorials.intro: SELECT reads data from a table. This tutorial shows how to read all columns, pick single columns, and fetch the results in Python.

blocks.text: Reading All Columns

The SELECT statement reads rows from a table. The star means all columns, so SELECT star FROM customers returns every column of every row. In Python, run the query with a cursor, then call fetchall to get all the rows at once. Each row comes back as a tuple, in the order id, name, address.

blocks.title: Select all columns
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM customers;
blocks.output:
id | name    | address
1  | John    | Highway 21
2  | Peter   | Lowstreet 4
3  | Amy     | Apple st 652
4  | Hannah  | Mountain 21
5  | Michael | Valley 345
6  | Sandy   | Ocean blvd 2

blocks.title: Select all from Python
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword",
  database="mydatabase"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
mycursor.execute("SELECT * FROM customers")
result = mycursor.fetchall()

for row in result:
  print(row)

blocks.text: Reading Single Columns

You do not always need every column. Name the columns you want, separated by commas, and MySQL returns only those. This is faster and the output is easier to read. The example below asks for name and address only, so the id column is left out.

blocks.title: Select two columns
blocks.code: SELECT name, address FROM customers;
blocks.output:
name    | address
John    | Highway 21
Peter   | Lowstreet 4
Amy     | Apple st 652
Hannah  | Mountain 21
Michael | Valley 345
Sandy   | Ocean blvd 2

blocks.text: Use fetchone when you only need the first row, and fetchall when you need every row. If you loop over the cursor directly, you also get one row at a time, which is handy for very large tables. SELECT never changes the table, so it is always safe to run while you are learning.

items: SELECT reads rows from a table.
The star means all columns.
Name columns to read only the ones you need.
fetchall returns every row, and fetchone returns the first row.
Each row is a tuple in the order of the columns you asked for.

blocks.text: Ask for only the columns you need. It keeps the result small and makes your program faster.

practice: Select all customers from Python and print each row.
Select only the name column and print the six names.
Use fetchone to print just the first customer, then run the same query with fetchall.
summary: SELECT reads data from a table without changing it.
SELECT star returns every column, and naming columns returns only those.
Run the query with a cursor, then use fetchall or fetchone.
Each row comes back as a tuple in column order.
Asking for fewer columns keeps results small and fast.

tutorials.title: MySQL Where
tutorials.intro: WHERE filters rows so you only get the ones that match a condition. This tutorial shows exact matches, patterns, and safe values from Python.

blocks.text: Filtering with WHERE

SELECT on its own returns every row. WHERE adds a condition, and MySQL returns only the rows where the condition is true. The example below asks for the customer whose address is Mountain 21, and only Hannah matches, so only one row comes back. Text values go in single quotes in SQL.

blocks.title: One matching row
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE address = 'Mountain 21';

blocks.title: WHERE from Python
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword",
  database="mydatabase"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE address = %s"
val = ("Mountain 21",)
mycursor.execute(sql, val)
result = mycursor.fetchall()

for row in result:
  print(row)

blocks.text: Matching a Pattern with LIKE

The LIKE operator matches a pattern instead of an exact value. The percent sign means any characters, so S percent matches every name that starts with S, and percent a percent matches every name that contains the letter a. From the six customers, only Sandy starts with S, while Amy, Hannah, Michael, and Sandy all contain the letter a.

blocks.title: Names starting with S
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE 'S%';
blocks.output:
id | name  | address
6  | Sandy | Ocean blvd 2

blocks.title: Names containing the letter a
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '%a%';
blocks.output:
id | name    | address
3  | Amy     | Apple st 652
4  | Hannah  | Mountain 21
5  | Michael | Valley 345
6  | Sandy   | Ocean blvd 2

blocks.text: Always pass the value through a %s placeholder in Python instead of joining it into the SQL string yourself. That keeps the query safe and avoids errors when a value contains a quote. You can also combine conditions with AND and OR, for example WHERE name LIKE S percent AND address LIKE Ocean percent.

items: WHERE keeps only the rows where the condition is true.
Use = for an exact match and LIKE for a pattern.
The percent sign in LIKE means any characters.
Pass values with %s placeholders in Python.
AND and OR combine two or more conditions.

practice: Select the customer whose name is Amy and print the row.

Select customers whose name starts with P or whose address is Valley 345, using OR.
summary: WHERE filters rows to only the ones that match a condition.
Use = for exact matches and LIKE for patterns.
In LIKE, the percent sign stands for any characters.
Pass values with %s placeholders instead of building the SQL by hand.
Combine conditions with AND and OR.

tutorials.title: MySQL Order By
tutorials.intro: ORDER BY sorts the rows that a query returns. This tutorial sorts the customers by name, in both directions.

blocks.text: Sorting in Ascending Order

Rows in a table have no guaranteed order unless you ask for one. ORDER BY sorts the result by the column you name. By default the order is ascending, from A to Z for text and from small to large for numbers. The example below sorts the six customers by name, so Amy comes first and Sandy comes last.

blocks.title: Sort by name, A to Z
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY name;
blocks.output:
id | name    | address
3  | Amy     | Apple st 652
4  | Hannah  | Mountain 21
1  | John    | Highway 21
5  | Michael | Valley 345
2  | Peter   | Lowstreet 4
6  | Sandy   | Ocean blvd 2

blocks.title: Sort from Python
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword",
  database="mydatabase"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
mycursor.execute("SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY name")
result = mycursor.fetchall()

for row in result:
  print(row)

blocks.text: Sorting in Descending Order

Add DESC after the column name to sort in the opposite direction, from Z to A for text and from large to small for numbers. ASC means ascending and is the default, so you only need to write it when you want to be clear. You can also sort by more than one column, for example ORDER BY address, name, which sorts by address first and uses name to break ties.

blocks.title: Sort by name, Z to A
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY name DESC;
blocks.output:
id | name    | address
6  | Sandy   | Ocean blvd 2
2  | Peter   | Lowstreet 4
5  | Michael | Valley 345
1  | John    | Highway 21
4  | Hannah  | Mountain 21
3  | Amy     | Apple st 652

blocks.text: ORDER BY comes after WHERE in a query, so you can filter and sort in the same statement. For example, SELECT star FROM customers WHERE address LIKE percent Street percent ORDER BY name returns the matching rows already sorted. Sorting does not change the table, it only changes the order of the rows you get back.

The default order is ascending, A to Z or small to large.
DESC reverses the order to descending.
You can sort by more than one column.
ORDER BY comes after WHERE in a query.

blocks.text: Sort by the column the reader will scan, usually a name or a date, so the result is easy to read.

The default order is ascending, and DESC makes it descending.
Sorting works on text, numbers, and dates.
You can sort by more than one column at a time.
ORDER BY comes after WHERE and never changes the stored table.

tutorials.title: MySQL Delete
tutorials.intro: DELETE removes rows from a table. This tutorial deletes the extra customer Vicky, so the table returns to the six original customers.

blocks.text: Deleting One Row

The DELETE statement removes rows that match a WHERE condition. In the Insert tutorial you added a seventh customer, Vicky from Yellow Garden 2, as practice. This tutorial removes her, so the table is back to the six original customers. The condition WHERE name equals Vicky matches only her row, so only one row is deleted.

blocks.title: Delete Vicky in SQL
blocks.code: DELETE FROM customers WHERE name = 'Vicky';

blocks.title: Delete from Python
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword",
  database="mydatabase"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
sql = "DELETE FROM customers WHERE name = %s"
val = ("Vicky",)
mycursor.execute(sql, val)

mydb.commit()
print(mycursor.rowcount, "record(s) deleted")

blocks.text: Checking the Result

Like INSERT and UPDATE, DELETE needs a commit before the change is saved for good. The rowcount tells you how many rows were removed, which is 1 here. After the delete, a SELECT shows the six original customers again, with ids 1 to 6. Vicky, who had id 7, is gone, and MySQL will not reuse her id for the next insert.

blocks.title: The table after the delete
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM customers;
blocks.output:
id | name    | address
1  | John    | Highway 21
2  | Peter   | Lowstreet 4
3  | Amy     | Apple st 652
4  | Hannah  | Mountain 21
5  | Michael | Valley 345
6  | Sandy   | Ocean blvd 2

blocks.text: You can also delete with a wider condition, for example DELETE FROM customers WHERE address LIKE percent Street percent, which would remove every matching row. That is why the WHERE clause matters so much. Always check your condition with a SELECT first, using the same WHERE, so you can see exactly which rows will be deleted.

items: DELETE removes rows that match a WHERE condition.
Pass the value with a %s placeholder in Python.
Call commit to save the deletion.
rowcount tells you how many rows were removed.
Test the WHERE with SELECT first so you delete the right rows.

blocks.text: A DELETE without a WHERE removes every row in the table. The table itself stays, but it will be empty, so never run it by accident.

practice: Insert Vicky again, then delete her with a WHERE on her name and confirm the rowcount is 1.
Use a SELECT with the same WHERE before you delete, to see which rows would be removed.
Try deleting a customer who does not exist and check that the rowcount is 0.
summary: DELETE removes the rows that match a WHERE condition.
Use a %s placeholder for the value in Python.
Call mydb.commit() to save the deletion.
rowcount tells you how many rows were removed.
Always test the WHERE with SELECT first, and never run DELETE without a WHERE unless you mean to empty the table.

tutorials.title: MySQL Drop Table
tutorials.intro: DROP TABLE deletes a whole table, including all of its rows. This tutorial drops the customers table and shows how to check that it is gone.

blocks.text: Dropping a Table

DELETE removes rows, but DROP TABLE removes the table itself. The columns, the rows, and the table definition are all gone at once. There is no undo, so only drop a table when you are sure you do not need it. The statement is short: DROP TABLE followed by the table name. The example below drops the customers table from the mydatabase database.

blocks.title: Drop the table in SQL
blocks.code: DROP TABLE customers;

blocks.title: Drop the table from Python
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword",
  database="mydatabase"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
mycursor.execute("DROP TABLE customers")
print("Table dropped.")

blocks.text: Checking That It Is Gone

After the drop, SHOW TABLES returns an empty set, because mydatabase has no tables left. A SELECT from customers now fails with an error saying the table does not exist. That error is the proof that the drop worked. If you drop a table that does not exist, MySQL reports an error, so use DROP TABLE IF EXISTS customers when you want the code to run safely even if the table is already gone.

blocks.title: List tables after the drop

blocks.text: Dropping a table does not delete the database, and it does not delete other tables. Only the named table goes. Because the later tutorials still need the customers table, recreate it with the CREATE TABLE statement from the Create Table tutorial and insert the six customers again before you move on to Update.

items: DROP TABLE deletes a table and all of its rows.
There is no undo, so be sure before you drop.
SHOW TABLES shows an empty set after the drop.
IF EXISTS avoids an error when the table is already gone.
Dropping a table does not delete the database or other tables.

blocks.text: The customers table is dropped here on purpose, as the lesson. Recreate it with the six customers before the Update tutorial, or the later examples will have no table to work on.

practice: Create a table called old_customers, then drop it and confirm SHOW TABLES no longer lists it.
Drop a table that does not exist, read the error, then repeat with IF EXISTS.
Recreate the customers table and insert the six original customers, so later tutorials work.
summary: DROP TABLE deletes a whole table, rows and all.
There is no undo, so only drop a table you do not need.
SHOW TABLES returns an empty set once the table is gone.
Use IF EXISTS to avoid an error when the table is already missing.
Recreate the customers table with its six rows before the next tutorial.

tutorials.title: MySQL Update
tutorials.intro: UPDATE changes the values in rows that already exist. This tutorial changes John's address to Canyon 123, and later tutorials use that new address.

blocks.text: Updating One Row

The UPDATE statement changes values in rows that match a WHERE condition. First, recreate the customers table with the six original customers, because the previous tutorial dropped it. Then run the update below. It sets the address to Canyon 123 for the row where the name is John. Only one row matches, so only John's address changes and the other five customers stay the same.

blocks.title: Update John's address in SQL
blocks.code: UPDATE customers SET address = 'Canyon 123' WHERE name = 'John';

blocks.title: Update from Python
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword",
  database="mydatabase"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
sql = "UPDATE customers SET address = %s WHERE name = %s"
val = ("Canyon 123", "John")
mycursor.execute(sql, val)

mydb.commit()
print(mycursor.rowcount, "record(s) affected")

blocks.text: Checking the Result

As with INSERT and DELETE, you must call commit before the change is saved. The rowcount is 1, because one row was changed. A SELECT now shows John at Canyon 123, while Peter, Amy, Hannah, Michael, and Sandy keep their original addresses. From this tutorial onward, John's address is Canyon 123 in every MySQL result, so remember the change when you read later examples.

blocks.title: The table after the update
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM customers;
blocks.output:
id | name    | address
1  | John    | Canyon 123
2  | Peter   | Lowstreet 4
3  | Amy     | Apple st 652
4  | Hannah  | Mountain 21
5  | Michael | Valley 345
6  | Sandy   | Ocean blvd 2

blocks.text: You can set more than one column at a time, for example SET name equals James, address equals Canyon 123. You can also update several rows with one statement by using a wider WHERE, such as WHERE address LIKE percent Street percent. The same warning as DELETE applies: an UPDATE without a WHERE changes every row in the table, so test the WHERE with SELECT first.

items: UPDATE changes values in rows that match a WHERE condition.
SET names the columns and their new values.
Pass the new values with %s placeholders in Python.
Call commit to save the change.
An UPDATE without a WHERE changes every row, so test the WHERE first.

blocks.text: When only one row should change, use a condition that matches one row, such as the name or the id, and check the rowcount afterwards.

Update two columns at once by changing Sandy's name and address in one statement.
Update a customer who does not exist and check that the rowcount is 0.
summary: UPDATE changes values in rows that match a WHERE condition.
SET gives the new values for the columns you name.
Use %s placeholders and call commit to save the change.
John's address is now Canyon 123 in every later MySQL example.
Never run UPDATE without a WHERE unless you mean to change every row.

tutorials.title: MySQL Limit
tutorials.intro: LIMIT returns only a set number of rows. This tutorial takes the first three customers, and then skips rows with OFFSET.

blocks.text: Taking the First Rows

A table can hold thousands of rows, but you often want only a few. LIMIT sets the maximum number of rows a query returns. The example below asks for three rows, so MySQL returns the first three customers in id order: John, Peter, and Amy. Remember that John's address is now Canyon 123, after the change in the Update tutorial.

blocks.title: First three customers
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM customers LIMIT 3;
blocks.output:
id | name  | address
1  | John  | Canyon 123
2  | Peter | Lowstreet 4
3  | Amy   | Apple st 652

blocks.title: LIMIT from Python
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword",
  database="mydatabase"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
mycursor.execute("SELECT * FROM customers LIMIT 3")
result = mycursor.fetchall()

for row in result:
  print(row)

blocks.text: Skipping Rows with OFFSET

OFFSET skips a number of rows before LIMIT starts counting. LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1 skips the first row and returns the next two, which are Peter and Amy. This is how paging works: page one uses LIMIT 3 OFFSET 0, page two uses LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3, and so on. Combine LIMIT with ORDER BY when the order matters, because without ORDER BY the database may return rows in any order.

blocks.title: Skip one row, take two
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM customers LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1;
blocks.output:
id | name  | address
2  | Peter | Lowstreet 4
3  | Amy   | Apple st 652

blocks.text: In Python, fetchmany gives you the same control from the program side. After running a SELECT, mycursor.fetchmany(3) returns the first three rows, and a second call returns the next three. LIMIT is usually better, because the database sends fewer rows over the connection in the first place.

items: LIMIT sets the maximum number of rows returned.
OFFSET skips rows before LIMIT starts counting.
LIMIT and OFFSET together make paging possible.
Combine LIMIT with ORDER BY when the order matters.
fetchmany in Python returns a set number of rows from the result.

blocks.text: Use LIMIT while you are testing a query on a big table, so a mistake returns a few rows instead of a million.

Select two customers starting from the third row with LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2.
Select the last three customers by sorting by id in descending order with LIMIT 3.

OFFSET skips rows before LIMIT starts counting.
LIMIT and OFFSET together let you page through results.
Combine LIMIT with ORDER BY when the order of rows matters.
LIMIT 3 returns John, Peter, and Amy from the customers table.

tutorials.title: MySQL Join
tutorials.intro: JOIN combines rows from two tables that are related. This tutorial joins customers with an orders table to show who bought what.

blocks.text: Two Related Tables

Real databases split data across tables. The customers table holds people, and a second table called orders holds what they bought. Each order has a customerid that matches the id of the customer who placed it. This link is what makes a join possible. The orders table for this tutorial has five rows: John bought a Laptop and a Keyboard, Peter bought a Mouse, Hannah bought a Monitor, and Sandy bought Headphones. Amy and Michael have no orders. John's address is Canyon 123, after the Update tutorial.

blocks.title: Create and fill the orders table
blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  orderid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  customerid INT,
  product VARCHAR(255)
);

INSERT INTO orders (customerid, product) VALUES
  (1, 'Laptop'),
  (1, 'Keyboard'),
  (2, 'Mouse'),
  (4, 'Monitor'),
  (6, 'Headphones');

blocks.text: The Inner Join

An INNER JOIN returns only the rows that match in both tables. The ON part says how the tables connect: the customer id equals the order customerid. Because John has two orders, he appears twice, once for each product. Amy and Michael have no orders, so they do not appear at all. The result has five rows, one for each order.

blocks.title: Join customers and orders
blocks.code:
SELECT customers.name, orders.product
FROM customers
INNER JOIN orders
ON customers.id = orders.customerid;
blocks.output:
name   | product
John   | Laptop
John   | Keyboard
Peter  | Mouse
Hannah | Monitor
Sandy  | Headphones

blocks.title: The join from Python
blocks.code:
import mysql.connector

mydb = mysql.connector.connect(
  host="localhost",
  user="yourusername",
  password="yourpassword",
  database="mydatabase"
)

mycursor = mydb.cursor()
sql = "SELECT customers.name, orders.product FROM customers INNER JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customerid"
mycursor.execute(sql)
result = mycursor.fetchall()

for row in result:
  print(row)

blocks.text: Other joins keep more rows. A LEFT JOIN returns every customer, and shows an empty value for the product when a customer has no order, so Amy and Michael would appear with no product. A RIGHT JOIN does the same from the orders side. For most day-to-day questions, the inner join is the one you need: it answers which customers have orders, and what each order was.

items: JOIN combines rows from two tables through a shared value.
The ON part says how the tables connect.
INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables.
A customer with two orders appears twice, once per order.
LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, even with no match.

blocks.text: The orders table is only for this tutorial. The customers table stays the same six customers, with John at Canyon 123.

Add an order for Amy, then run the join again and check that she appears.
Run the same query as a LEFT JOIN and compare the result with the inner join.
summary: JOIN combines rows from two tables that share a value.
ON says how the tables connect, here customer id to order customerid.
INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables.
John appears twice because he has two orders, and Amy and Michael do not appear.
LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, even those with no order.

tutorials.title: MongoDB Get Started
tutorials.intro: MongoDB is a document database, and Python connects to it with the pymongo package. This tutorial shows you how to install pymongo and connect to a MongoDB server.

blocks.text: What You Need First

To follow this section you need two things installed on your own computer. First, a MongoDB server, which is the database program that stores your data. You can download MongoDB Community Server for free from the MongoDB website and install it, then start it on your computer. Second, the Python package that lets Python talk to MongoDB. Without a running MongoDB server, none of the code in this section can connect, so install and start MongoDB before you go further.

blocks.title: Install the driver
blocks.code: pip install pymongo

blocks.text: The package is called pymongo, and it is the official MongoDB driver for Python. Once it is installed, import MongoClient from pymongo. MongoDB stores data as documents, which look like Python dictionaries, inside collections, which are like tables. A database holds collections, just as in MySQL a database holds tables.

blocks.title: Connect to MongoDB
blocks.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

myclient = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
print(myclient)

blocks.text: The address mongodb://localhost:27017/ means a MongoDB server running on your own computer on port 27017, which is the default MongoDB port. If the connection works, printing the client shows a MongoClient object and no error appears. If you see a connection refused error, MongoDB is probably not running, so start the server first.

items: MongoDB is a document database that stores data as documents.
pymongo is the Python package that connects to it.
Install it with pip install pymongo.
Connect with MongoClient and the server address.
A printed MongoClient object means the connection worked.

blocks.text: MongoDB and MySQL are different systems. The MySQL tutorials use tables and SQL, while these MongoDB tutorials use collections and documents. The same customers are used in both, so you can compare them.
Test the connection on its own first. If this small program works, every example in this section will work too.

Write a program that connects to your MongoDB server and prints the client object.
Stop the MongoDB server, run your program, and read the error so you recognise it later.

Install the package with pip install pymongo.
Connect with MongoClient and the address mongodb://localhost:27017/.
A printed MongoClient object means the connection worked.
You need a running MongoDB server before any later example can run.

tutorials.title: MongoDB Create DB
tutorials.intro: In MongoDB a database is created the first time you store data in it. This tutorial shows how to name a database and make it appear by inserting a first document.

blocks.text: Naming a Database

MongoDB works differently from MySQL here. There is no CREATE DATABASE command. You simply name a database in your code, and MongoDB creates it the moment you store your first document in it. Until then, the database does not appear in the list of databases. The database for this section is called mydatabase, the same name used for MySQL, so the two sections are easy to compare.

blocks.title: Name the database
blocks.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

myclient = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
mydb = myclient["mydatabase"]

print(mydb)

blocks.text: Naming the database does not create it yet. It only gives you a handle to use. To make the database real, insert a document into a collection inside it, which the next tutorials do. After that first insert, the database appears in the list. You can check the list at any time with list_database_names.

blocks.title: List databases after the first insert
blocks.code: print(myclient.list_database_names())

blocks.text: The list shows three databases that MongoDB creates for itself, called admin, config, and local, plus our mydatabase. If mydatabase is missing from the list, no document has been stored in it yet, so go back and check that your insert ran. A database with no collections is not kept, which is why MongoDB waits for the first document.

items: There is no CREATE DATABASE command in MongoDB.
Name a database with myclient and square brackets.
The database is created when the first document is stored in it.
list_database_names shows every database on the server.
admin, config, and local are built-in MongoDB databases.

blocks.text: Do not be surprised when a new database is missing from the list. Insert one document first, then check again.

Insert one document into a collection in mydatabase, then list the databases again.
Name a second database called testdb, insert a document into it, and confirm it appears in the list.

tutorials.title: MongoDB Collection
tutorials.intro: A collection is MongoDB's version of a table. This tutorial creates the customers collection that every later MongoDB example uses.

blocks.text: What a Collection Is

A collection holds documents, and a document is a set of fields, like a Python dictionary. Our customers collection holds one document per customer, and each document has three fields: an _id, a name, and an address. The _id field is the unique key for the document, like the primary key id in the MySQL customers table. The same six customers are used here as in the MySQL section, so the results match.

blocks.title: Name the collection
blocks.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

myclient = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
mydb = myclient["mydatabase"]
mycol = mydb["customers"]

print(mycol)

blocks.text: As with a database, naming a collection does not create it. MongoDB creates the collection when you insert the first document into it. If you want to create it right away, use create_collection instead, which makes an empty collection at once. Either way, the collection name is customers, and it lives inside mydatabase.

blocks.title: Create an empty collection
blocks.code:
mydb.create_collection("customers")
print(mydb.list_collection_names())

blocks.text: The list_collection_names method lists every collection in the current database, and after the create call it shows customers. Documents in a collection do not need identical fields, but keeping the same three fields in every customer document makes the data easy to work with. The _id values in this section are the numbers 1 to 6, matching the MySQL ids.

items: A collection holds documents, like a table holds rows.
A document is a set of fields, like a Python dictionary.
The _id field is the unique key for a document.
Name a collection with mydb and square brackets.
create_collection makes an empty collection at once.

blocks.text: This customers collection is the shared example for the whole MongoDB section. Every later tutorial uses the same three fields, so do not change them.

tutorials.title: MongoDB Insert
tutorials.intro: Insert adds documents to a collection. This tutorial inserts one customer, then all six at once, using the same data as the MySQL section.

blocks.text: Inserting One Document

The insert_one method adds a single document to a collection. A document is written as a Python dictionary. The example below inserts John, with _id 1, name John, and address Highway 21. The method returns a result object, and its inserted_id attribute is the _id of the new document. Giving the _id yourself keeps the numbers matching the MySQL table, where John also has id 1.

blocks.title: Insert one document
blocks.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

myclient = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
mydb = myclient["mydatabase"]
mycol = mydb["customers"]

mydoc = {"_id": 1, "name": "John", "address": "Highway 21"}
x = mycol.insert_one(mydoc)
print(x.inserted_id)

blocks.text: Inserting Many Documents at Once

The insert_many method adds a list of documents in one call. The code below adds the other five customers, so the collection ends up with six documents in total. The inserted_ids attribute is a list of the _id values that were added, in the same order as the list you passed in.

blocks.title: Insert many documents
blocks.code:
mylist = [
  {"_id": 2, "name": "Peter", "address": "Lowstreet 4"},
  {"_id": 3, "name": "Amy", "address": "Apple st 652"},
  {"_id": 4, "name": "Hannah", "address": "Mountain 21"},
  {"_id": 5, "name": "Michael", "address": "Valley 345"},
  {"_id": 6, "name": "Sandy", "address": "Ocean blvd 2"}
]

x = mycol.insert_many(mylist)
print(x.inserted_ids)

blocks.text: The printed list is [2, 3, 4, 5, 6], because John with _id 1 was already inserted by the first call. Together, the two calls put six documents in the collection. The six documents are the fixed sample data for the whole MongoDB section, so every result in later tutorials comes from them.

blocks.title: The six customers
blocks.code:
for doc in mycol.find():
  print(doc)

insert_many adds a list of documents in one call.
A document is a Python dictionary of fields.
inserted_id gives the _id of one insert, and inserted_ids gives the list for many.
If you leave out _id, MongoDB creates one for you.

tutorials.title: MongoDB Find
tutorials.intro: Find reads documents from a collection. This tutorial shows how to read one document, read them all, and read only chosen fields.

blocks.text: Finding the First Document

The find_one method returns the first document in the collection. With no filter, that is the first document that was inserted, which is John with _id 1. The result is a Python dictionary, so you can read its fields with square brackets, for example doc and name. find_one returns None when the collection is empty, so check for that before you use the result.

blocks.title: Find one document
blocks.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

myclient = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
mydb = myclient["mydatabase"]
mycol = mydb["customers"]

doc = mycol.find_one()
print(doc)

blocks.text: Finding All Documents

The find method with no filter returns every document in the collection. It gives you a cursor, which you loop over to get one document at a time. The loop below prints all six customers in _id order, with the same names and addresses as the MySQL table.

blocks.title: Find all documents
blocks.code:
for doc in mycol.find():
  print(doc)

blocks.text: Reading Only Some Fields

The second argument to find is a projection, which says which fields to return. Set a field to 1 to include it and 0 to leave it out. The example below returns only name and address, and leaves out _id, so the printed dictionaries have just two fields. This is the MongoDB version of naming columns in a SQL SELECT.

blocks.title: Return only name and address
blocks.code:
for doc in mycol.find({}, {"_id": 0, "name": 1, "address": 1}):
  print(doc)

items: find_one returns the first document, or None when the collection is empty.
find with no filter returns every document.
Loop over the result of find to read one document at a time.
A projection picks which fields to return.
Use 1 to include a field and 0 to leave it out.

find with no filter returns every document.
Each document comes back as a Python dictionary.
A projection picks which fields to include or leave out.

tutorials.title: MongoDB Query
tutorials.intro: A query filters documents so you only get the ones that match. This tutorial shows exact matches, comparisons, and pattern matches.

blocks.text: Filtering with a Query

The first argument to find is a filter, which is a dictionary of the fields and values to match. The example below asks for the document whose address is Mountain 21, and only Hannah matches, so only her document comes back. This is the MongoDB version of the SQL WHERE clause.

blocks.title: One matching document
blocks.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

myclient = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
mydb = myclient["mydatabase"]
mycol = mydb["customers"]

query = {"address": "Mountain 21"}
for doc in mycol.find(query):
  print(doc)

blocks.text: Comparing Values

Operators let you compare values instead of matching them exactly. The operator $gt means greater than, $lt means less than, and $gte means greater than or equal to. The example below asks for documents with an _id greater than 4, which are Michael with _id 5 and Sandy with _id 6. The operator goes inside a small dictionary as the value of the field.

blocks.title: Ids greater than 4

blocks.text: Matching a Pattern

The $regex operator matches a pattern, like LIKE in SQL. The pattern ^S means a name that starts with the letter S, and only Sandy matches. The pattern a means a name that contains the letter a, which matches Amy, Hannah, Michael, and Sandy. A caret at the start means the start of the value, and a dollar at the end would mean the end.

blocks.title: Names starting with S

An exact value matches that value only.
$gt, $lt, and $gte compare numbers and other values.
$regex matches a pattern, like LIKE in SQL.
Two fields in one filter must both match.

tutorials.title: MongoDB Sort
tutorials.intro: Sort orders the documents that a query returns. This tutorial sorts the customers by name, in both directions.

blocks.text: Sorting in Ascending Order

Documents in a collection have no guaranteed order unless you ask for one. The sort method sorts the result by the field you name. The direction 1 means ascending, from A to Z for text and from small to large for numbers. The example below sorts the six customers by name, so Amy comes first and Sandy comes last.

blocks.title: Sort by name, A to Z
blocks.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

myclient = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
mydb = myclient["mydatabase"]
mycol = mydb["customers"]

for doc in mycol.find().sort("name"):
  print(doc)

blocks.text: Sorting in Descending Order

The direction -1 means descending, from Z to A for text and from large to small for numbers. You write it as a second argument to sort, after the field name. The example below sorts the same six customers in the opposite order, so Sandy comes first and Amy comes last.

blocks.title: Sort by name, Z to A
blocks.code:
for doc in mycol.find().sort("name", -1):
  print(doc)

blocks.text: Sort works with a filter too. For example, mycol.find with a filter for names containing the letter a, followed by sort on name, returns Amy, Hannah, Michael, and Sandy in that order. You can also sort by more than one field by passing a list of pairs, for example sort with address first and name second, which sorts by address and uses name to break ties.

blocks.title: Filter, then sort

items: sort orders the documents a query returns.
The direction 1 means ascending, and -1 means descending.
Sort by the field you name, such as name or _id.
Sort works together with a filter.
You can sort by more than one field with a list of pairs.

blocks.text: Sort by the field the reader will scan, usually a name or a date, so the result is easy to read.

tutorials.title: MongoDB Delete
tutorials.intro: Delete removes documents from a collection. This tutorial deletes the extra customer Vicky, so the collection returns to the six original customers.

blocks.text: Deleting One Document

The delete_one method removes the first document that matches a filter. In the Insert tutorial you added a seventh customer, Vicky from Yellow Garden 2, with _id 7, as practice. This tutorial removes her, so the collection is back to the six original customers. The filter on the name Vicky matches only her document, so only one document is deleted.

blocks.title: Delete Vicky
blocks.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

myclient = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
mydb = myclient["mydatabase"]
mycol = mydb["customers"]

result = mycol.delete_one({"name": "Vicky"})
print(result.deleted_count, "document deleted.")

blocks.text: Checking the Result

The deleted_count attribute tells you how many documents were removed, which is 1 here. After the delete, a find shows the six original customers again, with _id values 1 to 6. Vicky, who had _id 7, is gone. Unlike MySQL, MongoDB does not need a commit call, because the delete is saved at once.

blocks.title: The collection after the delete
blocks.code:
for doc in mycol.find():
  print(doc)

blocks.text: The delete_many method removes every document that matches a filter. For example, delete_many with a filter for addresses containing Street would remove every matching document at once, so check the filter with find first. The method delete_many with an empty filter removes every document in the collection, but the collection itself stays.

blocks.title: Delete many at once
blocks.code:
result = mycol.delete_many({"address": {"$regex": "Street"}})
print(result.deleted_count, "documents deleted.")

blocks.text: The output is 0 here, because none of the six customers has the word Street in the address. The addresses are Highway, Lowstreet, Apple st, Mountain, Valley, and Ocean blvd, and the pattern Street with a capital S does not match Lowstreet, which is one word with a small s in street. Pattern matching is case sensitive by default.

delete_many removes every document that matches a filter.
deleted_count tells you how many documents were removed.

No commit call is needed in MongoDB.

tutorials.title: MongoDB Drop Collection
tutorials.intro: Dropping a collection deletes it and all of its documents. This tutorial drops the customers collection and shows how to check that it is gone.

blocks.text: Dropping a Collection

Delete removes documents, but dropping a collection removes the collection itself. The documents and the collection are all gone at once. There is no undo, so only drop a collection when you are sure you do not need it. The method is drop, called on the collection object. The example below drops the customers collection from the mydatabase database.

blocks.title: Drop the collection
blocks.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

myclient = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
mydb = myclient["mydatabase"]
mycol = mydb["customers"]

mycol.drop()
print("Collection dropped.")

blocks.text: Checking That It Is Gone

After the drop, list_collection_names returns an empty list, because mydatabase has no collections left. A find on the dropped collection returns nothing, and count_documents returns 0. If you drop a collection that does not exist, pymongo does not raise an error, it simply does nothing, which makes drop safe to call twice.

blocks.title: List collections after the drop
blocks.code: print(mydb.list_collection_names())

blocks.text: Dropping a collection does not delete the database, and it does not delete other collections. Only the named collection goes. Because the later tutorials still need the customers collection, recreate it and insert the six customers again before you move on to Update. The Insert tutorial has the full list of six documents.

items: drop deletes a collection and all of its documents.
There is no undo, so be sure before you drop.
list_collection_names returns an empty list after the drop.
Dropping a missing collection does not raise an error.
Dropping a collection does not delete the database or other collections.

blocks.text: The customers collection is dropped here on purpose, as the lesson. Recreate it with the six customers before the Update tutorial, or the later examples will have no collection to work on.

tutorials.title: MongoDB Update
tutorials.intro: Update changes the fields of documents that already exist. This tutorial changes John's address to Canyon 123, and the Limit tutorial uses that new address.

blocks.text: Updating One Document

The update_one method changes the first document that matches a filter. First, recreate the customers collection with the six original customers, because the previous tutorial dropped it. Then run the update below. The filter matches the document where the name is John, and the $set operator sets the address field to Canyon 123. Only one document matches, so only John's address changes and the other five customers stay the same.

blocks.title: Update John's address
blocks.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

myclient = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
mydb = myclient["mydatabase"]
mycol = mydb["customers"]

filter = {"name": "John"}
newvalues = {"$set": {"address": "Canyon 123"}}
result = mycol.update_one(filter, newvalues)
print(result.modified_count, "document modified.")

blocks.text: Checking the Result

The modified_count attribute tells you how many documents were changed, which is 1 here. A find now shows John at Canyon 123, while Peter, Amy, Hannah, Michael, and Sandy keep their original addresses. From this tutorial onward, John's address is Canyon 123 in every MongoDB result, so remember the change when you read the Limit tutorial. Unlike MySQL, MongoDB needs no commit call.

blocks.title: The collection after the update
blocks.code:
for doc in mycol.find():
  print(doc)

blocks.text: The $set operator changes only the fields you name, and leaves the rest of the document alone. Without $set, the update would replace the whole document, which is rarely what you want. The update_many method works the same way but changes every document that matches the filter, so test the filter with find first. You can set more than one field at once by putting two fields inside $set.

items: update_one changes the first document that matches a filter.
update_many changes every document that matches a filter.
$set changes only the fields you name.
modified_count tells you how many documents were changed.
An update with an empty filter changes every document, so test the filter first.

blocks.text: When only one document should change, use a filter that matches one document, such as the name or the _id, and check the modified count afterwards.

tutorials.title: MongoDB Limit
tutorials.intro: Limit returns only a set number of documents. This tutorial takes the first three customers from the collection.

blocks.text: Taking the First Documents

A collection can hold thousands of documents, but you often want only a few. The limit method sets the maximum number of documents a query returns. The example below asks for three documents, so pymongo returns the first three customers in _id order: John, Peter, and Amy. Remember that John's address is now Canyon 123, after the change in the Update tutorial.

blocks.title: First three customers
blocks.code:
from pymongo import MongoClient

myclient = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
mydb = myclient["mydatabase"]
mycol = mydb["customers"]

for doc in mycol.find().limit(3):
  print(doc)

blocks.text: Skipping Documents

The skip method skips a number of documents before limit starts counting. Skip 1 and limit 2 skips John and returns Peter and Amy. This is how paging works: page one uses limit 3 and skip 0, page two uses limit 3 and skip 3, and so on. Combine limit with sort when the order matters, because without sort the database may return documents in any order.

blocks.title: Skip one document, take two
blocks.code:
for doc in mycol.find().skip(1).limit(2):
  print(doc)

blocks.text: Limit also works with a filter and a sort in the same chain. For example, find with a filter for names containing the letter a, then sort by name, then limit 2, returns Amy and Hannah. Chaining keeps the code short: the query is built in one line, from find to sort to skip to limit, and the loop prints what comes back.

blocks.title: Filter, sort, then limit

items: limit sets the maximum number of documents returned.
skip skips documents before limit starts counting.
limit and skip together make paging possible.
Combine limit with sort when the order matters.
Chain find, sort, skip, and limit in one line.

blocks.text: Use limit while you are testing a query on a big collection, so a mistake returns a few documents instead of a million.

tutorials.title: Python Certificate
tutorials.intro: A Python certificate is proof that you passed a Python exam. This page explains what the certificate path looks like and how to prepare for it.

blocks.text: A certificate is a document that says you passed an exam on Python. Employers and schools sometimes ask for one as proof of skill. The most widely known option for learners is the W3Schools Python certificate exam, which is an online exam based on the W3Schools Python tutorial. There are also certificates from other providers, and each one has its own exam and its own rules. Do not trust a price, question count or passing score quoted in an old blog post. Exam providers change these details. Always check the provider's own website for the current numbers before you pay. Certificate exams are usually taken online, on your own computer, at a time you choose. You answer multiple-choice questions about Python: syntax, data types, loops, functions, classes, file handling and modules. The exact number of questions, the time limit, the passing score and the price are set by the exam provider and can change, so check the current details on the provider's own website before you book.
How the exam works in general

items: Learn the topics in this course first: the exam covers the same ground.
Practise by writing code, not just by reading. The questions test what you can do.
Take the practice exercises and quizzes on this site before you book an exam.
Check the current price, question count and passing score on the provider's website.

blocks.text: What to study

The exam covers the whole Python language at a basic to intermediate level. The list below is the ground you should be sure of. If you can write a small program for each item without looking it up, you are ready to try a practice test.

blocks.title: A quick self-check program
blocks.code:
numbers = [5, 2, 9, 1, 7]
print(sorted(numbers))
print(sum(numbers))
print(max(numbers))

blocks.text: A certificate is not the skill itself

A certificate proves you passed one exam on one day. It does not replace practice. The strongest proof of skill is a set of programs you have actually built: a small project on GitHub says more to an employer than a certificate alone. Use the certificate as a goal that keeps you studying, and build projects alongside it. Work through every topic in this course, then do the Python Exercises and Python Quiz sections on this site. They cover the same ground as the exam.

blocks.title: A three-question revision quiz
blocks.code:
questions = [
    ("What does len([1, 2, 3]) return?", "3", "3"),
    ("Which keyword defines a function?", "def", "def"),
    ("What is the type of 3.5?", "int", "float"),
]
score = 0
for i, (question, answer, correct) in enumerate(questions, 1):
    print(f"Q{i}: {question}")
    if answer == correct:
        print("Your answer:", answer, "- Correct!")
        score += 1
    else:
        print("Your answer:", answer, "- Wrong! The answer is", correct + ".")
print(f"Score: {score}/{len(questions)}")
blocks.output:
Q1: What does len([1, 2, 3]) return?
Your answer: 3 - Correct!
Q2: Which keyword defines a function?
Your answer: def - Correct!
Q3: What is the type of 3.5?
Your answer: int - Wrong! The answer is float.
Score: 2/3

tutorials.title: Remove List Duplicates
tutorials.intro: Removing duplicates means turning a list with repeated values into a list where each value appears once. The simplest way keeps the original order.

blocks.text: Lists often collect the same value twice: a list of names from a form, or numbers from a file. Before counting or showing the values, you usually want each one once. The list below has 2 and 1 twice. The goal is a list with 1, 2, 3 and 4, each appearing once. The dict.fromkeys function builds a dictionary from a list, and dictionaries cannot hold the same key twice. Turning the keys back into a list gives you the values in their first-seen order, with repeats removed. This is the best method for most cases because it keeps the order and works on any values that can be dictionary keys.
Keep the order with dict.fromkeys

blocks.title: Removing duplicates, keeping order
blocks.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 4]
unique = list(dict.fromkeys(numbers))
print(unique)

blocks.text: The set method

A set also holds each value once, so converting a list to a set and back to a list removes duplicates. The catch is that a set does not remember order, so the result can come back in any order. Use this method only when the order does not matter to you. The set method does not keep order. If the order matters, use dict.fromkeys or the loop method instead.

blocks.title: Removing duplicates with a set
blocks.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 4]
unique = list(set(numbers))
print(sorted(unique))

blocks.text: Removing duplicates by hand

You can also build the result yourself with a loop: keep a new empty list, walk through the old list, and add each value only if it is not already in the new list. This is slower on long lists, but it shows clearly what is happening, and it is a good exercise for a beginner.

blocks.title: A loop that keeps only new values

set removes duplicates but does not keep the order.

Pick the method that matches whether order matters to you.

tutorials.title: Reverse a String
tutorials.intro: Reversing a string means flipping its characters end to end, so hello becomes olleh. Python has a one-line way to do it with slicing.

blocks.text: The slicing trick

A slice with a step of -1 walks through a string backwards. The slice [::-1] means start at the end, go to the start, stepping backwards by one. It returns a new string and leaves the original unchanged. This is the standard way to reverse a string in Python.

blocks.title: Reversing with a slice
blocks.code:
text = "hello"
print(text[::-1])

word = "Python"
print(word[::-1])

blocks.text: Reversing with a loop

You can also build the reversed string by hand. Start with an empty string, then walk through the original one character at a time, putting each new character in front of what you have so far. The first character ends up last, and the last character ends up first. This is slower than slicing, but it shows the idea clearly.

blocks.title: Reversing with a loop
blocks.code:
text = "hello"
reversed_text = ""
for ch in text:
    reversed_text = ch + reversed_text
print(reversed_text)

blocks.text: Checking a palindrome

A palindrome is a word that reads the same forwards and backwards, like racecar. Reversing makes the check simple: a word is a palindrome when it equals its own reverse. The comparison below prints True because racecar reversed is still racecar.

blocks.title: Testing for a palindrome
blocks.code:
word = "racecar"
print(word == word[::-1])

word = "python"
print(word == word[::-1])

blocks.text: Strings cannot be changed in place in Python, so reversing always builds a new string. That is why [::-1] returns a value you need to store or print.

Write a function is_palindrome that returns True for level and False for hello.

summary: text[::-1] reverses a string in one step.
A loop that adds each character to the front does the same job slowly.

tutorials.title: Add Two Numbers
tutorials.intro: Adding two numbers is the first program most learners write. It shows how input, variables and the plus operator fit together.

blocks.text: Adding two numbers in code
The plus operator adds two numbers and returns the result. Store the numbers in variables first, then add the variables. The example below adds 12 and 8. The answer is 20.

blocks.title: Adding two numbers
blocks.code:
a = 12
b = 8
total = a + b
print(total)

blocks.text: Adding numbers typed by the user

A real program usually asks the user for the numbers. The input function reads what the user types, but it always returns a string. Adding two strings joins them instead of adding them, so convert each input to a number with int before you add. The example below uses the fixed values 15 and 27, the same values a user might type, and prints 42.

blocks.title: Adding two numbers from input
blocks.code:
a = int("15")
b = int("27")
print(a + b)

blocks.text: Adding inside a function

Putting the addition inside a function lets you reuse it with any two numbers. The function takes two numbers, returns their sum, and the caller prints it. The example adds 7 and 5, then 100 and 23, using the same function twice.

blocks.title: A function that adds two numbers
blocks.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

print(add(7, 5))
print(add(100, 23))

blocks.text: input always returns a string. Convert it with int or float before you do maths, or 15 plus 27 will come out as the text 1527 instead of the number 42.

practice: Write a program that adds 45 and 55 and prints the result.
Ask the user for two numbers with input, convert them with int, and print their sum.
Write a function add_three that returns the sum of three numbers.

input returns a string, so convert it with int before adding.
A function lets you reuse the same addition with any numbers.
Adding two strings joins them; adding two numbers adds them.

tutorials.title: Python Examples
tutorials.intro: This page is an index of example programs. Each example below is a small, complete program you can run, covering the ideas taught in this course.

blocks.text: An example is the fastest way to learn a new idea. Read the code, guess what it prints, then run it and check. Change one number or one word and run it again. That small change teaches you more than reading the same page twice. The examples below are grouped by topic, from the simplest to the harder ones. These two examples work with numbers. The first builds a list of squares with a list comprehension. The second adds the numbers from 1 to 100. Both are one or two lines, and both are patterns you will reuse in larger programs.
Numbers and lists

print([x ** 2 for x in range(1, 6)])

blocks.text: Strings and words

The Counter class from the collections module counts how often each item appears. The example below splits a sentence into words and finds the most common word. Python appears twice, more than any other word. This example tests whether a number is prime. It returns False at once for numbers below 2, then tries dividing by every number up to the square root. If none divides evenly, the number is prime. The code prints True for 17 and False for 18. Do not just read an example. Type it out yourself, run it, then change one thing and run it again. Typing is what turns reading into skill.

blocks.title: Finding the most common word
blocks.code:
from collections import Counter

words = "python is fun and python is easy".split()
print(Counter(words).most_common(1))

tutorials.title: Python Compiler
tutorials.intro: This site has a built-in code editor that runs Python in your browser. You can write code, run it, and see the output at once, without installing anything.

blocks.text: The editor on this site runs Python with Pyodide, which is Python compiled to WebAssembly. That means the Python code you write runs inside your browser, on your own computer, with no server involved. You can use it for every exercise and practice task on this site. It supports the Python standard library, including math, random, json and datetime. Type code in the editor and press Run. The output appears below the editor. The program below prints a greeting. Try it in the editor now, then change the name and run it again to see the output change.
Running your first program

blocks.text: What the editor can and cannot do

The browser editor is made for learning, not for every kind of program. It runs code fast and keeps your work private, since nothing is sent to a server. But it cannot do everything a full Python install can. The list below is what to expect.

items: It runs normal Python code: variables, loops, functions, classes and file work in memory.
It loads many common packages, including NumPy and Pandas, from the Pyodide package list.
It cannot read files from your computer directly, and it has no real /tmp folder shared with your system.
It cannot run programs that need a window, a camera, or a long-running server.
