tutorials.title: Python Quiz
tutorials.intro: The quiz tests what you remember from this course with multiple-choice questions. This page explains how the quiz works and gives you sample questions with answers.

blocks.text: Each quiz question has four options and one correct answer. You pick an answer and the quiz tells you at once whether it was right. At the end you see your score and the questions you missed, so you know which topics to revise. The quiz covers the whole course, from variables to modules. Question: what is the type of the value 3.5 in Python? The options are int, float, str and bool. The answer is float, because 3.5 has a decimal point. An int has no decimal point, a str is text in quotes, and a bool is True or False.
Sample question 1: data types

blocks.title: Checking the type in code
blocks.code: print(type(3.5))

blocks.text: Sample question 2: lists
Question: what does len([1, 2, 3]) return? The options are 2, 3, 4 and 6. The answer is 3, because the list holds three items. The len function counts the items in a list, a string or a dictionary.

blocks.title: Counting a list in code
blocks.code: print(len([1, 2, 3]))

blocks.text: Sample question 3: loops

Question: how many times does the loop for i in range(3) run? The options are 2, 3, 4 and 0. The answer is 3, because range(3) gives the values 0, 1 and 2. Range stops before the number you give it, so it gives three values, not four. Question: which keyword defines a function in Python? The options are func, def, function and define. The answer is def. You write def, then the function name, then brackets with any parameters, then a colon. When you miss a quiz question, do not just note the right answer. Open the tutorial for that topic and read it again, then write one small program that uses the idea.

tutorials.title: Python Practice Problems
tutorials.intro: Practice problems are the way to turn reading into skill. This page gives you a set of problems with solutions, from easy to medium.

blocks.text: Reading a tutorial shows you an idea. Writing a program that uses the idea is what makes it stick. Practice problems sit between the two: they give you a clear goal and leave the code to you. Work through them in order, and do not skip the easy ones. The easy ones build the habits the hard ones depend on. Write a function that returns the factorial of a number: the product of all whole numbers from 1 up to that number. The factorial of 5 is 5 times 4 times 3 times 2 times 1, which is 120. The solution uses a loop and a running total that starts at 1.
Problem 1: factorial

blocks.title: Solution: factorial of 5

blocks.text: Problem 2: sum of digits

Add up the digits of the number 1234. The digits are 1, 2, 3 and 4, and they add up to 10. The solution turns the number into a string, walks through its characters, turns each back into a number, and adds them up.

blocks.title: Solution: sum of the digits of 1234
blocks.code:
number = 1234
total = 0
for ch in str(number):
    total += int(ch)
print(total)

blocks.text: Problem 3: remove duplicates

Remove the duplicates from the list [1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 4] while keeping the order. The dict.fromkeys trick builds a dictionary from the list, which drops repeats, then turns the keys back into a list in their first-seen order. One problem a day beats ten problems in one sitting. Pick a problem, solve it, then change it slightly and solve it again. When these problems feel easy, move to the Challenges page, which has harder problems that combine more ideas. If you cannot solve a problem in fifteen minutes, read the solution, close it, and write it again from memory. That is still practice, and it still teaches.

blocks.title: Solution: removing duplicates
blocks.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 4]
print(list(dict.fromkeys(numbers)))

tutorials.title: Python Server
tutorials.intro: Running Python on a server means your Python code answers requests from the internet, instead of running once on your own computer. This is how websites and APIs work.

blocks.text: A program on your computer runs once and prints to your screen. A server program keeps running and waits. When a browser or an app sends it a request, it runs some code and sends back a response, usually a web page or some data. The same Python you already know powers the logic; the server part is just the waiting and answering. Python comes with a small web server in its standard library, so you need no extra package to try one. The code below starts a server on your own computer at port 8000. It serves the files in the folder where you run it. Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser while it runs, and you will see a listing of that folder.
A minimal server with the standard library

blocks.title: Starting a simple file server
blocks.code: python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1

blocks.text: A server that runs your code

A file server only sends files. A real web app runs your code for each request. The example below is a tiny server written with the standard library. It answers every request with the text Hello from the server. When you run it, it prints a line saying it is serving, then waits. Press Ctrl and C to stop it. The servers on this page listen on 127.0.0.1, which means only your own computer can reach them. That is the safe way to learn. Opening a server to the whole internet needs care with security and is a separate topic.

blocks.title: A tiny server that answers Hello
blocks.code:
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(b"Hello from the server")

server = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8000), Handler)
print("Serving on http://127.0.0.1:8000")
server.serve_forever()

blocks.text: From a tiny server to a framework

The standard library server above is good for learning, but real sites use a framework. Flask is a small framework that makes routing and pages easy. Django is a large framework that adds a database, forms and an admin site. Both run the same idea: your Python code answers requests. Learn Flask first if you want the smallest step up from this page, and Django when you want everything included.

items: http.server is built in and good for learning and serving files.
Flask is a small framework for small sites and APIs.
Django is a full framework for large sites with a database.
A server keeps running and answers requests; a script runs once and ends.

practice: Run python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 in a folder and open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser.
Run the tiny Hello server above and open its address in your browser.
Change the Hello server to answer with your name, then restart it and check the page.
summary: A server keeps running, waits for requests, and sends back responses.
Python has a built-in file server: python -m http.server 8000.
The http.server module lets you write a server that runs your own code.
Flask and Django are the frameworks real sites use on top of this idea.

tutorials.title: Python Syllabus
tutorials.intro: The syllabus is the full list of topics in this course, in the order you should learn them. Use it as a map: check off each topic as you finish it.

blocks.text: Part 1 and 2: basics and control flow

items: Python introduction, getting started, syntax and comments.
Variables, data types, numbers, strings and booleans.
Operators, if else, match, while loops and for loops.
Functions, lambda, arrays, and scope.

blocks.text: Part 3 and 4: data, files and modules

items: Lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, and string methods.
File handling: reading, writing and deleting files.
Modules, dates, math, JSON and regular expressions.
Errors, exceptions, user input and string formatting.

blocks.text: Part 5 and 6: objects and libraries

items: Classes and objects, inheritance, iterators and polymorphism.
NumPy, Pandas, SciPy and Django tutorials.
Certificate exam preparation and the How To guides.
Examples, exercises, quizzes, challenges and practice problems.

blocks.text: A quick check of where you are

The course has six parts. The first part covers the basics: installing Python, writing your first program, and using variables and data types. The second part covers control flow: conditions, loops and functions. The third part covers data: lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries and strings. The fourth part covers files, modules and errors. The fifth part covers classes and objects. The sixth part covers the libraries: NumPy, Pandas, SciPy and Django. The code below is a small self-check. If you can read it and say what it prints before you run it, you have covered the basics. It builds a list of squares with a list comprehension and prints the largest one. Do not skip ahead to the libraries. NumPy and Pandas are much easier once lists, loops and functions feel natural.

blocks.title: A syllabus self-check
blocks.code:
squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(1, 6)]
print(squares)
print(max(squares))

tutorials.title: Python Study Plan
tutorials.intro: A study plan turns a long course into small weekly goals. This plan covers the whole course in eight weeks, with one hour of study a day.

blocks.text: Weeks 1 to 4: basics, functions and data

items: Week 1: install Python, write your first program, learn variables, numbers and strings.
Week 2: learn operators, if else, while loops and for loops. Write ten small loop programs.
Week 3: functions, lambda and scope. Write a small calculator with functions.
Week 4: lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries. Build a phone book program with a dictionary.

blocks.text: Weeks 5 and 6: files, modules and classes

items: Week 5: file handling, modules, dates, JSON and error handling.
Week 6: classes and objects, inheritance and iterators. Build a small bank account class.

blocks.text: Weeks 7 and 8: libraries and revision

items: Week 7: NumPy and Pandas. Load a CSV file and find its averages.
Week 8: SciPy and Django basics, then the full quiz and the practice problems. Revise weak topics.

blocks.text: The daily habit

The plan assumes one hour a day, five days a week. Each day has one topic to read and one small program to write. The weekend is for review: redo the exercises from the week and fix anything that still feels hard. If you miss a day, do not try to catch up by doubling the next day. Just continue from where you stopped. Every study day ends the same way: write one program without looking at the tutorial. The program below is the kind of daily check the plan uses. It adds the numbers from 1 to 100, and the answer is 5050. If you can write it from memory, the basics are sticking. Track your days, not your hours. A tick on the calendar for each day you studied keeps you going longer than counting minutes.

blocks.title: A daily check program
blocks.code: print(sum(range(1, 101)))

blocks.title: Looking up one week's plan

    5: "File handling, modules, dates, JSON, errors",
    6: "Classes, objects, inheritance, bank account class",
    7: "NumPy and Pandas, load a CSV and find averages",
    8: "SciPy and Django basics, quiz and practice problems",
}
week = 3
print(f"Week {week}: {plan[week]}")

Each week has a clear topic and a small project to build.
Weekends are for review, not for new topics.
End each day by writing one program from memory.

tutorials.title: Python Interview Q&A
tutorials.intro: Interviewers ask a small set of Python questions again and again. This page covers the most common ones, with short answers and a code example for each.

blocks.text: Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language. High-level means it hides machine details and reads close to plain English. Interpreted means the code runs line by line without a separate compile step. It is used for web apps, data analysis, automation and machine learning. A list is mutable, which means you can change it after you make it: add, remove or replace items. A tuple is immutable, which means you cannot change it after you make it. Use a list when the data changes, and a tuple when the data should stay fixed, like coordinates or a record from a database.
Question 2: list versus tuple

blocks.title: A list changes, a tuple does not
blocks.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
numbers.append(4)
print(numbers)

point = (3, 4)
print(point)

blocks.text: Question 3: what is a dictionary?

A dictionary stores key and value pairs, like a phone book that maps names to numbers. Looking up a value by its key is fast, even in a large dictionary. Keys must be unique and unchangeable, while values can be anything.

blocks.title: A dictionary lookup
blocks.code:
phone_book = {"Asha": 98765, "Ravi": 87654}
print(phone_book["Asha"])

blocks.text: Question 4: what does the __init__ method do?

The __init__ method runs when you create an object from a class. It sets up the object, usually by storing the values you pass in. In the example below, creating a Dog stores its name, and the bark method uses that name. You use try and except. The code that might fail goes in the try block, and the code that runs when it fails goes in the except block. The example below tries to divide by zero, which raises an error, and the except block prints a friendly message instead of crashing. In an interview, answer in your own words first, then offer a short example. A one-line answer with no example sounds memorised; an example shows you can actually use the idea.

blocks.title: A class with __init__
Handling an error with try and except

summary: Python is a high-level, interpreted language used for web, data and automation.
Lists can change; tuples cannot.
A dictionary maps unique keys to values for fast lookups.
__init__ sets up a new object; try and except handle errors.

tutorials.title: Python Training
tutorials.intro: Training is the full learning path this site offers: read a topic, try it in the editor, do the exercises, and finish with a small project. This page explains how the path fits together.

blocks.text: The training path

This site teaches Python in four steps that repeat for every topic. First you read the tutorial, which explains one idea with examples. Then you try the idea in the built-in editor, which runs Python in your browser. Then you do the exercises and the quiz for that topic. Finally you use the idea in a small project. The path is the same from your first program to Django, only the ideas get bigger.
Step 1: read and understand

Start with the tutorial for the topic. Read the explanation, then read the code examples and guess their output before you check it. The syllabus page lists every topic in order, and the study plan page spreads them across eight weeks. Do not skip the reading: the examples make sense only when you know what idea they show.
Step 2: practise in the editor

Open the built-in editor and type the example yourself. Change one value and run it again. The program below is the kind of first step the training uses: a loop that prints the squares of the numbers 1 to 5. If you can change it to print cubes instead, you understood the loop.

blocks.title: A practice step in the editor
blocks.code:
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i * i)

blocks.text: After the editor, do the exercises, the quiz and the challenges for the topic. The exercises test one idea at a time, the quiz tests what you remember, and the challenges ask you to combine ideas. If you miss a question, reread that tutorial and try again. The score matters less than the gaps it shows you. At the end of each part of the course, build something real with what you learned. A phone book uses dictionaries. A diary app uses file handling. A marks analyser uses Pandas. A project is the proof that the training worked, and it is also the thing you show to an employer or a teacher. Pick one project per part and finish it before moving on. Training works when it is regular. One hour a day, five days a week, beats a ten-hour session once a month.
Step 4: build a project

blocks.title: A tiny project piece: a phone book

practice: Pick one topic you have finished and do its exercises again without looking at the answers.
Build a phone book program that adds a name, looks one up, and lists all names.
Choose your project for the part of the course you are on, and write down its first three steps.
summary: Training on this site is read, practise, test, then build.
The editor, exercises, quiz and challenges support every topic.
Each part of the course ends with a small project.
Regular short sessions work better than rare long ones.
